20.document_title: Private Education in New Zealand: History, Funding, Integration, and Academic Achievement
20.document_summary: This comprehensive document provides an in-depth overview of private education in New Zealand from the 1820s to the 2000s, examining its historical development, funding mechanisms, and academic outcomes. It traces the evolution from missionary schools in the 1820s through Catholic school establishment in 1877 to evangelical Christian school expansion from the 1960s. By the 2000s, New Zealand had approximately 100 private schools and over 300 state-integrated schools. A critical turning point occurred in the 1970s when Catholic schools faced a funding crisis, leading to the 1975 Private Schools Conditional Integration Act, which allowed private schools to receive government funding while maintaining their special character. The document examines three main categories: state-integrated schools (primarily Catholic institutions receiving government funding), elite private schools modeled on English institutions charging $12,000-$34,000 annually with excellent academic results, and Māori church boarding schools established in the 1840s-1850s that produced many of the country's Māori leaders. Schools like St Stephen's and Wesley College successfully transitioned to state-integrated status from 1976 onwards, serving mixed populations of Māori, Pacific Island, and Pākehā students. The document explores tensions between maintaining religious character and secular education principles, discusses school fee variations, and highlights how these institutions served disadvantaged students while achieving exam results comparable to mainstream education.

31.document_title: Apirana Turupa Ngata: Māori Leader, Reformer, and Cultural Pioneer (1874-1950)
31.document_summary: This comprehensive biographical document chronicles the life and legacy of Apirana Turupa Ngata (1874-1950), a pioneering Māori leader and reformer who profoundly shaped twentieth-century Māori society. Born at Te Araroa on the East Coast, Ngata became the first Māori to complete a university degree in New Zealand, earning a BA in political science and LLB. Rather than practicing law, he dedicated himself to Māori social and economic reform. As Eastern Māori MP from 1905-1943, Ngata revolutionized Ngāti Porou's agricultural development, expanding sheep farming to 180,919 sheep by 1916 and establishing the Waiapu Farmers' Co-operative in 1912. He assisted in drafting crucial legislation including the Māori Lands Administration Act 1900 and Native Land Act 1909, and mobilized Māori recruitment during WWI. During the 1920s-1940s, Ngata served as Native Minister (1928-1932) and established the Board of Māori Ethnological Research in 1923, promoting cultural activities and founding a Māori school of arts at Rotorua in 1927. He orchestrated land consolidation among Māori tribes and initiated extensive development schemes providing employment and community regeneration. Though a 1934 commission criticized his administrative style, Ngata remained influential and continued cultural work, including organizing Treaty of Waitangi centennial celebrations in 1940. His final years were marked by scholarly work with the Polynesian Society and recognition with an honorary LittD in 1948. Ngata died on July 14, 1950, leaving an enduring legacy as a vital contributor to early twentieth-century Māori revival through land development, cultural preservation, and identity maintenance.

32.text:
[Page 1] Ngata, Apirana Turupa Apirana Turupa Ngata was born at Te Araroa on the East Coast on 3 July 1874. He had connections with the leaders of Ngāti Porou . His hapū included Te Whānau a Te Ao, Ngāti Rangi, Te Whānau a Karuai and Ngāti Rākairoa. His father, Paratene Ngata , was a storekeeper, a progressive farmer, a Native Land Court assessor and an expert in tribal lore. His paternal great uncle Rāpata (Rōpata) Wahawaha had led Ngāti Porou troops on the side of the Crown during the wars of the 1860s. Apirana Ngata was greatly influenced by both men and spent some of his early years living in Rāpata's household. Throughout his life he followed their policy of loyalty to the Crown and empire. His mother, Kāterina Naki (or Ēnoka), was the daughter of an itinerant Scot, Abel Knox, and Ngata once said that this Pākehā ancestry was the source of his methodical habits, but otherwise he did not regard it as important. It was his upbringing as a Māori and a speaker of Māori, under the watchful care of Paratene and Rāpata, that he valued more. Nevertheless, they were insistent that he be educated in the learning and skills of the Pākehā so that he could turn them to the benefit of Ngāti Porou and the Māori people.

33.document_title: Hēnare Kōhere Ngata: Māori Leader, Accountant, and Legacy
33.document_summary: This comprehensive biographical account chronicles the life and legacy of Hēnare Kōhere Ngata (1917-2011), a pioneering Māori leader and the first Māori to qualify as an independent accountant. Born in Waiomatatini to Sir Apirana Ngata, Hēnare was educated at Te Aute College and Victoria University. During World War II, he served as a Second Lieutenant in the 28th Māori Battalion and endured four years of imprisonment. After the war, he completed his BA and BCom in economics, and in 1953 established the first independent Māori accountancy practice in Gisborne, serving major Māori organizations including the Mangatū Incorporation. Throughout his career, Hēnare was instrumental in Māori political affairs, serving on the New Zealand Māori Council (1962-1984) and as National Party Māori vice president (1967-1969), championing Māori land rights and treaty settlements. Recognized with an OBE (1967) and KBE (1982), he remained devoted to Māori causes throughout his life. The document also reflects on his death and legacy, noting his father Sir Apirana's prophetic statement that proved equally applicable to Hēnare's life of dedicated service. His contributions to Māori affairs, including establishing the C Company Trust and supporting historical publications about the 28th Māori Battalion, continue to influence Māori land law and family heritage.

34.text:
[Page 7] In December 1928 Ngata was suddenly propelled into office as native minister when the United Party surprisingly won enough seats in the general election to form a government. He was ranked third in the cabinet, chaired important committees and occasionally acted as deputy prime minister. He was now 54. Always a hard worker, frequently far into the night, Ngata could get by with very little sleep, often mere catnaps. He entered into his new ministry with a ferocious energy that left men half his age, especially his hapless staff, trailing in his wake. Ngata pressed ahead with his land development schemes, using state funds, shifting his consolidators straight on to development work, and initiating schemes all over the country wherever he could find underdeveloped Māori land and local communities willing to work it. There was seldom any lack of enthusiasm, since the new schemes provided work for unemployed or under employed men, women and children, who worked as communal groups as of old. The land was cleared of bush or scrub, ploughed, grassed, fenced and stocked on the assumption that it could be sub divided into individual farms at a later date. 37.document_title: Materoa Ngārimu Reedy: A Māori Leader and Cultural Custodian
37.document_summary: Materoa Ngārimu Reedy (1881-1944) was a prominent Māori leader from Ngāti Porou who became a significant cultural and political figure. Born at Maraeke, Whareponga, she married John Marshall Reedy in 1903 and together they built a successful agricultural and pastoral enterprise, including sheep, cattle, dairy farming, and a renowned racing stable. Materoa gained prominence through her role in allocating over 30,000 acres of tribal lands through the Native Land Court, her skilled oratory, and extensive knowledge of tribal history and traditions. She collaborated closely with Apirana Ngata on cultural preservation efforts, contributed waiata to his collection Ngā mōteatea, and was an expert weaver. A staunch Anglican and United Party supporter, she led the Eastern Māori Patriotic Association during WWI and received recognition from the Prince of Wales. Her son Arnold served in the 28th Battalion, and her nephew Te Moana-nui-a-Kiwa Ngārimu posthumously won the Victoria Cross. Materoa died in 1944 following a motor accident, leaving a legacy of cultural knowledge passed to her children.

39.text:
[Page 4] In 1905 Ngata contested the Eastern Māori parliamentary seat against the long standing incumbent, Wī Pere . With solid support from Ngāti Porou, Ngata won by over 750 votes. He was to retain the seat, surviving challenge after challenge, until 1943, becoming in that time 'father' of the House. He was a superb parliamentarian. A skilled debater, he could fill the parliamentary galleries whenever he rose to speak. He took his duties very seriously and shunned much of the social side of parliamentary life. He was a diligent member of the Native Affairs Committee and soon became Carroll's right hand man. He served with the chief justice, Sir Robert Stout , on the 1907 8 Native Land Commission. They were critical of the government's use of pre emption to purchase Māori land below value, and recommended that tribes with very little remaining land should have it permanently reserved. However, they conceded that other tribes with ample lands, for instance in the central North Island, could be encouraged to sell or lease some of it. Finally, they castigated governments of the past for having done nothing to encourage or assist Māori to farm their own land. Ngata also assisted John Salmond in drafting the Native Land Act 1909, a massive consolidating measure. In that year Ngata was rewarded by appointment to the Executive Council as member representing the native race and was given a minor cabinet post in charge of Māori councils. He lost these positions when Sir Joseph Ward 's ministry was defeated in 1912. Because he remained faithful to the Liberal party, Ngata did not again attain cabinet office until 1928.

[Page 2] Although she was not fluent in English, Arihia Ngata was never ill at ease in Pākehā company and accompanied Apirana at public functions with grace and confidence. She was described as 'a tiny woman, shy and very gentle', and her tactful and sympathetic presence was a foil to her husband's more assertive approach. 40.document_title: Arihia Kane Ngata: A Life of Service and Cultural Leadership
40.document_summary: Arihia Kane Ngata (1879-1929) was a prominent Māori woman born at Whareponga on the East Coast of the North Island. She married Apirana Ngata in 1895 and became the cornerstone of one of the most important households in Ngāti Porou. Despite her husband's frequent absences in Parliament, Arihia excelled as a homemaker, raising 11 surviving children and becoming a cultural ambassador. She organized fund-raising events during World War I, earning an MBE in 1918, and supported her husband's economic development schemes. Her home, Te Wharehou (The Bungalow), became a meeting place for young people and tribal leaders. Arihia was known for her grace, gentleness, and ability to bridge Māori and Pākehā worlds. She died on 18 April 1929 from dysentery contracted at the Māhinārangi hui, leaving a lasting legacy honored through the Lady Arihia trophy and the Arihia Memorial Hall.

His mother, Kāterina Naki (or Ēnoka), was the daughter of an itinerant Scot, Abel Knox, and Ngata once said that this Pākehā ancestry was the source of his methodical habits, but otherwise he did not regard it as important. It was his upbringing as a Māori and a speaker of Māori, under the watchful care of Paratene and Rāpata, that he valued more. Nevertheless, they were insistent that he be educated in the learning and skills of the Pākehā so that he could turn them to the benefit of
Ngāti Porou and the Māori people.

2.fileDescription: This comprehensive document provides an in-depth historical and cultural account of Ngāti Porou, a major Māori iwi (tribe) from New Zealand's East Coast region. It traces the tribe's origins to ancestor Porourangi and their spiritual connection to Māui mythology, with Mt Hikurangi and the Waiapu river serving as sacred tribal symbols. The document details genealogical descent through key ancestors including Paikea, Toi, and various sub-tribes such as Ngāi Tuere, Te Wahineiti, Uepōhatu, Ngāti Ruanuku, and Ngāti Ira. It chronicles major historical events including pre-European tribal conflicts, the 1820s Ngāpuhi musket raids, the introduction of Christianity in 1834, the Treaty of Waitangi in 1840, and the 1865 civil war between Hauhau converts and traditionalists. The document emphasizes the tribe's fierce independence and territorial claims shaped by geographical landmarks and strategic marriages. It highlights the transformative leadership of Sir Apirana Ngata from the 1890s onwards, whose initiatives in education, farming, cultural revival, and military service significantly advanced the tribe. Population data shows growth from 4,164 members in 1901 to 71,049 by 2013, with major concentrations in Auckland, Gisborne, and Wellington. The 2010 Treaty settlement of $110 million and the establishment of Te Rūnanga o Ngāti Porou in 1987 reflect ongoing efforts to strengthen economic, social, and cultural sovereignty.

3.fileDescription: This comprehensive biographical document chronicles the life and legacy of Apirana Turupa Ngata (1874-1950), a pioneering Māori leader and reformer who profoundly shaped twentieth-century Māori society. Born at Te Araroa on the East Coast, Ngata became the first Māori to complete a university degree in New Zealand, earning a BA in political science and LLB. Rather than practicing law, he dedicated himself to Māori social and economic reform. As Eastern Māori MP from 1905-1943, Ngata revolutionized Ngāti Porou's agricultural development, expanding sheep farming to 180,919 sheep by 1916 and establishing the Waiapu Farmers' Co-operative in 1912. He assisted in drafting crucial legislation including the Māori Lands Administration Act 1900 and Native Land Act 1909, and mobilized Māori recruitment during WWI. During the 1920s-1940s, Ngata served as Native Minister (1928-1932) and established the Board of Māori Ethnological Research in 1923, promoting cultural activities and founding a Māori school of arts at Rotorua in 1927. He orchestrated land consolidation among Māori tribes and initiated extensive development schemes providing employment and community regeneration. Though a 1934 commission criticized his administrative style, Ngata remained influential and continued cultural work, including organizing Treaty of Waitangi centennial celebrations in 1940. His final years were marked by scholarly work with the Polynesian Society and recognition with an honorary LittD in 1948. Ngata died on July 14, 1950, leaving an enduring legacy as a vital contributor to early twentieth-century Māori revival through land development, cultural preservation, and identity maintenance.

chunkHighlights.text: In 1905 Ngata contested the Eastern Māori parliamentary seat against the long-standing incumbent, Wī Pere . With solid support from Ngāti Porou, Ngata won by over 750 votes. He was to retain the seat, surviving challenge after challenge, until 1943, becoming in that time 'father' of the House. He was a superb parliamentarian. A skilled debater, he could fill the parliamentary galleries whenever he rose to speak. He took his duties very seriously and shunned much of the social side of parliamentary life. He was a diligent member of the Native Affairs Committee and soon became Carroll's right-hand man. He served with the chief justice, Sir Robert Stout , on the 1907–8 Native Land Commission. They were critical of the government's use of pre-emption to purchase Māori land below value, and recommended that tribes with very little remaining land should have it permanently reserved. However, they conceded that other tribes with ample lands, for instance

in the central North Island, could be encouraged to sell or lease some of it. Finally, they castigated governments of the past for having done nothing to encourage or assist Māori to farm their own land.

Ngata also assisted John Salmond in drafting the Native Land Act 1909, a massive consolidating measure. In that year Ngata was rewarded by appointment to the Executive Council as member representing the native race and was given a minor cabinet post in charge of Māori councils. He lost these positions when Sir Joseph Ward 's ministry was defeated in 1912. Because he remained faithful to the Liberal party, Ngata did not again attain cabinet office until 1928.

6.fileDescription: This comprehensive document traces the history of Te Tiriti o Waitangi (Treaty of Waitangi) from its signing in 1840 through to modern legal recognition. The treaty, signed between the British Crown and over 500 Māori chiefs on 5-6 February 1840, was drafted in English and translated to Māori by missionary Henry Williams. Critical differences between versions created ongoing disputes: Article One differed on sovereignty versus governance; Article Two guaranteed chiefs "te tino rangatiratanga" (chieftainship) while giving the Crown land-buying rights; Article Three granted Māori British subject protections. From 1860-1940, the Crown systematically dishonored treaty promises through land confiscation, the Native Land Court, and legislation undermining Māori rights, despite Māori resistance through the Kīngitanga (Māori King movement), petitions, and alternative institutions. The pivotal transformation occurred with the Treaty of Waitangi Act 1975, which established the Waitangi Tribunal to investigate Crown breaches. The tribunal's jurisdiction expanded in 1985 to cover all Crown actions since 1840, fundamentally changing the treaty's role from a largely ignored historical document to a central element of New Zealand law and governance. Subsequent parliamentary legislation incorporated treaty principles into law, leading to widespread legal recognition and formal settlements between the Crown and iwi.

chunkHighlights.text: Māori hopes rise

Despite the continuing sale of Māori land, relations between the government and Māori began to improve in the first decades of the 20th century. This gave Māori new hope that the government would respect their treaty rights.

An educated Māori elite increasingly participated in both the Māori and European worlds, and began to address Māori social problems. The most prominent member of this group was Apirana Ngata of Ngāti Porou, member of Parliament for the Eastern Māori electorate from 1905 to 1943. In the 1920s Ngata introduced schemes to develop Māori land and consolidate fragmented landholdings. Māori farming ventures received government funding for the first time.

7.fileDescription: This comprehensive document provides an extensive overview of New Zealand's East Coast region (Te Tairāwhiti), encompassing geography, history, culture, economy, and contemporary development. The region comprises East Cape and Poverty Bay, including Gisborne city, characterized by isolated hill country connected by two state highways. Geographically, it features major rivers (Waiapu, Ūawa, Waipāoa, Motu), extensive Poverty Bay flats, and significant natural hazards including earthquakes, erosion, and cyclones due to its location on the Pacific-Australian plate boundary. Historically, four related Māori tribes—Ngāti Porou, Te Aitanga-a-Māhaki, Rongowhakaata, and Ngāi Tāmanuhiri—have inhabited the region for centuries, with European contact beginning in 1769. The region experienced significant conflict in the 1860s, followed by European settlement from the 1870s. Between 1870-1940, the settler population grew from 1,200 to 25,000, with extensive forest clearing and agricultural expansion, though this came at substantial cost to Māori through land dispossession of approximately 453,600 hectares. Infrastructure development progressed through the 20th century, with rail connectivity to Napier established in 1942. Today, the East Coast has the highest percentage of Māori population (48.9%) of any New Zealand region, with 62 marae and strong cultural heritage. The modern economy includes agriculture, forestry, fishing, and emerging industries such as vineyards and wood processing. Gisborne, designated a city in 1955, serves as the regional hub with approximately 43,656 residents (2013). The region is renowned for surfing beaches, the annual Rhythm and Vines music festival, and cultural contributions including notable writers and artists.

chunkHighlights.text: Apirana Ngata, kin to Rāpata Wahawaha, and the first Māori graduate of a New Zealand university, further developed the incorporation system that had been pioneered (although not lastingly) in blocks like Mangatū. This entailed organising multiple small landholdings into a single entity for operational farming purposes. In 1912 Ngata established the Waiapu Farmers Co-operative Company, partly as a way of giving Ngāti Porou access to credit. Ngata also promoted dairying on the Waiapu valley flats in the 1920s. As a government minister he was instrumental in the Native Land and Native Land Claims Adjustment Amendment Act 1929, which made provision for state assistance for the development of Māori land.

8.fileDescription: This comprehensive document traces Māori agriculture in New Zealand from pre-European times through the contemporary era. Māori cultivated traditional crops like kūmara and taro before adopting European farming methods after 1769. Between 1830-1850s, Māori developed highly successful commercial agriculture, controlling coastal shipping and food exports, building mills, and growing wheat and livestock. This prosperity declined after the Native Lands Act 1862, which individualized land ownership and enabled confiscation of agricultural lands. The document examines land fragmentation and management structures addressing it. Following abolition of communal land claims, individual ownership led to rapid title fragmentation, with average titles containing 73 owner interests by 2008. The Māori Land Development Scheme (1929) introduced by Sir Apirana Ngata provided solutions through title amalgamation. Two primary frameworks emerged: ahuwhenua trusts (750,187 hectares) and Māori incorporations (207,157 hectares). The document chronicles Māori farming development, particularly among Ngāti Porou farmers, with sheep farming in Waiapu valley expanding from 52,786 sheep in 1900 to 500,000 by 1927. Ngata established the Ahuwhenua Trophy in 1932 as a Māori Farmer of the Year award. Today, Māori manage approximately 1.5 million hectares (5% of New Zealand's total), controlling 720,000 hectares through trusts and incorporations, contributing over 15% of sheep and beef exports, with agricultural and forestry production valued at approximately $750 million annually.

chunkHighlights.text: Apirana Ngata played a vital role in the 20th century in developing a national scheme that amalgamated Māori land and provided funding to farm it. His success was largely due to his experience of farming on the East Coast amongst his Ngāti Porou people, as well as his knowledge of European law.

9.fileDescription: This comprehensive document traces Māori history from Polynesian origins to contemporary times. Māori ancestors arrived in New Zealand by canoe before 1300 CE, establishing communal societies governed by tapu and mana. European arrival from the 1600s-1800s brought Christianity, literacy, and the Treaty of Waitangi (1840), followed by land wars and population decline to under 50,000 by 1900. The 20th century witnessed cultural revival through leaders like Apirana Ngata and Te Puea Hērangi, with renewed focus on language, arts, and traditions. The Waitangi Tribunal (established 1975) addressed historical grievances and facilitated land claims settlements. By 2019, approximately 800,000 Māori lived primarily in urban centers with established educational institutions and political representation. Contemporary Māori society demonstrates remarkable achievements in media, business, and tourism while maintaining cultural adaptation through integration of European and modern elements. Challenges persist including higher disease rates, literacy concerns, housing disparities, and unemployment. Today, Māori culture continues evolving through language revitalization programs and prominent figures in arts, film, and politics.

chunkHighlights.text: invigoration of the culture and of political influence.
Apirana Ngata

The dynamic and inspirational leader Apirana Ngata typified the energy of those determined to respond to the losses of the 19th century, and to bring about widespread rejuvenation of Māori people, society and culture.
The period between 1900 and 1950 is dominated by the work of Ngata and his group. Their numerous initiatives and enterprises included:
entry into Parliament (and at times membership of the cabinet)
the formation of the Pioneer and Maori Battalions which saw action in the world wars
the introduction of widespread health reforms under Buck and Pōmare
the reform of land tenure arrangements.

Ngata also led a remarkable renaissance in Māori knowledge and culture. With the assistance of Pei Te Hurinui Jones of Ngāti Maniapoto, he researched and wrote the monumental four-volume collection of traditional song poetry entitled Nga moteatea . He oversaw the building of carved meeting houses throughout the country, and was instrumental in the restoration of many others.

10.fileDescription: This comprehensive document traces the evolution of Māori political participation and representation in New Zealand from 1853 to 2023. Initially excluded from voting due to property requirements, Māori gained representation through four dedicated electorates created in 1867. Early Māori MPs were independents until the 1890s when they aligned with major parties like the Liberal and Reform parties. Notable early figures include James Carroll (first Māori Cabinet minister), Apirana Ngata, and Māui Pōmare. The 20th century witnessed the emergence of significant independent Māori political movements, including the Rātana movement (1920s) as the first pan-Māori political group, which formed a crucial alliance with Labour from 1936 to 1996. Key figures such as Iriaka Rātana (first Māori woman MP, 1949), Whetū Tirikātene-Sullivan, and Matiu Rata shaped Māori political discourse. Electoral reforms in 1967 allowed Māori to stand in general electorates, and the 1996 MMP system significantly increased representation opportunities. The document covers modern Māori political parties including New Zealand First, Te Pāti Māori (co-led by Tariana Turia and Pita Sharples from 2005-2023), and the Mana Party led by Hone Harawira. By 2023, Te Pāti Māori won six Māori electorates, demonstrating the evolution of Māori political engagement focused on land rights, Treaty of Waitangi ratification, and self-determination.

## Sir Āpirana Ngata — A Giant of Aotearoa

Sir Āpirana Turupa Ngata stands as one of the most towering figures in New Zealand history — a statesman, scholar, and champion of Māori revitalisation whose legacy continues to shape the nation today.

### Early Life

Born on 3 July 1874 at Te Araroa on the East Coast, Ngata had deep connections to the leaders of Ngāti Porou [[1]](cite://1/1). His father, Paratene Ngata, was a progressive farmer, a Native Land Court assessor and an expert in tribal lore, while his great-uncle Rāpata Wahawaha had led Ngāti Porou troops during the wars of the 1860s [[1]](cite://1/2). Both men profoundly shaped Āpirana's outlook and values.

His family were insistent that he be educated in the learning and skills of the Pākehā world, so that those skills could be turned to the benefit of Ngāti Porou and the Māori people — a vision he would fulfil spectacularly [[1]](cite://1/3).

### A Historic First

Ngata became the first Māori to graduate with a university degree in New Zealand, setting an example for his people and the nation [[2]](cite://2/1). This achievement was not merely personal — it was the opening move in a lifelong campaign to secure a better future for Māori.

### Political Career

In 1905, Ngata won the Eastern Māori parliamentary seat, defeating the long-standing incumbent Wī Pere by over 750 votes, and held it until 1943 — becoming 'father' of the House [[3]](cite://3/1). He was regarded as a superb parliamentarian and skilled debater who could fill the parliamentary galleries whenever he rose to speak [[3]](cite://3/2).

He served as native minister from 1928 to 1934, ranked third in cabinet and occasionally acting as deputy prime minister [[4]](cite://4/1). Even after losing his seat in 1943, he remained influential as an elder statesman, coaching successive ministers of Māori affairs [[5]](cite://5/1).

### Land Development

Ngata's contribution to Māori land development was transformative. From the 1920s onwards, he introduced schemes to consolidate fragmented Māori landholdings and secure government funding for Māori farming ventures — the first time this had ever happened [[6]](cite://6/1). As minister, he pressed ahead with land development across the country, clearing bush, ploughing, fencing, and stocking land, and bringing in machinery wherever it was available [[4]](cite://4/2).

His success was grounded in his own experience of farming on the East Coast among his Ngāti Porou people, as well as his deep knowledge of European law [[7]](cite://7/1). He was also instrumental in the Native Land and Native Land Claims Adjustment Amendment Act 1929, which enshrined state assistance for the development of Māori land in law [[8]](cite://8/1).

### Cultural Renaissance

Beyond politics, Ngata led a remarkable renaissance in Māori knowledge and culture [[9]](cite://9/1). He:

- Researched and co-wrote the monumental four-volume collection of traditional song poetry, *Ngā Moteatea*, with the assistance of Pei Te Hurinui Jones of Ngāti Maniapoto [[9]](cite://9/2)
- Oversaw the building of carved meeting houses (wharenui) throughout the country and was instrumental in restoring many others [[9]](cite://9/3)
- Promoted sports — including rugby, hockey, and tennis — through intertribal competition as a means of cultural and community cohesion [[2]](cite://2/2)

### The Māori Battalion

Ngata helped organise Māori participation in both World Wars and is remembered as 'the father of the Māori Battalion' [[2]](cite://2/3). He was a key driver of the formation of the 28 (Māori) Battalion, whose structure acknowledged tribal connections by grouping members of related iwi together [[10]](cite://10/1).

### Legacy

Ngata made a vital contribution to the revival of the Māori people at a time when both population and morale were at their lowest ebb [[2]](cite://2/4). His intelligence, tact, persistence and political skill brought him considerable success, and the positive impact of his initiatives is still felt today [[2]](cite://2/5)[[11]](cite://11/1). His explanation of the Treaty of Waitangi has remained so influential that it has been distributed widely and referenced in national political debates generations after his death in 1950 [[12]](cite://12/1)[[13]](cite://13/1).

He was, in the words of those who documented his life, a man of ferocious energy and deep commitment to his people — a leader who worked not just for Ngāti Porou, but for all Māori and for Aotearoa as a whole [[4]](cite://4/3)[[11]](cite://11/2).

Would you like to explore more about Ngata's land development schemes and their lasting impact on Māori farming and land ownership?

1.document_title: Māori: History, Culture, and Contemporary Society in New Zealand
1.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces Māori history from Polynesian origins to contemporary times. Māori ancestors arrived in New Zealand by canoe before 1300 CE, establishing communal societies governed by tapu and mana. European arrival from the 1600s-1800s brought Christianity, literacy, and the Treaty of Waitangi (1840), followed by land wars and population decline to under 50,000 by 1900. The 20th century witnessed cultural revival through leaders like Apirana Ngata and Te Puea Hērangi, with renewed focus on language, arts, and traditions. The Waitangi Tribunal (established 1975) addressed historical grievances and facilitated land claims settlements. By 2019, approximately 800,000 Māori lived primarily in urban centers with established educational institutions and political representation. Contemporary Māori society demonstrates remarkable achievements in media, business, and tourism while maintaining cultural adaptation through integration of European and modern elements. Challenges persist including higher disease rates, literacy concerns, housing disparities, and unemployment. Today, Māori culture continues evolving through language revitalization programs and prominent figures in arts, film, and politics.

2.text:
[Page 14] Māori hopes rise Despite the continuing sale of Māori land, relations between the government and Māori began to improve in the first decades of the 20th century. This gave Māori new hope that the government would respect their treaty rights. An educated Māori elite increasingly participated in both the Māori and European worlds, and began to address Māori social problems. The most prominent member of this group was Apirana Ngata of Ngāti Porou, member of Parliament for the Eastern Māori electorate from 1905 to 1943. In the 1920s Ngata introduced schemes to develop Māori land and consolidate fragmented landholdings. Māori farming ventures received government funding for the first time.

2.document_title: Te Tiriti o Waitangi: A Comprehensive History from 1840 to Modern Legal Recognition
2.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the history of Te Tiriti o Waitangi (Treaty of Waitangi) from its signing in 1840 through to modern legal recognition. The treaty, signed between the British Crown and over 500 Māori chiefs on 5-6 February 1840, was drafted in English and translated to Māori by missionary Henry Williams. Critical differences between versions created ongoing disputes: Article One differed on sovereignty versus governance; Article Two guaranteed chiefs "te tino rangatiratanga" (chieftainship) while giving the Crown land-buying rights; Article Three granted Māori British subject protections. From 1860-1940, the Crown systematically dishonored treaty promises through land confiscation, the Native Land Court, and legislation undermining Māori rights, despite Māori resistance through the Kīngitanga (Māori King movement), petitions, and alternative institutions. The pivotal transformation occurred with the Treaty of Waitangi Act 1975, which established the Waitangi Tribunal to investigate Crown breaches. The tribunal's jurisdiction expanded in 1985 to cover all Crown actions since 1840, fundamentally changing the treaty's role from a largely ignored historical document to a central element of New Zealand law and governance. Subsequent parliamentary legislation incorporated treaty principles into law, leading to widespread legal recognition and formal settlements between the Crown and iwi.

3.document_title: Māori Land, Agriculture, and Farming Development in New Zealand: History, Management Structures, and Contemporary Practice
3.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces Māori agriculture in New Zealand from pre-European times through the contemporary era. Māori cultivated traditional crops like kūmara and taro before adopting European farming methods after 1769. Between 1830-1850s, Māori developed highly successful commercial agriculture, controlling coastal shipping and food exports, building mills, and growing wheat and livestock. This prosperity declined after the Native Lands Act 1862, which individualized land ownership and enabled confiscation of agricultural lands. The document examines land fragmentation and management structures addressing it. Following abolition of communal land claims, individual ownership led to rapid title fragmentation, with average titles containing 73 owner interests by 2008. The Māori Land Development Scheme (1929) introduced by Sir Apirana Ngata provided solutions through title amalgamation. Two primary frameworks emerged: ahuwhenua trusts (750,187 hectares) and Māori incorporations (207,157 hectares). The document chronicles Māori farming development, particularly among Ngāti Porou farmers, with sheep farming in Waiapu valley expanding from 52,786 sheep in 1900 to 500,000 by 1927. Ngata established the Ahuwhenua Trophy in 1932 as a Māori Farmer of the Year award. Today, Māori manage approximately 1.5 million hectares (5% of New Zealand's total), controlling 720,000 hectares through trusts and incorporations, contributing over 15% of sheep and beef exports, with agricultural and forestry production valued at approximately $750 million annually.

4.document_title: Māori Political Representation in New Zealand: From 1853 to 2023
4.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the evolution of Māori political participation and representation in New Zealand from 1853 to 2023. Initially excluded from voting due to property requirements, Māori gained representation through four dedicated electorates created in 1867. Early Māori MPs were independents until the 1890s when they aligned with major parties like the Liberal and Reform parties. Notable early figures include James Carroll (first Māori Cabinet minister), Apirana Ngata, and Māui Pōmare. The 20th century witnessed the emergence of significant independent Māori political movements, including the Rātana movement (1920s) as the first pan-Māori political group, which formed a crucial alliance with Labour from 1936 to 1996. Key figures such as Iriaka Rātana (first Māori woman MP, 1949), Whetū Tirikātene-Sullivan, and Matiu Rata shaped Māori political discourse. Electoral reforms in 1967 allowed Māori to stand in general electorates, and the 1996 MMP system significantly increased representation opportunities. The document covers modern Māori political parties including New Zealand First, Te Pāti Māori (co-led by Tariana Turia and Pita Sharples from 2005-2023), and the Mana Party led by Hone Harawira. By 2023, Te Pāti Māori won six Māori electorates, demonstrating the evolution of Māori political engagement focused on land rights, Treaty of Waitangi ratification, and self-determination.

It concludes with treaty settlements (Rongowhakaata: $22 million in 2011; Ngāi Tāmanuhiri: $11 million in 2011) and census data showing tribal population growth from 1991-2013.

7.document_title: Ngāti Porou: Comprehensive History, Tribal Identity, and Development
7.document_summary: This comprehensive document provides an in-depth historical and cultural account of Ngāti Porou, a major Māori iwi (tribe) from New Zealand's East Coast region. The document details genealogical descent through key ancestors including Paikea, Toi, and various sub-tribes such as Ngāi Tuere, Te Wahineiti, Uepōhatu, Ngāti Ruanuku, and Ngāti Ira. It chronicles major historical events including pre-European tribal conflicts, the 1820s Ngāpuhi musket raids, the introduction of Christianity in 1834, the Treaty of Waitangi in 1840, and the 1865 civil war between Hauhau converts and traditionalists. The document emphasizes the tribe's fierce independence and territorial claims shaped by geographical landmarks and strategic marriages. It highlights the transformative leadership of Sir Apirana Ngata from the 1890s onwards, whose initiatives in education, farming, cultural revival, and military service significantly advanced the tribe. Population data shows growth from 4,164 members in 1901 to 71,049 by 2013, with major concentrations in Auckland, Gisborne, and Wellington. 9.document_title: East Coast Region of New Zealand: Comprehensive Regional Guide
9.document_summary: This comprehensive document provides an extensive overview of New Zealand's East Coast region (Te Tairāwhiti), encompassing geography, history, culture, economy, and contemporary development. The region comprises East Cape and Poverty Bay, including Gisborne city, characterized by isolated hill country connected by two state highways. Geographically, it features major rivers (Waiapu, Ūawa, Waipāoa, Motu), extensive Poverty Bay flats, and significant natural hazards including earthquakes, erosion, and cyclones due to its location on the Pacific-Australian plate boundary. Historically, four related Māori tribes—Ngāti Porou, Te Aitanga-a-Māhaki, Rongowhakaata, and Ngāi Tāmanuhiri—have inhabited the region for centuries, with European contact beginning in 1769. The region experienced significant conflict in the 1860s, followed by European settlement from the 1870s. Between 1870-1940, the settler population grew from 1,200 to 25,000, with extensive forest clearing and agricultural expansion, though this came at substantial cost to Māori through land dispossession of approximately 453,600 hectares. Infrastructure development progressed through the 20th century, with rail connectivity to Napier established in 1942. Today, the East Coast has the highest percentage of Māori population (48.9%) of any New Zealand region, with 62 marae and strong cultural heritage. The modern economy includes agriculture, forestry, fishing, and emerging industries such as vineyards and wood processing. Gisborne, designated a city in 1955, serves as the regional hub with approximately 43,656 residents (2013). The region is renowned for surfing beaches, the annual Rhythm and Vines music festival, and cultural contributions including notable writers and artists.

21.document_title: Apirana Turupa Ngata: Māori Leader, Reformer, and Cultural Pioneer (1874-1950)
21.document_summary: This comprehensive biographical document chronicles the life and legacy of Apirana Turupa Ngata (1874-1950), a pioneering Māori leader and reformer who profoundly shaped twentieth-century Māori society. Born at Te Araroa on the East Coast, Ngata became the first Māori to complete a university degree in New Zealand, earning a BA in political science and LLB. Rather than practicing law, he dedicated himself to Māori social and economic reform. As Eastern Māori MP from 1905-1943, Ngata revolutionized Ngāti Porou's agricultural development, expanding sheep farming to 180,919 sheep by 1916 and establishing the Waiapu Farmers' Co-operative in 1912. He assisted in drafting crucial legislation including the Māori Lands Administration Act 1900 and Native Land Act 1909, and mobilized Māori recruitment during WWI. During the 1920s-1940s, Ngata served as Native Minister (1928-1932) and established the Board of Māori Ethnological Research in 1923, promoting cultural activities and founding a Māori school of arts at Rotorua in 1927. He orchestrated land consolidation among Māori tribes and initiated extensive development schemes providing employment and community regeneration. Though a 1934 commission criticized his administrative style, Ngata remained influential and continued cultural work, including organizing Treaty of Waitangi centennial celebrations in 1940. His final years were marked by scholarly work with the Polynesian Society and recognition with an honorary LittD in 1948. Ngata died on July 14, 1950, leaving an enduring legacy as a vital contributor to early twentieth-century Māori revival through land development, cultural preservation, and identity maintenance.

22.text:
[Page 1] Ngata, Apirana Turupa Apirana Turupa Ngata was born at Te Araroa on the East Coast on 3 July 1874. He had connections with the leaders of Ngāti Porou . His hapū included Te Whānau a Te Ao, Ngāti Rangi, Te Whānau a Karuai and Ngāti Rākairoa. His father, Paratene Ngata , was a storekeeper, a progressive farmer, a Native Land Court assessor and an expert in tribal lore. His paternal great uncle Rāpata (Rōpata) Wahawaha had led Ngāti Porou troops on the side of the Crown during the wars of the 1860s. Apirana Ngata was greatly influenced by both men and spent some of his early years living in Rāpata's household. Throughout his life he followed their policy of loyalty to the Crown and empire. His mother, Kāterina Naki (or Ēnoka), was the daughter of an itinerant Scot, Abel Knox, and Ngata once said that this Pākehā ancestry was the source of his methodical habits, but otherwise he did not regard it as important. It was his upbringing as a Māori and a speaker of Māori, under the watchful care of Paratene and Rāpata, that he valued more. Nevertheless, they were insistent that he be educated in the learning and skills of the Pākehā so that he could turn them to the benefit of Ngāti Porou and the Māori people.

23.document_title: Hēnare Kōhere Ngata: Māori Leader, Accountant, and Legacy
23.document_summary: This comprehensive biographical account chronicles the life and legacy of Hēnare Kōhere Ngata (1917-2011), a pioneering Māori leader and the first Māori to qualify as an independent accountant. Born in Waiomatatini to Sir Apirana Ngata, Hēnare was educated at Te Aute College and Victoria University. During World War II, he served as a Second Lieutenant in the 28th Māori Battalion and endured four years of imprisonment. After the war, he completed his BA and BCom in economics, and in 1953 established the first independent Māori accountancy practice in Gisborne, serving major Māori organizations including the Mangatū Incorporation. Throughout his career, Hēnare was instrumental in Māori political affairs, serving on the New Zealand Māori Council (1962-1984) and as National Party Māori vice president (1967-1969), championing Māori land rights and treaty settlements. Recognized with an OBE (1967) and KBE (1982), he remained devoted to Māori causes throughout his life. The document also reflects on his death and legacy, noting his father Sir Apirana's prophetic statement that proved equally applicable to Hēnare's life of dedicated service. His contributions to Māori affairs, including establishing the C Company Trust and supporting historical publications about the 28th Māori Battalion, continue to influence Māori land law and family heritage.

[Page 7] In December 1928 Ngata was suddenly propelled into office as native minister when the United Party surprisingly won enough seats in the general election to form a government. He was ranked third in the cabinet, chaired important committees and occasionally acted as deputy prime minister. He was now 54. Always a hard worker, frequently far into the night, Ngata could get by with very little sleep, often mere catnaps. He entered into his new ministry with a ferocious energy that left men half his age, especially his hapless staff, trailing in his wake. Ngata pressed ahead with his land development schemes, using state funds, shifting his consolidators straight on to development work, and initiating schemes all over the country wherever he could find underdeveloped Māori land and local communities willing to work it. There was seldom any lack of enthusiasm, since the new schemes provided work for unemployed or under employed men, women and children, who worked as communal groups as of old. The land was cleared of bush or scrub, ploughed, grassed, fenced and stocked on the assumption that it could be sub divided into individual farms at a later date. 27.document_title: Materoa Ngārimu Reedy: A Māori Leader and Cultural Custodian
27.document_summary: Materoa Ngārimu Reedy (1881-1944) was a prominent Māori leader from Ngāti Porou who became a significant cultural and political figure. Born at Maraeke, Whareponga, she married John Marshall Reedy in 1903 and together they built a successful agricultural and pastoral enterprise, including sheep, cattle, dairy farming, and a renowned racing stable. Materoa gained prominence through her role in allocating over 30,000 acres of tribal lands through the Native Land Court, her skilled oratory, and extensive knowledge of tribal history and traditions. She collaborated closely with Apirana Ngata on cultural preservation efforts, contributed waiata to his collection Ngā mōteatea, and was an expert weaver. A staunch Anglican and United Party supporter, she led the Eastern Māori Patriotic Association during WWI and received recognition from the Prince of Wales. Her son Arnold served in the 28th Battalion, and her nephew Te Moana-nui-a-Kiwa Ngārimu posthumously won the Victoria Cross. Materoa died in 1944 following a motor accident, leaving a legacy of cultural knowledge passed to her children.

29.text:
[Page 4] In 1905 Ngata contested the Eastern Māori parliamentary seat against the long standing incumbent, Wī Pere . With solid support from Ngāti Porou, Ngata won by over 750 votes. He was to retain the seat, surviving challenge after challenge, until 1943, becoming in that time 'father' of the House. He was a superb parliamentarian. A skilled debater, he could fill the parliamentary galleries whenever he rose to speak. He took his duties very seriously and shunned much of the social side of parliamentary life. He was a diligent member of the Native Affairs Committee and soon became Carroll's right hand man. He served with the chief justice, Sir Robert Stout , on the 1907 8 Native Land Commission. They were critical of the government's use of pre emption to purchase Māori land below value, and recommended that tribes with very little remaining land should have it permanently reserved. However, they conceded that other tribes with ample lands, for instance in the central North Island, could be encouraged to sell or lease some of it. Finally, they castigated governments of the past for having done nothing to encourage or assist Māori to farm their own land. Ngata also assisted John Salmond in drafting the Native Land Act 1909, a massive consolidating measure. In that year Ngata was rewarded by appointment to the Executive Council as member representing the native race and was given a minor cabinet post in charge of Māori councils. He lost these positions when Sir Joseph Ward 's ministry was defeated in 1912. Because he remained faithful to the Liberal party, Ngata did not again attain cabinet office until 1928.

30.document_title: Arihia Kane Ngata: A Life of Service and Cultural Leadership
30.document_summary: Arihia Kane Ngata (1879-1929) was a prominent Māori woman born at Whareponga on the East Coast of the North Island. She married Apirana Ngata in 1895 and became the cornerstone of one of the most important households in Ngāti Porou. Despite her husband's frequent absences in Parliament, Arihia excelled as a homemaker, raising 11 surviving children and becoming a cultural ambassador. She organized fund-raising events during World War I, earning an MBE in 1918, and supported her husband's economic development schemes. Her home, Te Wharehou (The Bungalow), became a meeting place for young people and tribal leaders. Arihia was known for her grace, gentleness, and ability to bridge Māori and Pākehā worlds. She died on 18 April 1929 from dysentery contracted at the Māhinārangi hui, leaving a lasting legacy honored through the Lady Arihia trophy and the Arihia Memorial Hall.

New Zealand First leader Winston Peters has brandished copies of Sir Apirana's account on several occasions, including televised election campaign debates last year. 32.document_title: Historic Waka 'Hinepāpara' Emerges from Far North's Ōmahuta Forest
32.document_summary: Ngāti Rēhia hapū in the Bay of Islands has unveiled a newly carved waka named 'Hinepāpara', marking the first time in nearly a century that a waka has been shaped in a forest in Northland. The 14-metre waka, weighing 1.2 tonnes and seating 24 paddlers, was carved from a kauri that fell in Ōmahuta Forest a decade ago. Lead builder Billy Harrison and carvers Renata Tane and Anthony Collins worked alongside the Department of Conservation to prevent kauri dieback spread. The project represents a return to ancestral waka-building practices, with the hull designed for river use on Te Awa o Ngā Rangatira. Almost 300 people attended the blessing ceremony, and the waka will undergo sea trials before an official launch in early 2026. This achievement connects the community to their identity and whakapapa, with every carving carrying cultural significance and purpose.

36.document_title: Kiingi Tuheitia to be Laid to Rest Alongside His Ancestors at Maunga Taupiri
36.document_summary: Kiingi Tuheitia Pootatau Te Wherowhero VII, the Māori king, is laid to rest at Taupiri Maunga following his funeral service on September 5, 2024. Thousands of mourners paid respects at Tuurangawaewae Marae. A special waka carries the king along the Waikato River to his burial site. The funeral marks the transition from the physical to spiritual realm, steeped in ancient Māori tradition. Uniquely, the ceremony simultaneously farewells the previous monarch and welcomes the new Māori monarch through the Whakawahinga ceremony, beginning at 10 am. The proceedings include the new monarch's seating on the throne, coronation with the bible, anointing, and funeral rites. All ceremony parts are open to the public, with roads closing at 6 am.

[Page 1] Thousands pour into Tūrangawaewae Marae for Koroneihana celebrations ByTnatanahira Māori news journalist 2025 09 02 18:31:04+12:00 Koroneihana celebrations at Tūrangawaewae Marae. Tūrangawaewae Marae heaved under the weight of Tainui Waka today, as thousands of mourners and Kiingitanga followers flooded into Ngāruawāhia for the annual Koroneihana celebrations. Tuesday marked Ngā Kawe Mate o Tainui Waka the first day of the celebrations where people gathered to mourn their whānau who have died over the past year. Many of them clutched pictures of their loved as ones as they made their way through the gate and it took nearly 40 minutes for everyone to get in. The annual koroneihana celebrations mark the ascension of the Maori monarch, Te Arikinui Kuini Nga wai hono i te po. It is also an opportunity to reflect on the legacy of her father Kiingi Tuheitia Potatau Te Wherowhero VII, who died in August last year. Long time Kiingitanga spokesperson Rahui Papa said that even one year on from his Kiingi Tuheitia's death, he still missed him. "With the air of sadness there's always the era of opportunity and I suppose he's left an awesome legacy for Te Arikinui Kuini Ngā wai hono i te po to follow along in the footsteps of Kotahitanga and into the future." Papa also remembered Huti Waitere, a stalwart of the movement. "Uncle Huti, he was the one that raised the flags in the days of King Korokii, right through the days of Te Atairangikaahu, right through the days of Tuuheitia, and just passed away just a few months ago now his tamariki take on the mantle." he said. "It's those stalwart kaumaatua that have been here throughout, generation upon generation of Ariki. Those are the ones at the top of my mind." Fiona Hunter came with whānau to remember their mother Erihipeti Monga, the last of 21 brothers and sisters. Hunter told RNZ she remembered seeing Kiingi Tuheitia at various marae around the rohe and shared the grief many will still be feeling. "Kare e kore kei konei i tātou katoa te maumahara i ā ia hoki, me te tini me te mano." Maia Jade Karena came to remember her Aunty Ra. She said Te Arikinui Kuini Nga wai hono i te po's relatively young age was an inspiration to her generation. "It's cool, especially with some of her values coming through, with rangatahi being more present and more seen," Karena said. "It's nice to see that the younger generations are getting more involved as well including myself. It's really cool to see these values being passed down." Papa said while politicians were always invited to attend the celebrations, they would not be the focus this year. "Politics of the day will be a secondary focus, or a thirdly focus, or a fourthly focus" he said "It's going to be about our Tamariki, it's going to be about our pakeke, it's going to be about celebration, it's going to be about being us being Māori all day, every day." Koroneihana will run from Tuesday through to Saturday, with Te Arikinui Kuini Nga wai hono i te po due to give her first speech on Friday. [Page 1] 'Carried on behalf of all of us': Northland iwi Ngātiwai defends the mana of moko ByLayla Bailey Mcdowell Māori News Journalist 2025 06 26 13:33:19+12:00 Northland iwi Ngātiwai is encouraging te iwi Māori to take pride in their identity and wear their moko proudly, following Winston Peters' comments calling Rawiri Waititi's mataora "scribbles". Peters, who is of Ngātiwai descent, made the remark during a Parliamentary debate on the suspension of Te Pāti Māori MPs, referring to Waititi as "the one in the cowboy hat" with "scribbles on his face." He was made to apologise by the Speaker of the House. Ngātiwai Kaumātua Taipari Munro said he wanted his people to understand that wearing moko mataora, moko kauae, or even moko rāpa puhoro were decisions made not just for the individual, but on behalf of whānau, hapū, and iwi. "You carry those markings because of you and your people," Munro told RNZ. "I was appalled that he [Peters] should do that. Because those moko marks are carried on behalf of all of us. Even though we mustn't have it on our own faces specifically, it's carried on behalf of all of us. "Winston had no right to say what he said. It was absolutely insulting and below the belt. "And also, you do that to your own people? I thought we'd come out of that quagmire, that we were at a place where we support and advocate for our people and for kaupapa Māori." Munro said the progress Māori had made over decades was being eroded under the current government. "And then you have a Māori stand up in the House and talk like that? No, that was absolutely disgraceful." Munro said moko was a living symbol for iwi, and seeing others wear them was a source of immense pride. "When I see those who carry moko, I know they carry it on behalf of myself, my whānau, my hapū on behalf of Ngātiwai. "It's been carried for us. And so that's just the immense pride." "Waiho mā tō koutou iwi a Ngātiwai e mokohia kahore anō koutou kia haere mai ki kōnei ki te rapu i ēnei mākā mōu anahe erangi kua haere mai koutou ki te whiwhi i ngā māka o te tā moko hei tohu mō tātou katoa mō Ngātiwai whānui. "Let these sacred markings be received by you on behalf of Ngātiwai, not for yourself alone, but as a living symbol for us all, for the wider Ngātiwai whānui. They speak to our presence, to the enduring mana of our ancestors, and to the fact that we are still here."' In an earlier statement to RNZ, NZ First leader Winston Peters said he was proud of his Ngātiwai whakapapa and his Tainui connections. He said he was also proud of his European ancestry and their culture. "And all of my ancestors who have worn traditional tā moko that have been rightly bestowed upon them and I always have been. That is why I have fought for, and so often succeeded for, justifiable Māori causes, and have done more for Māori than all of those critics all put together." In the statement he did not directly address his use of the word 'scribbles', but instead criticised Te Pāti Māori. "Every Māori who understands tradition, respect, and heritage understands that it is not a right for anyone to decide for themselves one day to have a traditional tā moko tattoo," he said. "We now have a bunch of radical cultural elitists in the Māori Party who are claiming to represent all of Māoridom and think by wearing tā moko they have a monopoly of thought over all of our representation. "Pointing out the shallowness of their thinking is not racist, nor is it a reflection on any Māori in New Zealand it is in fact the opposite." Munro believed the insult was not just directed at Te Pāti Māori. "When he hurled that insult out, it went to all Māori, as far as I'm concerned," he said. "I don't know who sees those things as just being something individual. I hope that us Māori don't see it like that because those are proud markings that come from our ancestors." Now that Aotearoa has marked Matariki, Munro said it was time for Māori to stand firm in their identity and mana motuhake. "E te iwi Māori, kia manawanui,kia ū ki te mana Māori motuhake, i heke iho mai o tātou mātua tūpuna ki a tātou. "This is a call to all Māori, embrace your identity and take pride in who you are, honour our ancestors." "I'd be telling them, i roto i tō tātou reo, so that they truly understand that this is where this person, this rangatira here, is coming from." "Look forward to the new year, plan well, and bring the dreams and aspirations of our people to the floor." [Page 1] ByCoco Lance RNZ Pacific Digital Journalist 2025 09 05 11:20:02+12:00 The relationship between peoples across Te Moana nui a Kiwa and Aotearoa runs deep, with Māori and Pacific leaders often crossing oceans and borders to honour what Kiingitanga spokesperson Rahui Papa called "our cousins of the Pacific." RNZ Pacific spoke with attendees about this enduring connection, and how it continues to evolve as Koroneihana marks one year since the ascension of Te Arikinui Kuini Nga wai hono i te po. Matalaoa Lafaele Barlow and Lisa Meto Fox, delegates from the Pacific General Assembly in Tāmaki Makaurau, said the significance this year runs deep. "This isn't just about showing up to an event. Every day, we are trying to awhi (support) our young people coming through. What's so symbolic about this Koroneihana is that our Queen is so young, she is our vision, and we are following beside her, after her. So it's great to be here…and also acknowledge that many of our Pacific whakapapa Maori," Lafaele Barlow said. "It's really important that Pacific people, especially in Aotearoa and around the Pacific, show kotahitanga, and solidarity with te ao Maori. Particularly at this time, with this political climate," Meto Fox added. For Rhoen Hemara, a student from Te Wānanga o Takiura, the long standing history between the Pacific and Aotearoa is alive in moments like these. "Even though the Pacific is so vast and the islands are spread out, we are all still connected," Hemara said. Having that hononga (connection) means we stay linked. Our tūpuna used the Pacific like a highway, so it only makes sense that we continue to show up, in their name and honour. Youth voices this year shared similar sentiments that Te Arikinui, at just 28, embodies a fresh, rangatahi led future. Pacific youth delegate Maia Lusia Anitele'a emphasised this. "Being here as Pacific youth, it's important to bridge the gap between rangatahi Māori, as well, if we have to fight issues together, both being minorities, both being indigenous peoples… we need to come together, have unity, and… support such a great thing," Anitele'a said. 1.fileDescription: This comprehensive biographical document chronicles the life and legacy of Apirana Turupa Ngata (1874-1950), a pioneering Māori leader and reformer who profoundly shaped twentieth-century Māori society. Born at Te Araroa on the East Coast, Ngata became the first Māori to complete a university degree in New Zealand, earning a BA in political science and LLB. Rather than practicing law, he dedicated himself to Māori social and economic reform. As Eastern Māori MP from 1905-1943, Ngata revolutionized Ngāti Porou's agricultural development, expanding sheep farming to 180,919 sheep by 1916 and establishing the Waiapu Farmers' Co-operative in 1912. He assisted in drafting crucial legislation including the Māori Lands Administration Act 1900 and Native Land Act 1909, and mobilized Māori recruitment during WWI. During the 1920s-1940s, Ngata served as Native Minister (1928-1932) and established the Board of Māori Ethnological Research in 1923, promoting cultural activities and founding a Māori school of arts at Rotorua in 1927. He orchestrated land consolidation among Māori tribes and initiated extensive development schemes providing employment and community regeneration. Though a 1934 commission criticized his administrative style, Ngata remained influential and continued cultural work, including organizing Treaty of Waitangi centennial celebrations in 1940. His final years were marked by scholarly work with the Polynesian Society and recognition with an honorary LittD in 1948. Ngata died on July 14, 1950, leaving an enduring legacy as a vital contributor to early twentieth-century Māori revival through land development, cultural preservation, and identity maintenance.

chunkHighlights.text: Ngata, Apirana Turupa

Apirana Turupa Ngata was born at Te Araroa on the East Coast on 3 July 1874. He had connections with the leaders of Ngāti Porou . His hapū included Te Whānau -a-Te Ao, Ngāti Rangi, Te Whānau -a-Karuai and Ngāti Rākairoa. His father, Paratene Ngata , was a storekeeper, a progressive farmer, a Native Land Court assessor and an expert in tribal lore. His paternal great-uncle Rāpata (Rōpata) Wahawaha had led Ngāti Porou troops on the side of the Crown during the wars of the 1860s. Apirana Ngata was greatly influenced by both men and spent some of his early years living in Rāpata's household. Throughout his life he followed their policy of loyalty to the Crown and empire. His mother, Kāterina Naki (or Ēnoka), was the daughter of an itinerant Scot, Abel Knox, and Ngata once said that this Pākehā ancestry was the source of his methodical habits, but otherwise he did not regard it as important. It was his upbringing as a Māori and a speaker of Māori, under the watchful care of Paratene and Rāpata, that he valued more. Nevertheless, they were insistent that he be educated in the learning and skills of the Pākehā so that he could turn them to the benefit of
Ngāti Porou and the Māori people.

2.fileDescription: This comprehensive document provides an in-depth historical and cultural account of Ngāti Porou, a major Māori iwi (tribe) from New Zealand's East Coast region. It traces the tribe's origins to ancestor Porourangi and their spiritual connection to Māui mythology, with Mt Hikurangi and the Waiapu river serving as sacred tribal symbols. The document details genealogical descent through key ancestors including Paikea, Toi, and various sub-tribes such as Ngāi Tuere, Te Wahineiti, Uepōhatu, Ngāti Ruanuku, and Ngāti Ira. It chronicles major historical events including pre-European tribal conflicts, the 1820s Ngāpuhi musket raids, the introduction of Christianity in 1834, the Treaty of Waitangi in 1840, and the 1865 civil war between Hauhau converts and traditionalists. The document emphasizes the tribe's fierce independence and territorial claims shaped by geographical landmarks and strategic marriages. It highlights the transformative leadership of Sir Apirana Ngata from the 1890s onwards, whose initiatives in education, farming, cultural revival, and military service significantly advanced the tribe. Population data shows growth from 4,164 members in 1901 to 71,049 by 2013, with major concentrations in Auckland, Gisborne, and Wellington. The 2010 Treaty settlement of $110 million and the establishment of Te Rūnanga o Ngāti Porou in 1987 reflect ongoing efforts to strengthen economic, social, and cultural sovereignty.

3.fileDescription: This comprehensive biographical document chronicles the life and legacy of Apirana Turupa Ngata (1874-1950), a pioneering Māori leader and reformer who profoundly shaped twentieth-century Māori society. Born at Te Araroa on the East Coast, Ngata became the first Māori to complete a university degree in New Zealand, earning a BA in political science and LLB. Rather than practicing law, he dedicated himself to Māori social and economic reform. As Eastern Māori MP from 1905-1943, Ngata revolutionized Ngāti Porou's agricultural development, expanding sheep farming to 180,919 sheep by 1916 and establishing the Waiapu Farmers' Co-operative in 1912. He assisted in drafting crucial legislation including the Māori Lands Administration Act 1900 and Native Land Act 1909, and mobilized Māori recruitment during WWI. During the 1920s-1940s, Ngata served as Native Minister (1928-1932) and established the Board of Māori Ethnological Research in 1923, promoting cultural activities and founding a Māori school of arts at Rotorua in 1927. He orchestrated land consolidation among Māori tribes and initiated extensive development schemes providing employment and community regeneration. Though a 1934 commission criticized his administrative style, Ngata remained influential and continued cultural work, including organizing Treaty of Waitangi centennial celebrations in 1940. His final years were marked by scholarly work with the Polynesian Society and recognition with an honorary LittD in 1948. Ngata died on July 14, 1950, leaving an enduring legacy as a vital contributor to early twentieth-century Māori revival through land development, cultural preservation, and identity maintenance.

chunkHighlights.text: In 1905 Ngata contested the Eastern Māori parliamentary seat against the long-standing incumbent, Wī Pere . With solid support from Ngāti Porou, Ngata won by over 750 votes. He was to retain the seat, surviving challenge after challenge, until 1943, becoming in that time 'father' of the House. He was a superb parliamentarian. A skilled debater, he could fill the parliamentary galleries whenever he rose to speak. He took his duties very seriously and shunned much of the social side of parliamentary life. He was a diligent member of the Native Affairs Committee and soon became Carroll's right-hand man. He served with the chief justice, Sir Robert Stout , on the 1907–8 Native Land Commission. They were critical of the government's use of pre-emption to purchase Māori land below value, and recommended that tribes with very little remaining land should have it permanently reserved. However, they conceded that other tribes with ample lands, for instance

in the central North Island, could be encouraged to sell or lease some of it. Finally, they castigated governments of the past for having done nothing to encourage or assist Māori to farm their own land.

Ngata also assisted John Salmond in drafting the Native Land Act 1909, a massive consolidating measure. In that year Ngata was rewarded by appointment to the Executive Council as member representing the native race and was given a minor cabinet post in charge of Māori councils. He lost these positions when Sir Joseph Ward 's ministry was defeated in 1912. Because he remained faithful to the Liberal party, Ngata did not again attain cabinet office until 1928.

6.fileDescription: This comprehensive document traces the history of Te Tiriti o Waitangi (Treaty of Waitangi) from its signing in 1840 through to modern legal recognition. The treaty, signed between the British Crown and over 500 Māori chiefs on 5-6 February 1840, was drafted in English and translated to Māori by missionary Henry Williams. Critical differences between versions created ongoing disputes: Article One differed on sovereignty versus governance; Article Two guaranteed chiefs "te tino rangatiratanga" (chieftainship) while giving the Crown land-buying rights; Article Three granted Māori British subject protections. From 1860-1940, the Crown systematically dishonored treaty promises through land confiscation, the Native Land Court, and legislation undermining Māori rights, despite Māori resistance through the Kīngitanga (Māori King movement), petitions, and alternative institutions. The pivotal transformation occurred with the Treaty of Waitangi Act 1975, which established the Waitangi Tribunal to investigate Crown breaches. The tribunal's jurisdiction expanded in 1985 to cover all Crown actions since 1840, fundamentally changing the treaty's role from a largely ignored historical document to a central element of New Zealand law and governance. Subsequent parliamentary legislation incorporated treaty principles into law, leading to widespread legal recognition and formal settlements between the Crown and iwi.

chunkHighlights.text: Māori hopes rise

Despite the continuing sale of Māori land, relations between the government and Māori began to improve in the first decades of the 20th century. This gave Māori new hope that the government would respect their treaty rights.

An educated Māori elite increasingly participated in both the Māori and European worlds, and began to address Māori social problems. The most prominent member of this group was Apirana Ngata of Ngāti Porou, member of Parliament for the Eastern Māori electorate from 1905 to 1943. In the 1920s Ngata introduced schemes to develop Māori land and consolidate fragmented landholdings. Māori farming ventures received government funding for the first time.

7.fileDescription: This comprehensive document traces Māori agriculture in New Zealand from pre-European times through the contemporary era. Māori cultivated traditional crops like kūmara and taro before adopting European farming methods after 1769. Between 1830-1850s, Māori developed highly successful commercial agriculture, controlling coastal shipping and food exports, building mills, and growing wheat and livestock. This prosperity declined after the Native Lands Act 1862, which individualized land ownership and enabled confiscation of agricultural lands. The document examines land fragmentation and management structures addressing it. Following abolition of communal land claims, individual ownership led to rapid title fragmentation, with average titles containing 73 owner interests by 2008. The Māori Land Development Scheme (1929) introduced by Sir Apirana Ngata provided solutions through title amalgamation. Two primary frameworks emerged: ahuwhenua trusts (750,187 hectares) and Māori incorporations (207,157 hectares). The document chronicles Māori farming development, particularly among Ngāti Porou farmers, with sheep farming in Waiapu valley expanding from 52,786 sheep in 1900 to 500,000 by 1927. Ngata established the Ahuwhenua Trophy in 1932 as a Māori Farmer of the Year award. Today, Māori manage approximately 1.5 million hectares (5% of New Zealand's total), controlling 720,000 hectares through trusts and incorporations, contributing over 15% of sheep and beef exports, with agricultural and forestry production valued at approximately $750 million annually.

chunkHighlights.text: Apirana Ngata played a vital role in the 20th century in developing a national scheme that amalgamated Māori land and provided funding to farm it. His success was largely due to his experience of farming on the East Coast amongst his Ngāti Porou people, as well as his knowledge of European law.

8.fileDescription: This comprehensive document provides an extensive overview of New Zealand's East Coast region (Te Tairāwhiti), encompassing geography, history, culture, economy, and contemporary development. The region comprises East Cape and Poverty Bay, including Gisborne city, characterized by isolated hill country connected by two state highways. Geographically, it features major rivers (Waiapu, Ūawa, Waipāoa, Motu), extensive Poverty Bay flats, and significant natural hazards including earthquakes, erosion, and cyclones due to its location on the Pacific-Australian plate boundary. Historically, four related Māori tribes—Ngāti Porou, Te Aitanga-a-Māhaki, Rongowhakaata, and Ngāi Tāmanuhiri—have inhabited the region for centuries, with European contact beginning in 1769. The region experienced significant conflict in the 1860s, followed by European settlement from the 1870s. Between 1870-1940, the settler population grew from 1,200 to 25,000, with extensive forest clearing and agricultural expansion, though this came at substantial cost to Māori through land dispossession of approximately 453,600 hectares. Infrastructure development progressed through the 20th century, with rail connectivity to Napier established in 1942. Today, the East Coast has the highest percentage of Māori population (48.9%) of any New Zealand region, with 62 marae and strong cultural heritage. The modern economy includes agriculture, forestry, fishing, and emerging industries such as vineyards and wood processing. Gisborne, designated a city in 1955, serves as the regional hub with approximately 43,656 residents (2013). The region is renowned for surfing beaches, the annual Rhythm and Vines music festival, and cultural contributions including notable writers and artists.

chunkHighlights.text: Apirana Ngata, kin to Rāpata Wahawaha, and the first Māori graduate of a New Zealand university, further developed the incorporation system that had been pioneered (although not lastingly) in blocks like Mangatū. This entailed organising multiple small landholdings into a single entity for operational farming purposes. In 1912 Ngata established the Waiapu Farmers Co-operative Company, partly as a way of giving Ngāti Porou access to credit. Ngata also promoted dairying on the Waiapu valley flats in the 1920s. As a government minister he was instrumental in the Native Land and Native Land Claims Adjustment Amendment Act 1929, which made provision for state assistance for the development of Māori land.

9.fileDescription: This comprehensive document traces Māori history from Polynesian origins to contemporary times. Māori ancestors arrived in New Zealand by canoe before 1300 CE, establishing communal societies governed by tapu and mana. European arrival from the 1600s-1800s brought Christianity, literacy, and the Treaty of Waitangi (1840), followed by land wars and population decline to under 50,000 by 1900. The 20th century witnessed cultural revival through leaders like Apirana Ngata and Te Puea Hērangi, with renewed focus on language, arts, and traditions. The Waitangi Tribunal (established 1975) addressed historical grievances and facilitated land claims settlements. By 2019, approximately 800,000 Māori lived primarily in urban centers with established educational institutions and political representation. Contemporary Māori society demonstrates remarkable achievements in media, business, and tourism while maintaining cultural adaptation through integration of European and modern elements. Challenges persist including higher disease rates, literacy concerns, housing disparities, and unemployment. Today, Māori culture continues evolving through language revitalization programs and prominent figures in arts, film, and politics.

chunkHighlights.text: invigoration of the culture and of political influence.
Apirana Ngata

The dynamic and inspirational leader Apirana Ngata typified the energy of those determined to respond to the losses of the 19th century, and to bring about widespread rejuvenation of Māori people, society and culture.
The period between 1900 and 1950 is dominated by the work of Ngata and his group. Their numerous initiatives and enterprises included:
entry into Parliament (and at times membership of the cabinet)
the formation of the Pioneer and Maori Battalions which saw action in the world wars
the introduction of widespread health reforms under Buck and Pōmare
the reform of land tenure arrangements.

Ngata also led a remarkable renaissance in Māori knowledge and culture. With the assistance of Pei Te Hurinui Jones of Ngāti Maniapoto, he researched and wrote the monumental four-volume collection of traditional song poetry entitled Nga moteatea . He oversaw the building of carved meeting houses throughout the country, and was instrumental in the restoration of many others.
