15.fileDescription: This comprehensive article documents the remarkable recovery efforts of takahē, New Zealand's endangered flightless birds, whose population is rising 10% annually through coordinated conservation initiatives. The narrative follows Department of Conservation rangers Jason and Maddie van de Wetering on tracking expeditions in the Gouland Downs of Kahurangi National Park, monitoring 30 takahē wearing radio transmitters. The piece explores takahē biology and behavior, including their unique digestive system requiring 19 hours of daily feeding and complex social structures with partner-swapping. The article examines conservation challenges, particularly stoat predation which kills up to 20% of the population during mast seasons, and the dilemma of using aerial 1080 poison for pest control. It documents the transition from captive-breeding methods using puppets at Burwood Breeding Centre to natural parenting approaches, successfully producing approximately 25 chicks annually at Burwood and similar numbers across 20 other sanctuaries. The narrative includes the discovery of Pipper, a 12-year-old female, dead in Shiner Brook, contrasted with hope as her adopted daughter Tupuānuku incubates three eggs. Alternative pest control solutions like PAPP remain years away from approval. Despite ongoing obstacles including limited suitable habitat and predator threats, the recovery program aims to restore takahē to their former range across the South Island.

chunkHighlights.text: As takahē learn and evolve, so does the effort to save them.
With a gentleness like reverence, Maddie replaces the eggs. It’s so late that Sirius is gleaming above the Saxon Ridge. Weka shriek from the woods. We call it a long day.
[Chapter Break]

Derek Grzelewski wrote about takahē in this magazine 20 years ago, quoting then-recovery programme manager Dave Crouchley as saying: “For now, our aim is to breed up enough birds so that we have the problem of where to put them.”

Problem accomplished. Burwood now produces some 25 chicks a year, and a similar number are produced at 20 other sanctuary sites around the country. Crouchley did his bit—now his successors have to figure out where to put them, and that’s a thorny, if luxurious, problem. There are few safe places for takahē to go.

“Potentially, there’s a lot of nice habitat in the South Island,” says the takahē programme’s scientific adviser, Andrew Digby, “but with open areas like that come cats and ferrets, which are a real problem.”

Jason van de Wetering defies a drenching southerly near the Tubman Range to listen for the tell-tale beep of takahē. Another 10 birds are scheduled for release this summer, but the Gouland Downs is only a small, suitable island in a sea of habitat otherwise denied to takahē by cats, ferrets and stoats.

And there’s the rub: those pests are impossible to control at any sizeable scale. Takahē are only here on the Gouland Downs thanks to a vagary of topography. Cats and ferrets seem reluctant to breach a dissuasive perimeter of beech and broadleaf forest that separates the Downs from more-appealing farmland on the national park’s eastern reach.

And then there are stoats, which routinely kill a few juvenile takahē every year in the Murchison Mountains. But when the beech trees mast, losses go stratospheric: in a 2007 mast season, prodigious seedfall

prompted stoats to breed to full capacity, seizing their chance to feast on the extra rats and mice nourished by the cornucopia. When the seed ran out and rodent numbers fell, hungry stoats turned on the takahē—40 per cent of the adult population was slaughtered in a single season. Trapping has since been stepped up, but undeterred by a phalanx of 3500 traps, stoats still kill up to 20 per cent of Murchison takahē in mast seasons.
Kahurangi National Park, by contrast, has had years of concerted pest control with aerial 1080.
“And that’s the main reason takahē are here,” says Digby.
“Stoats are at very low numbers here. If we could just get that landscape-scale pest control in other places, we’d have takahē everywhere in the South Island.”
But that would mean more aerial poisoning, and no-one knows yet whether takahē and 1080 can mix: “That’s the biggest question we face,” says Digby.

17.fileDescription: Two senior takahē, 13-year-old Autahi and 16-year-old Hopi, have arrived at Wellington's Zealandia wildlife sanctuary to spend their retirement. Transferred from the Department of Conservation's Burwood Takahē Centre near Te Anau, they join three other takahē at the sanctuary, bringing the total to five. These vulnerable birds, with only 520 remaining in the species, were welcomed by local iwi and Zealandia staff. The takahē will remain separated from existing residents due to their territorial nature. This relocation highlights the species' remarkable conservation story—rediscovered in the 1940s after being declared extinct 50 years earlier—and provides visitors with rare access to view these inaccessible mountain-dwelling birds.

https://www.rnz.co.nz/national/programmes/morningreport/audio/20190
33841/zealandia-welcomes-pair-of-senior-takahe A pair of senior takahē are set to make Wellington wildlife sanctuary Zealandia their new home. The duo, 13-year-old Autahi and 16-year-old Hopi, come from the Department of Conservation's Burwood Takahē Centre near Te Anau and will bring the number of takahē currently living wild at Zealandia to five. Zealandia general manager conservation and restoration, Jo Ledington, told Morning Report the pair had made a special trip from the south early on Wednesday morning. "They were captured at Burwood near Te Anau, and they'll be driven up to Queenstown, and then a direct flight to Wellington." The South Island takahē are two of just 520 of the species remaining, and were welcomed by members of Taranaki Whānui ki Te Upoko o Te Ika, Ngāti Toa Rangatira and Ngāi Tahu, alongside Zealandia staff and volunteers. Autahi and Hopi will join Waitaa and Bendigo, a young couple who were presumed infertile, however produced a "miracle" chick in 2025. While the new residents will be welcomed, takahē are known to be territorial, so they will remain separated from the others. Ledington said this could mean they are hard to spot for visitors for a little while until they get settled. Zealandia chief executive Dr Danielle Shanahan said takahē have a way of marching their way into the hearts of Zealandia's visitors and staff. "Takahē are such an incredible example of why we should never give up when it comes to nature. A small population of the species was rediscovered in the Murchison Mountains in the 1940s, 50 years after being declared extinct." Takahē are usually found in inaccessible habitats such as remote mountains, meaning their presence at Zealandia allows people to see the vulnerable species. 18.fileName: Our Changing World: Backcountry takahē make a comeback.pdf
18.filePath: pdf/Our Changing World: Backcountry takahē make a comeback.pdf
18.fileDescription: Takahē, a flightless New Zealand bird twice believed extinct, are making a remarkable comeback through intensive conservation efforts. Rediscovered in 1948 in the Murchison Mountains, the species has grown from a small population to approximately 500 birds through breeding programs at Burwood Takahē Centre and establishment of security populations on predator-free islands. Recent reintroduction efforts include releases in Kahurangi National Park (2018) and two new wild populations in the Upper Whakatipu region: Greenstone Station (2023) and the Rees Valley (2025). While stoat predation remains a significant threat, extensive trap lines and dedicated conservation teams from Southern Lakes Sanctuary and local wildlife trusts are actively monitoring and protecting the birds. Backcountry trampers now regularly spot takahē in the wild, marking a significant conservation success story.

chunkHighlights.text: Our Changing World: Backcountry takahē make a comeback

In Shelter Rock Hut,near the head of the Rees Valley, the visitor book
comment section is sprinkled with excited notes about bird sightings.
Twice believed to be extinct, takahē, the ultimate comeback bird, are
now being spotted in the wild by backcountry trampers in the upper
Whakatipu. [wk_audio]4dcb6a69-c39e-43a3-a7d0-e595f39a362e Follow
Our Changing World on Apple, Spotify, iHeartRadio or wherever you listen to your podcasts Bringing the birds back It was 1948 when takahē were rediscovered for the second time by Dr Geoffrey Orbell's party in the remote Murchison Mountains. With only a small population remaining, intensive management of the birds was deemed necessary. In the 1980s, Burwood Takahē Centre was created to manage breeding and chick rearing. 'Security populations' were established on offshore predator-free islands. A Specially Protected Area was created in the Murchison Mountains to protect the remaining wild population, with access by permit only. The hard work of DOC's takahē recovery team paid off, though not without a few setbacks along the way. The takahē population grew, hitting an estimated 300 in 2016. In 2018, takahē were reintroduced to Kahurangi National Park with the hope of establishing a second wild population. Things didn't go perfectly to plan, with a spate of bird deaths in the second year after release, and concerns about the suitability of the habitat. In 2023, the population hit 500 birds, and in August, 18 takahē were released on to Ngāi Tahu land at Greenstone Station in the Upper Whakatipu, to set up a third wild population. After two promising active breeding seasons, the birds took a bit of a hit earlier this year, with five thought to be killed by just one or two stoats. But after a step-up in trapping effort, it's believed the culprits have been caught. Return to the Rees A few valleys over from the Greenstone, the braids of the Rees River ribbon their way from the high alpine head to feed into Lake Whakatipu at Glenorchy. With a mixture of introduced grasses, beech forest edges, and alpine tussock, it is hoped this valley will prove to be good takahē country. Fifty-one birds have been released since February this year. There have been two mortalities - but neither
are thought to have been due to predation. One bird, named Frost,

caused a bit of excitement when he walked all the way from the Rees Valley into Glenorchy village, where he was found on a golf course. He was relocated back into the valley, and thankfully now seems content to stay in the backcountry. But it's stoats rather than wanderlust that remain the biggest concern, says Chrissy Becker-Fifield. Chrissy is part of the Glenorchy field team for Southern Lakes Sanctuary - an organisation involved with checking traps and monthly monitoring of the takahē in the Rees, alongside other roles including coordinating volunteers for local conservation group the Routeburn-Dart Wildlife Trust. Extensive trap lines had to be established before takahē could be released here. The Routeburn-Dart Wildlife Trust have long been trapping in some areas of the upper Whakatipu, as have the landowners of the Rees Valley Station. But with the work of the Southern Lakes Sanctuary, the traps now extend further into the valley and across alpine saddles to connect to other trap lines in both the Dart and Matukituki valleys. More releases are planned before the end of the year, and those involved have high hopes for the takahē's newest home. Sign up to the Our Changing World monthly newsletter for episode backstories,

19.fileName: Nature's milestones you may have missed.pdf
19.filePath: pdf/Nature's milestones you may have missed.pdf
19.fileDescription: This article highlights significant conservation milestones achieved in New Zealand's wildlife in 2024-2025. Key achievements include takahē populations reaching carrying capacity in the Murchison Ranges after 50 years of monitoring, with birds now dispersing to new territories via the Routeburn tramping track. Tokoeka kiwi chick survival rates dramatically improved to 70% following predator control operations. Kiwi populations have expanded from Wellington's Remutaka Ranges to Upper Hutt, with a 55% increase since 2011. The critically endangered Sinbad skink population, found only on a 320-metre vertical cliff face in Milford Sound, faces translocation challenges due to low numbers. Other successes include the first captive breeding of giant wētā in decades, record Northern Albatross breeding seasons, and successful pest control efforts. These milestones demonstrate the effectiveness of long-term conservation efforts and resource management by the Department of Conservation.

chunkHighlights.text: Now, here are some gains for nature you might not have heard about. Original takahē discovery site in the Murchison Ranges reaches full capacity as the population thrives This year was likely the last in which rangers would need to rigorously monitor the population of takahē in the Murchison Ranges, with the population reaching capacity. Glen Greaves, senior ranger in the Department of Conservation's (DOC) takahē recovery team, said the species was rediscovered at this site 76 years ago, and the population had been closely monitored for the past 50. "We think it's around 250, we don't know exactly - it's 50,000 hectares of mountainous terrain, so we have to give it an estimate - but we're pretty

certain its between 220 and 260 birds." That meant the site was at
carrying capacity. It was a huge area, but the usable land was a lot smaller - and takahē needed up to 100 hectares per pair. They still faced challenges, he said. "It's a really tough site, it's not takahē Nirvana. It receives really cold winters, some pretty extreme weather events, its topography is really challenging for the birds as well, we have a lot of misadventure - you know, birds falling off cliffs and drowning in ponds and rivers during flood events." But those challenges meant pests had only just arrived, and that had allowed takahē to thrive. "We think the size of the population means it's quite resilient and we can now take a step back." It had been 20 years of involvement for Greaves, and a labour of love for the team. "We'll miss it, it's definitely the most exciting and rewarding place to go and visit, being such a historically important site for takahē, but it's just an awesome place. "But it's also a big tick in the success box as well, being able to step back means that we can put those resources into new sites." Trampers spotting takahē on the Routeburn In another "massive milestone" for takahē, Greaves said birds from the Greenstone Valley population had begun to disperse outwards in search of new territory, via the popular tramping track, the Routeburn. In 2023, 28 birds were released onto a working station owned by Ngāi Tahu. But in the search for new territory, the birds were taking the path of least resistance. That meant trampers were catching a sighting, with many sending in pictures and reporting what band colours they spotted, which Greaves said was encouraged by DOC. For centuries takahē have only been in the Murchison Mountains and offshore islands, and the Murchison Mountains are closed to the public. "So for the public to be able to see these birds in their natural landscapes, in a place they've been absent for centuries, is huge." Tokoeka kiwi chick survival rate up to 70 percent The Fiordland tokoeka, or Southern Brown kiwi, population at Shy Lake on the remote Wet Jacket peninsula in Fiordland officially reversed its decline with a population growth of about two percent per year. monitoring the population since 2017 when every single chick was killed
by stoats, and the population was declining by two percent. DOC ranger
and project lead for tokoeka, Chris Dodd, said two predator control
operations in 2020 and 2023 knocked back stoats and about 20 percent
of kiwi chicks survived for the following two years. This past season,

area. Island restoration Some islands are being restored to something
resembling their original ecology, with unwanted animals entirely eradicated. Larger browsing animals such as wild cattle and goats are the first to go, followed by smaller predators – cats and possums, stoats and weasels, and eventually rats. Existing patches of native vegetation are enlarged, often with the help of planting programmes. Some sparse populations have become abundant once again. Other species were reintroduced to their former homes, while some islands became sanctuaries for animals never previously found there. Kākāpō were once plentiful, but when only a few remained in Fiordland and on Stewart Island (Rakiura), they were moved to Whenua Hou/Codfish, Maud and Little Barrier islands, and in 2003 to Fiordland’s Chalky Island (Te Kākahu-o-Tamatea). Public sanctuaries Most conservation restrict access to prevent disturbance or the arrival of unwanted pests. But several are open to the public. Kāpiti Island near Wellington and Tiritiri Matangi near Auckland have similar histories. Once cleared for farming, they now have no animal pests, and native forest has been re-established – over 250,000 native trees were planted on Tiritiri Matangi. Both are refuges for saddlebacks, kōkako, stitchbirds, little spotted kiwi and takahē. Not far from Kāpiti is Mana Island, also a bird sanctuary, and noted for its ‘colony’ of concrete gannets, built to tempt real gannets to breed there. Betty gets her goats In the 1970s the government decided to kill wild goats and sheep on Arapawa Island, in the Marlborough Sounds. Protesters claimed the animals were descendants of those left by James Cook. DNA tests showed some were genetically unique. Many were culled, but others were sent to farms and wildlife parks. Betty Rowe led the rescue campaign and established a sanctuary on Arapawa Island. retrieved_chunks.text: Feral cats had developed a taste for kākāpō, and within five years these bushwise and feisty predators halved the remaining kākāpō population. Just as in Fiordland, searchers realised they were riding a bow-wave of extinction. This time, however, they would take more radical measures. Between 1982 and 1992, all 61 surviving Stewart Island kākāpō were caught and transferred to safe island sanctuaries: Whenua Hou, Te Hoiere/Maud Island and Hauturu/Little Barrier Island, in the Hauraki Gulf . The kākāpō’s wild days were over. From now on, constant inter-island transfers and airlifts out of trouble would become the norm in kākāpō life. While a long-term solution to their predicament was being sought, the birds would remain refugees in their own homeland. One evening in early April 1999, as the seasons were turning and winter storms were edging in from the Southern Ocean, I walked with photographer Rod Morris through wet rimu forest down from the summit of Whenua Hou. We each carried a plastic cat box housing a kākāpō. The boxes were heavy, and every few hundred metres we stopped to swap hands and to catch a glimpse of the birds: a youngster named Sirocco in Morris’s cage, a female called Hoki in mine. The birds had just been ferried in from Pearl Island—at the entrance of Port Pegasus, on the eastern side of Stewart Island—their temporary home while 1396-hectare Whenua Hou Nature Reserve was being purged of any remaining vermin. Back in the mid-1980s, possums had been eradicated from Whenua Hou, and even egg-stealing weka removed, and now, having been blitzed with 22 air-dropped tonnes of poison pellets, the island had been declared a predator-free “kākāpōrium”—the safest haven the birds would ever know. At the release site I opened the grille door of my cage and Hoki stomped out angrily, dragging her brown tail like a hand-baggage trolley, and vanished in the undergrowth. Hoki was the star of several media appearances in the early 1990s when, rescued as a starving chi…

retrieved_chunks.text: Female kākāpō are devoted mothers, but since they are all solo parents they must leave their eggs and chicks unguarded for long periods each night while they forage. Before the advent of mammalian predators, their absences were of little consequence, but ground-level nests of eggs or chicks are like fast-food outlets to rats and their ilk, and now the only safe place for kākāpō to breed is on predator-free islands. Even in these havens, kākāpō workers take no chances, installing infrared movement sensors and surveillance cameras at all nests.

retrieved_chunks.text: By the mid-1970s, the deer population was finally brought under control. But for takahe it was almost too late. Tussock is slow to recover from heavy browsing—up to 20 years, suggests a recent study—and without food the takahe population began to collapse. By the early 1980s, there were just over 100 takahe left. Feeding is at the centre of takahe life. At least 70 per cent of a bird’s waking hours are consumed by the search for nourishment. In fact, it’s not even the search, it’s the act of eating. The bases (tillers) of tussocks and other grasses that make up a wild takahe’s diet require a fair tug to extract. There can be little doubt that without the major conservation effort that followed there would not be a wild takahe in Fiordland today. The valleys were topdressed to speed up the recovery of the tussock, and eggs were shuffled between nests to ensure that each pair would bring up a chick, but both actions had little tangible effect. The real breakthrough came with the establishment of Burwood Bush Rearing Unit near Te Anau—a takahe “factory” stocked with surplus eggs collected in the wild. On the inside, the unit resembles a small maternity ward, though you wear sterilised white gumboots instead of slippers. Oven-size incubators hum reassuringly, papier-mfiché “mother” takahe hang above heat-pad nests, their brooding calls played from tape recorders, and the young are fed with a takahe puppet—a blue glove with a red wooden beak. The chicks almost never see the puppeteers. Freshly hatched chicks are initially placed with one of six pairs of resident birds for a period of two weeks, the birds’ own offspring being removed. The parents don’t seem to notice the substitution, and may take a succession of these infant impostors. At about two weeks of age, all the chicks are brought into the brooding unit to be reared by the puppets. Our Changing World on Apple, Spotify, iHeartRadio or wherever you listen to your podcasts Bringing the birds back It was 1948 when takahē were rediscovered for the second time by Dr Geoffrey Orbell's party in the remote Murchison Mountains. With only a small population remaining, intensive management of the birds was deemed necessary. In the 1980s, Burwood Takahē Centre was created to manage breeding and chick rearing. 'Security populations' were established on offshore predator-free islands. A Specially Protected Area was created in the Murchison Mountains to protect the remaining wild population, with access by permit only. The hard work of DOC's takahē recovery team paid off, though not without a few setbacks along the way. The takahē population grew, hitting an estimated 300 in 2016. In 2018, takahē were reintroduced to Kahurangi National Park with the hope of establishing a second wild population. Things didn't go perfectly to plan, with a spate of bird deaths in the second year after release, and concerns about the suitability of the habitat. In 2023, the population hit 500 birds, and in August, 18 takahē were released on to Ngāi Tahu land at Greenstone Station in the Upper Whakatipu, to set up a third wild population. After two promising active breeding seasons, the birds took a bit of a hit earlier this year, with five thought to be killed by just one or two stoats. Now, here are some gains for nature you might not have heard about. Original takahē discovery site in the Murchison Ranges reaches full capacity as the population thrives This year was likely the last in which rangers would need to rigorously monitor the population of takahē in the Murchison Ranges, with the population reaching capacity. Glen Greaves, senior ranger in the Department of Conservation's (DOC) takahē recovery team, said the species was rediscovered at this site 76 years ago, and the population had been closely monitored for the past 50. "We think it's around 250, we don't know exactly - it's 50,000 hectares of mountainous terrain, so we have to give it an estimate - but we're pretty certain its between 220 and 260 birds." That meant the site was at
carrying capacity. It was a huge area, but the usable land was a lot smaller - and takahē needed up to 100 hectares per pair. They still faced challenges, he said. "It's a really tough site, it's not takahē Nirvana. It receives really cold winters, some pretty extreme weather events, its topography is really challenging for the birds as well, we have a lot of misadventure - you know, birds falling off cliffs and drowning in ponds and rivers during flood events." But those challenges meant pests had only just arrived, and that had allowed takahē to thrive. "We think the size of the population means it's quite resilient and we can now take a step back." It had been 20 years of involvement for Greaves, and a labour of love for the team. "We'll miss it, it's definitely the most exciting and rewarding place to go and visit, being such a historically important site for takahē, but it's just an awesome place. "But it's also a big tick in the success box as well, being able to step back means that we can put those resources into new sites." retrieved_chunks.text: [Page 9] Feral cats had developed a taste for kākāpō, and within five years these bushwise and feisty predators halved the remaining kākāpō population. Just as in Fiordland, searchers realised they were riding a bow wave of extinction. This time, however, they would take more radical measures. Between 1982 and 1992, all 61 surviving Stewart Island kākāpō were caught and transferred to safe island sanctuaries: Whenua Hou, Te Hoiere/Maud Island and Hauturu/Little Barrier Island, in the Hauraki Gulf . The kākāpō’s wild days were over. From now on, constant inter island transfers and airlifts out of trouble would become the norm in kākāpō life. While a long term solution to their predicament was being sought, the birds would remain refugees in their own homeland. One evening in early April 1999, as the seasons were turning and winter storms were edging in from the Southern Ocean, I walked with photographer Rod Morris through wet rimu forest down from the summit of Whenua Hou. We each carried a plastic cat box housing a kākāpō. The boxes were heavy, and every few hundred metres we stopped to swap hands and to catch a glimpse of the birds: a youngster named Sirocco in Morris’s cage, a female called Hoki in mine. The birds had just been ferried in from Pearl Island—at the entrance of Port Pegasus, on the eastern side of Stewart Island—their temporary home while 1396 hectare Whenua Hou Nature Reserve was being purged of any remaining vermin. Back in the mid 1980s, possums had been eradicated from Whenua Hou, and even egg stealing weka removed, and now, having been blitzed with 22 air dropped tonnes of poison pellets, the island had been declared a predator free “kākāpōrium”—the safest haven the birds would ever know. At the release site I opened the grille door of my cage and Hoki stomped out angrily, dragging her brown tail like a hand baggage trolley, and vanished in the undergrowth. Hoki was the star of several media appearances in the early 1990s when, rescued as a sta…

[Page 13] Creating a stoat proof enclave for kiwi was a priority for McLennan, and he chose Puketukutuku because, like a fortress, it could be easily defended. Across the narrow neck of the peninsula he ran a double trapline, and then, with the help of a professional hunter, eradicated all the stoats inside the enclosure. He thus effectively turned the peninsula into a predator free island, a kiwi haven. In 1998, all of his chicks survived. [chapter break] The concept of island sanctuaries is not new. In 1894, Richard Henry masterminded the transfer of some 750 kiwi and kakapo to Resolution Island, in Fiordland. But he underestimated the enemy. Stoats swam across from the mainland, and 14 years of work was undone. Despite that setback, many of our offshore islands have now been turned into refuges for species that elsewhere are either extinct or extremely rare. Some of them were natural sanctuaries on account of their distance from the mainland or their inaccessibility, and only needed to have landings strictly controlled. Others, in the fashion of McLennan’s peninsula, have had to be restored through painstaking trapping of noxious animals and subsequent vigilance against reinvasion. Whatever their past, these islands now serve as insular aviaries, genetic safe houses which offer endangered species an evolutionary second chance, the opportunity of an assisted comeback. For kiwi, there is no more telling example than Kapiti, a sliver of mountainous, rain soused land lying off the west coast north of Wellington. Former home of Te Rauparaha, then the site of a whaling station, then a ne’er do well sheep farm, in 1897 the island was turned into a wildlife sanctuary. The cleared forest slowly grew back, and the resident caretakers methodically eradicated the vermin. Between 1980 and 1986, 22,500 possums were removed from this 2000 ha island, and a week before my visit the reserve was officially declared rat free.

[Page 1] It is four in the morning, and I am sitting alone on the rain soaked soil of an island at the edge of Foveaux Strait, hunched against the pre dawn cold and endless southwesterlies. I have been in the thick blackness of this southern night for six hours already, waiting for the approaching dawn to silhouette the forest canopy with patches of grey. My only company lies a couple of metres away, in a tangle of rotting rata stumps and roots: a tiny grey chick which looks as cold and disconsolate as I feel. It is H2, a seven day old kakapo and one of the very latest additions to the embattled parrot’s population. While I shiver in layers of expensive polypropylene and synthetic fabrics, H2 has only the finest coating of grey down for warmth and resembles nothing more than a patch of mould on the forest floor. As a volunteer nest minder, I am spending two weeks looking after this fragile addition to the kakapo world while its mother, Heather, forages in the surrounding rimu forest of Codfish Island/Whenua Hou. Fatigued by 10 days of scant and intermittent sleep and up to four hours’ walking on waterlogged tracks each day, I find my biggest challenge is simply to stay awake. It’s rough and it’s raw, but what I’m doing is the reality of conservation in this country. Forget photo opportunities and cuddling one of the world’s rarest birds. Saving this species requires patience, sturdy boots and getting used to rivulets of water trickling down your neck. Nest minders, including the author (viewing a video monitor connected to an infrared camera at the nest). The cables, batteries and electronic gadgetry involved in the project had to be kept operational in the demanding outdoor conditions by Kakapo Recovery Programme scientist Graeme Elliott.

[Page 1] If we’re serious about Predator Free 2050—about ridding New Zealand of every last rat, stoat and possum—then Fiordland poses its sternest backcountry test. If we can pull it off here, we can pull it off in any of our national parks. What makes this land so difficult—and so important? Lining up a limb, DOC biodiversity ranger Bex Jackson readies to fire a lead sinker into the canopy of a beech tree, site of a long tailed bat roost in the Iris Burn. Behind her, senior ranger Emmanuel Oyston holds the fishing line the pair will use to haul a climbing rope up to the roost. Since DOC began rodent control in 2014, this bat colony at Rocky Point has doubled in size. Looking at this part of the country, I’m not so sure. Fiordland National Park—12,600 square kilometres, barely scratched by road or track, suffering some of the planet’s foulest meteorology. It will be raining here for more than half the year—eight metres of rain disembogues annually over Milford Sound. Chill southerlies mean the forest is defeated at just 1000 metres of altitude: above is gaunt granite, some of the oldest rock in the land. The single biggest problem with pests in this park is getting to them. Glaciers have carved a confusing coastline—is that a passage or a peninsula? An island or an isthmus? You’ll need a boat, a good one—or a helicopter, and lots of fuel. Any endeavour here has to plan for immensity, hindrance, contingency and the consent of that funereal firmament.

retrieved_chunks.text: [Page 5] Fiordland National Park occupies 15 per cent of the conservation estate, but gets less than one per cent of DOC’s budget, so it fell to Treasury to stump up for the first Battle for Our Birds pest control campaign in 2014, when the Kepler bats got some breathing space after an aerial 1080 drop. The population graph levelled off, then started to climb after another 1080 drop in 2016. The female population here at Rocky Point has since doubled, which sounds encouraging until you learn that amounted to only 65 in 2017. We had held more than half of them in our hands. [Chapter Break] “Out you get,” orders Andrew Smart, and the gaggle of tourists turn their cameras from a couple of panhandling kea to Oska, a six year old Czechoslovakian wire haired pointer, as he jumps from the ute. Oska’s fluoro orange Conservation Dogs jacket brightens a rainy scene at Monkey Creek, on the Hollyford road. Smart, who is a biodiversity ranger and the manager of DOC’s whio recovery programme, knows that a few pairs of the blue ducks hang out nearby. By now, if the season’s been kind, they should have ducklings with them, and he wants to know how they got on. We wade into the chill riffles. ## Saving Two Taonga: Kākāpō and Takahē Recovery Compared

Both the kākāpō and takahē recovery programmes represent some of New Zealand's most intensive and long-running conservation efforts — yet the two species have required quite different strategies, shaped by their distinct biology, habitats, and the threats they face.

![embed-1](embed://1)

## The Core Difference: Islands vs Mainland

Perhaps the starkest contrast between the two programmes is their relationship with habitat. The kākāpō recovery has been built almost entirely around predator-free offshore islands. Between 1982 and 1992, all 61 surviving Stewart Island kākāpō were transferred to safe island sanctuaries — Whenua Hou, Te Hoiere/Maud Island, and Hauturu/Little Barrier Island — and their wild days on the mainland effectively came to an end. [[1]](cite://1/1) The kākāpō's flightless, ground-nesting habits and inability to escape mammalian predators made this total relocation unavoidable. [[2]](cite://2/1)

The takahē programme, by contrast, has always maintained a wild mainland population — the only one remaining — in the Murchison Mountains of Fiordland, which was rediscovered in 1948. [[3]](cite://3/1) This population has been treated as the ecological heartland of the species, even while offshore island populations were established as a genetic safety net. [[4]](cite://4/1) More recently, takahē have been reintroduced into Kahurangi National Park and, as of 2023, onto Ngāi Tahu land at Greenstone Station in the Upper Whakatipu, establishing a third wild mainland population. [[5]](cite://5/1)

## Intensity of Hands-On Management

Both programmes have been defined by intensive human intervention, but the kākāpō programme has perhaps reached the furthest extreme. Every known bird has a name, a transmitter, and a detailed family tree. [[6]](cite://6/1) Nest minding — where volunteers and rangers camp beside nests overnight to monitor chicks while mothers forage — has been standard practice, with infrared cameras, surveillance equipment, and even physically modified nests all part of the toolkit. [[7]](cite://7/1) Supplementary feeding, artificial insemination, egg incubation, and chick hand-rearing are all routine during breeding seasons. [[8]](cite://8/1)

The takahē programme developed its own intensive approach from the 1980s, when eggs began to be incubated in safe facilities and chicks raised in enclosures near Te Anau. [[3]](cite://3/2) The Burwood Takahē Centre was established as a dedicated captive-rearing facility, now producing around 25 chicks a year, with a similar number raised at 20 other sanctuary sites around the country. [[9]](cite://9/1) Both programmes also deploy transmitters to track birds, with DOC rangers using receivers — and in the takahē's case, even dogs — to locate individuals in the field. [[10]](cite://10/1)

## Predator Control: The Takahē's Achilles Heel

While the kākāpō programme sidesteps the predator problem largely by removing birds to predator-free islands, the takahē recovery has had to grapple directly with predators on the mainland. Stoats are the takahē's greatest foe: in a single mast season in 2007, stoats — fuelled by a boom in rodent numbers — slaughtered 40 percent of the Murchison Mountains adult population. [[9]](cite://9/2) Trapping has been significantly scaled up since, with over 3,500 traps deployed in the Murchisons, though stoats still kill up to 20 percent of birds there in bad mast years. [[9]](cite://9/3)

In Kahurangi National Park, years of aerial 1080 pest control have kept stoat numbers very low, which is cited as the main reason takahē have been able to establish there at all. [[9]](cite://9/4) The question of whether 1080 and takahē can safely coexist at scale has been described as "the biggest question" facing the takahē programme. [[9]](cite://9/5)

## Breeding Constraints and Recovery Pace

The two species face different biological constraints. Kākāpō only breed every two to four years, tied to the masting of rimu trees, making population growth painfully slow. [[8]](cite://8/2) By contrast, the takahē population has been growing at around 10 percent a year, reaching 500 birds in 2023 and with the Murchison Mountains population now considered to be at carrying capacity. [[5]](cite://5/2)[[11]](cite://11/1)

The kākāpō population has grown from a low of around 50 birds in the early 1990s to over 230 adults, with 2026 shaping up as the biggest breeding season on record — 92 new chicks alive as of mid-2026. [[6]](cite://6/2)[[12]](cite://12/1) However, kākāpō remain listed as Nationally Critical. [[12]](cite://12/2)

## A Shared Evolution: Moving Towards Lighter-Touch Management

Interestingly, both programmes are now at a similar philosophical crossroads: after decades of intense hands-on management, both are beginning to step back.

For the takahē, the Department of Conservation (DOC) began trialling a "do nothing" model as early as 2012, after more than six decades of intensive intervention, to test whether populations could sustain themselves with reduced oversight. [[13]](cite://13/1) Now, with the Murchison Mountains population at capacity, DOC has signalled it can redirect resources to new sites. [[11]](cite://11/2)

For kākāpō, 2026 marks the first season in which a "lighter touch" approach has been formally introduced across two of the three breeding islands — leaving more eggs to hatch in nests rather than incubators, reducing supplementary feeding, and prioritising checks only for genetically valuable eggs and chicks. [[14]](cite://14/1) Some chicks this season will not even be named — a symbolic step towards returning the birds to their own natural rhythms. [[6]](cite://6/3)

The long-term vision for both species is similar: self-sustaining wild populations roaming their ancestral landscapes. For kākāpō, that dream may eventually hinge on Predator Free Rakiura — a community-led effort to rid Stewart Island of feral cats and rats, which could one day allow kākāpō to return to their former island home without intensive management. [[15]](cite://15/1)

Would you like to explore how the kākāpō's unique breeding biology — particularly its dependence on rimu masting — has shaped the specific management tools the recovery programme has had to develop?

1.document_title: New Zealand's Threatened Species: Conservation Status, Strategies, and Recovery Efforts
1.document_summary: This comprehensive document provides an overview of New Zealand's threatened species and conservation efforts. It defines threatened species as native plants and animals with critically low populations facing extinction risk, with New Zealand having 2,788 threatened species (37% of birds, 34% of plants). Main causes of decline include habitat destruction, invasive predators like rats and possums, and over-harvesting. New Zealand uses an eight-tier classification system for conservation status based on threats, endemism, vulnerability, and cultural importance. Conservation strategies include island sanctuaries, pest control, captive breeding, and habitat restoration. Notable successes include the black robin recovery (7 to 250 individuals), takahē recovery program, and tuatara reintroduction programs. The document presents case studies of endangered species including the Mahoenui giant wētā, Peraxilla mistletoes, kiwi, and tuatara. About 30% of New Zealand is protected conservation land. Recent efforts have expanded beyond visible species to include freshwater fish and plants, with a shift toward restoring entire habitats. Key challenges include funding limitations, many species poorly understood (1,455 fungi species classified as 'data deficient'), an estimated 50,000 unidentified native species potentially at risk, and preventing 'zombie species' that survive only in cultivation.

2.document_title: Stewart Island/Rakiura: Comprehensive Guide to New Zealand's Third Largest Island
2.document_summary: Stewart Island/Rakiura is New Zealand's third largest island located south of the South Island. The Māori name "Rakiura" means "glowing skies," referencing the aurora australis, while the English name honors William Stewart, first mate of the sealer Pegasus. Covering 1,680 square kilometers with approximately 85% protected as Rakiura National Park (established 2002), the island features diverse vegetation zones from coastal shrublands to alpine tussock lands, with over half covered by podocarp and hardwood forests. The island supports exceptional biodiversity including 15,000 southern tokoeka (Stewart Island kiwi), kākāpō, three penguin species, fur seals, and sea lions, with 21 endemic alpine plant species. Historically, Polynesians reached the island by the late 1200s, with permanent Māori settlement following primarily around coastal areas for fishing and harvesting tītī (muttonbirds). European contact began with James Cook in 1770, followed by sealers, whalers, and missionaries. Since the 1850s, the island's economy has centered on sheep farming, timber milling, and fishing, with fishing becoming dominant by 2013. Tourism evolved from the 1890s to a major industry attracting 30,000 annual visitors. Key geographic features include Paterson Inlet (8,900 hectares), Mason Bay with 200-metre dunes, Ulva Island (predator-free scenic reserve), Port Pegasus with granite domes, and the Southern Circuit tramping track (71.5 km). Oban (Halfmoon Bay) serves as the main township with 378 residents in 2013.

3.text:
[Page 13] area. Island restoration Some islands are being restored to something resembling their original ecology, with unwanted animals entirely eradicated. Larger browsing animals such as wild cattle and goats are the first to go, followed by smaller predators cats and possums, stoats and weasels, and eventually rats. Existing patches of native vegetation are enlarged, often with the help of planting programmes. Some sparse populations have become abundant once again. Other species were reintroduced to their former homes, while some islands became sanctuaries for animals never previously found there. Kākāpō were once plentiful, but when only a few remained in Fiordland and on Stewart Island (Rakiura), they were moved to Whenua Hou/Codfish, Maud and Little Barrier islands, and in 2003 to Fiordland’s Chalky Island (Te Kākahu o Tamatea). Public sanctuaries Most conservation restrict access to prevent disturbance or the arrival of unwanted pests. But several are open to the public. Kāpiti Island near Wellington and Tiritiri Matangi near Auckland have similar histories. Once cleared for farming, they now have no animal pests, and native forest has been re established over 250,000 native trees were planted on Tiritiri Matangi. Both are refuges for saddlebacks, kōkako, stitchbirds, little spotted kiwi and takahē. Not far from Kāpiti is Mana Island, also a bird sanctuary, and noted for its ‘colony’ of concrete gannets, built to tempt real gannets to breed there. Betty gets her goats In the 1970s the government decided to kill wild goats and sheep on Arapawa Island, in the Marlborough Sounds. Protesters claimed the animals were descendants of those left by James Cook. DNA tests showed some were genetically unique. Many were culled, but others were sent to farms and wildlife parks. Betty Rowe led the rescue campaign and established a sanctuary on Arapawa Island. Marine reserves To create areas where people could not disturb the ocean, seabed and seashore, the Marine Reserves Act was passed in 1971. The first reserve was at Goat Island, north of Auckland (now Cape Rodney Ōkakari Point Marine Reserve). The second was the ocean around the Poor Knights Islands, noted for islands subtropical fish. Others include islands off the Coromandel Peninsula, Tūhua (Mayor Island) in Bay of Plenty, Kāpiti Island, Long Island in the Marlborough Sounds, Tonga Island in Abel Tasman National Park, Elizabeth Island in Fiordland and Ulva Island near Stewart Island.

3.document_title: New Zealand's Nearshore Islands: History, Conservation, and Human Settlement
3.document_summary: This comprehensive document explores New Zealand's over 600 nearshore islands within 50 kilometres of the main islands, covering their geological formation, historical significance, and contemporary conservation status. The islands are distributed around the North Island (Great Barrier, Rangitoto, Bay of Islands) and southern regions (Marlborough Sounds, Fiordland). Historically, Māori utilized these islands for harvesting seafood, birds, and resources like argillite rock, obsidian, and adzite, including tītī (muttonbirds). European contact began in the late 1700s-1800s with sealers, whalers, and explorers like James Cook. Island industries included 19th-century mining, farming, and the world's first regular pigeon airmail service on Great Barrier Island (1897-1908). The document details quarantine facilities on Quarantine Island (Dunedin), Ōtamahua (Christchurch), and Matiu (Wellington), which housed disease victims, leprosy patients, and wartime internees. Today, islands serve as nature reserves hosting endangered species including tuatara, kākāpō, kiwi, and rare plants like Pennantia baylisiana. Conservation efforts began with Resolution Island in 1891 and include successful eradication programs and species reintroduction initiatives.

Tongariro National Park, established in 1894, was New Zealand's first national park, created through an agreement between Ngāti Tūwharetoa chief Horonuku Te Heuheu and the Crown to preserve ancestral volcanoes. The document traces the significant shift from initial recreation and tourism focus to conservation and ecological protection, with the National Parks Act 1952 establishing centralized management. The West Coast extends over 500 kilometres along the South Island's western coast with only 32,148 residents spread across 8.7% of the land area. Geologically, the region features sedimentary rocks, coal measures, distinctive karst landforms like Pancake Rocks, and sits along the Alpine Fault. The landscape was shaped by glaciation, with high rainfall (2,000-3,000mm annually near coast, exceeding 10,000mm in mountains) supporting native forests and abundant wildlife including endangered kiwi species. Historically, Māori settlement began after 1250-1300 CE, with pounamu (greenstone) discovery becoming significant. Various iwi, including Waitaha, Ngāti Wairangi, and Poutini Ngāi Tahu, occupied the region. European exploration began with Abel Tasman (1642) and James Cook (1770), followed by the transformative gold rush triggered by alluvial gold discovery near Hokitika in mid-1864, which peaked at approximately 28,700 residents by late 1867. The region became a cradle of socialism and labour activism, particularly through coal miners' strikes like the 1908 Blackball strike. Economically, the region developed through resource extraction including gold mining (peaking at 15+ tonnes in 1866-67), coal mining (reaching 1 million tonnes by 1907), and timber production. Modern development includes dairy farming, commercial fishing (whitebaiting, blue cod, groper), and tourism. The 1965 Haast Pass road opening transformed the region into a major tourist destination. The region is home to 1.9 million hectares of protected areas including five national parks. Cultural heritage includes literary works by Keri Hulme and Eleanor Catton, strong rugby traditions, and a thriving craft sector including pounamu carving. The Māori community experienced renaissance following the 1998 Ngai Tahu Claim Settlement Act, which returned control of pounamu resources and provided financial settlements.

16.document_title: Māori Land Rights, Indigenous Law, and Colonial Legislation in New Zealand: A Historical and Legal Analysis
16.document_summary:
This document examines the complex relationship between Māori traditional law and British colonial legislation in New Zealand from pre-Treaty times to 2011. It traces how Māori operated under a sophisticated customary law system based on concepts like mana, tapu, rahui, and utu before the Treaty of Waitangi (1840). Traditional Māori land rights were based on ahi kā (occupation) and various take (rights), contrasting sharply with colonial land laws that clashed with Māori communal land concepts.

The analysis documents systematic land dispossession through key colonial legislation including the Land Claims Ordinance 1841, Native Land Purchase Ordinance 1846, New Zealand Settlements Act 1863, and Native Lands Acts 1862-1865. The Native Land Court individualized Māori land titles to facilitate European settlement, causing severe hardship through distant hearings, high costs, and lengthy delays. The 1.3 million hectares confiscated under the Settlements Act exemplifies the scale of dispossession.

From the 1970s onward, Māori protests prompted significant legislative reforms recognizing customary rights and treaty principles. Key reforms include the Waitangi Tribunal (1975), Te Ture Whenua Māori Act 1993, Resource Management Act 1991, and landmark cases like Tom Te Weehi's 1986 fishing rights case. The document also addresses the intersection of Māori indigenous property rights with European marine law, demonstrating how Māori claims to traditional rights over marine areas are grounded in pre-existing legal traditions. By 2011, legislation increasingly incorporated Treaty of Waitangi principles and recognized Māori spiritual, cultural, and property rights.

18.document_title: Te hī ika – Māori Fishing: Traditional Practices, Cultural Heritage, and Contemporary Fisheries Management
18.document_summary:
This comprehensive document explores Māori fishing practices across traditional, historical, and contemporary contexts. It covers the spiritual significance of fishing in Māori tradition, including the god Tangaroa and legendary figures like Māui and Kupe. Traditional fishing methods included nets made from flax, hooks, lines, spears, and pots, with fishing being a tapu (sacred) activity involving specific rituals and karakia (incantations). Fishing grounds were carefully managed by tribes with expert knowledge of optimal fishing times and seasons, and fish were preserved through steaming and drying for tribal feasts.

Early European observers like Captain Cook and Joseph Banks noted Māori fishing expertise and the enormous scale of their operations, including nets up to 900 metres long. Large-scale tribal expeditions involved hundreds of people in canoes, with catches distributed among families and exchanged with inland tribes. In 1852, 1,792 canoes brought 45 tons of fish to Auckland, demonstrating the significance of Māori fishing to early European settlements.

Following European settlement, traditional fishing declined due to land loss, European commercial competition, and regulatory restrictions. The 1992 Sealord deal granted Māori 50% ownership of New Zealand's largest fishing company and 22% of total quota. The Māori Fisheries Act 2004 established governance structures including Te Ohu Kaimoana. Today, Māori control over a third of New Zealand's fishing industry, with many tribes operating successful seafood companies, balancing commercial operations with customary fishing and traditional food preparation.

19.text:
[Page 4] No other creature in the pantheon of New Zealand’s endemic fauna has ever attracted so much attention, effort and funding, and none is more critically endangered and vulnerable. Yet for all the kākāpō’s ecological charisma and PR celebrity, few people ever get it in the wild—and not just because its sanctuaries are out of bounds to all but key personnel. You could walk its island forests and scrublands for days and never see a bird. The kākāpō evolved with blind and total faith in its perfect camouflage, and the birds blend into the foliage so well that trying to see them is like picking the 3D shapes out of Magic Eye pictures.

19.document_title: Kākāpō: Bird on the Brink - Conservation Efforts and Recovery Success
19.document_summary: This comprehensive document chronicles the remarkable conservation journey of the kākāpō, New Zealand's critically endangered flightless nocturnal parrot. Once abundant throughout New Zealand's islands, the species declined dramatically to just 18 males in Fiordland by the 1980s, with only 62 birds remaining by the early 2000s due to introduced predators and historical human hunting. The breakthrough came with the discovery of a 200-strong population on Stewart Island in 1977, including the first identified female since the early 1900s. The recovery program involved relocating all surviving kākāpō to predator-free island sanctuaries including Whenua Hou, Maud Island, and Little Barrier Island between 1982-1992. Key conservation innovations include helicopter access to remote populations, hand-rearing of chicks, inter-island transfers, electronic surveillance systems, and supplementary feeding programs. The species' unique lekking courtship behavior, where males inflate and boom low-frequency calls from elaborately maintained bowl-shaped arenas, was crucial to understanding their breeding patterns. Despite their appearance as ecological relics, kākāpō demonstrate adaptability and have become marathon survivors with lifespans potentially exceeding 60 years. The dedicated recovery team has achieved significant breeding successes, transforming wild kākāpō into managed refugees in their own homeland. The long-term vision includes establishing free-living, self-sustaining populations on subantarctic islands like Campbell Island, representing an unprecedented turning point in the species' survival.

20.text:
[Page 1] Each year, New Zealanders vote for Forest & Bird’s Te Manu Rongonui o te Tau / Bird of the Year to select a winner. Last year it was our flightless, nocturnal, long living kākāpō, which clings to existence on just three predator free islands around New Zealand. They were abundant in New Zealand before humans arrived, but have teetered on the edge of extinction since the early 1900s and reached an all time low of about 50 in the early ‘90s. Now there are just over 200, but are still listed as Nationally Critical. Rakiura/Stewart Island kākāpō are in good genetic health despite inbreeding, according to a study of 50 kākāpō genomes published in September.

20.document_title: Troubled Lives of the A-listers: New Zealand's Endangered and Recovering Bird Species
20.document_summary: This article examines New Zealand's most beloved bird species and their conservation status. While iconic birds like kākāpō, kea, and hoiho face critical threats from predators, habitat loss, and disease, there are encouraging signs of recovery. The kākāpō, despite numbering only 200, maintains genetic health. Kea populations are declining despite protection, with lead poisoning affecting up to 64% of some populations. However, success stories include the North Island kōkako's recovery to 1,600 pairs and the successful hand-rearing of a tara iti chick. Urban bird sanctuaries have enabled species like tūī, kererū, and piwakawaka to return to cities. The article highlights that native birds evolved without mammalian predators, making them particularly vulnerable to introduced species, while more recent arrivals like fantails show greater resilience.

21.text:
[Page 18] “Kākāpō are extinct throughout their natural range,” he began, “and there is no way of returning them there, at least in the short to medium term. If they are to survive in a free living state, then it must be outside their former range. But where? It is fair to expect that the number of kākāpō will steadily, if slowly, increase, and that the small islands where they are being kept will soon reach their holding capacity. What are we going to do then? There aren’t many options, because kākāpō need a lot of space, and a self sustaining population of several hundred birds would require many thousands of hectares. They cannot coexist with predatory mammals, so the mainland is out, and they need a dominant masting plant species in order to breed. We’re looking at all the possi bilities—including the subantarctic.” His eyes had the gleam of a man who sees a prize which is not yet within his grasp. “Campbell?” I asked. “It’s a candidate, and a good one. It is large—over 11,000 hectares—and after last year’s rat eradication project it should now be free of all alien mammals. It has a wide variety of plants, including abundant snow tussock, which could provide the necessary high energy food to enable kākāpō to breed. The climate shouldn’t worry them. Kākāpō are adapted to cool, damp, subalpine conditions. Their down is particularly dense, and under their skin they have a layer of fat up to 15 millimetres thick.” Placing the birds so far outside their former range might seem a form of banishment, Merton admitted, but it would also be like putting our feathery treasures on term deposit in a safe offshore bank, where no calamity and no fund cutting or staff downsizing could affect them. Although kākāpō are unable to fly they have well developed wings which they use for balance when climbing—an activity at which they excel—and for braking during short downward leaps. If the species’ flight towards oblivion is arrested—as now seems likely—it will be thanks to the Herculean effort of a coterie of conservation workers in gathering and applying knowledge about this most singular of birds. Merton reminded me that the Chatham Islands black robin, once the rarest bird in the world, no longer depends on precious conservation dollars for its survival, but thrives in two self sustaining populations without management. “We absolutely must do the same for kākāpō,” he said. I listened eagerly and soaked up his radiant enthusiasm, for it seemed that his lifetime task of seeing the kākāpō through its crisis might be nearing completion. Later, I walked with him to the small plane that would whisk this 62 year old battler, with his shy smile and big backpack, to where he was happiest—among his big green parrots. As I drove away I thought of Douglas Adams, the literary hitchhiker of the galaxy, who in 1989 went on a whirlwind tour to see some of the world’s most iconic threatened species. He wrote a book about his experiences, called Last Chance to See, which contains a chapter on kākāpō. Adams rushed to New Zealand to see the kākāpō before it disappeared, but as it has turned out he needn’t have hurried. Here, thanks to Merton, his Wildlife Service and DOC colleagues and an army of volunteers, the rerun of the dodo story looks set to have a happy ending. “If you look [a kākāpō] in its large, round, greeny brown face,” Adams wrote, “it has a look of serenely innocent incomprehension that makes you want to hug it and tell it that everything will be all right.” Perhaps now, for the first time ever, we can honestly say it will be. The post Kākāpō: Bird on the brink appeared first on New Zealand Geographic .

But it has contributed fundamentally to our own birdlife, with bird breeders imparting their knowledge on incubation and hand rearing techniques to DOC, underpinning conservation work such as kākāpō breeding programmes. “There’s just this massive untapped resource of people with decades of experience… It’s a real shame. If they were to put together the right regulations and work with breeders, I know of at least 20 or 30 who would have no problem breeding pure red crowned, yellow crowned, orange fronted, Antipodes Island parakeets, kea, kākā,” says van Hooff, “and they would do it all free of change. For the love of birds.” He points out that even if parrots do escape, “people get them back. They’re a bird of value.” (The society is firmly against deliberate releases. According to van Hooff, “We don’t condone people releasing parrots into the wild. It is not okay. It’s not fair on the bird, either.”)

23.document_title: Takahe Recovery Program: Conservation Challenges, Strategies, and Collaborative Approaches in New Zealand
23.document_summary: This comprehensive document examines the Department of Conservation's takahe recovery program, one of New Zealand's most intensive wildlife conservation efforts. The takahe, an endangered flightless bird endemic to New Zealand, faces critical survival challenges in the Murchison Mountains of Fiordland. After over 60 years of intensive intervention including captive breeding at Burwood Bush Rearing Unit and population management on predator-free islands, the wild population remains precarious at approximately 110-120 birds, having declined from 160 following a 2007 beech-mast event that triggered a stoat population explosion. The document chronicles a significant paradigm shift in conservation strategy: moving from intensive human intervention toward minimal intervention approaches, with the Murchison population being left largely unmanaged to test self-sustainability while establishing an insurance population in controlled environments. Key conservation challenges include predator control through 1,600 traplines across 500 sq km, harsh alpine habitat, avalanche risks, and poor nutritional food sources. Modern monitoring techniques using GPS technology and radio-telemetry have replaced invasive helicopter methods. The document highlights innovative collaborative approaches involving multiple stakeholders: the Kepler Challenge race organizers, Kids Restore New Zealand, the Wapiti Foundation, and local Te Anau businesses through "Buy a Box" programmes. Emerging technologies such as PAPP toxin and self-resetting CO2-powered traps offer new hope for protecting takahe and other native birds.

24.text:
[Page 13] Over the years, this programme has been through some shaky times, partly because there are still so many unknowns about the birds, but also because of the hobbling effects of political pressure and bureaucratic constraints. Following an external review in 1994, executive control over budget, strategy, staff and all things kākāpō was put in the hands of three people: Paul Jansen, Graeme Elliott and Merton—all of whom have clocked up many years in grassroots conservation. Jansen, the programme leader, has quietly emphatic manners and the reputation of a man who gets things done. Elliott, the team’s scientist, is a thinker and electronics tinkerer, responsible for much of the innovative technology now employed in the field. Merton, with unrivalled knowledge and experience of kākāpō, is the prime architect of the close order management strategy for the birds, adapted from his black robin work. Since 1995, the trio has put the kākāpō on a fast track to recovery—well, fast in kākāpō terms. In the avian world, where life is but a short sprint, kākāpō are the marathon runners—possibly the longest lived of all birds. Many of those alive today were already mature adults when they were found in the mid 1970s, and biologists estimate a typical kākāpō life span to be around 60 years, perhaps more. Like tuatara, they seem timeless. Their metabolism is so unhurried they can digest foods containing toxins that would kill humans or make them sick, like the leaves and fruit of the native tutu, and poroporo berries—both kākāpō favourites. And still the bizarre night parrots keep surprising their caretakers. Graeme Elliott, in an effort to breathe a little more enthusiasm into the birds’ courtship, has tried injecting selected rimu trees with a hormone to induce the trees to produce more fruit—so far the most consistent kākāpō aphrodisiac. He has also developed a “boom box”—a portable, weatherproof stereo system which, placed near a lek, automatically comes on at night, blaring out the boom! boom! sound to spur the males into song. In 1998, kākāpō bred successfully on Te Hoiere/Maud Island—but without the benefit of a boom box and without a rimu tree in sight. The event on Maud was all the more significant for taking place in an extremely modified environment, showing that, despite appearing to be stuck in an ecological time warp, the kākāpō is an adaptable creature. Maud Island is the 309 hectare tip of a mountain that was flooded when the sea level rose. It was farmed until 1975, when the Royal New Zealand Forest and Bird Society successfully campaigned to buy it and turn it into a nature reserve. Most of the island had been cleared of its original forest, and one corner had been planted in pines. Remarkably, it was in the radiata that the kākāpō nested. Many kākāpō now reside on Whenua Hou, an island west of Stewart Island which was cleared of possums, weka and rats to create a safe haven. Locating the birds on the 1396 hectare scrub and forest covered island is a challenge made easier by the use of radio telemetry, but the method is not foolproof: the kākāpō’s transmitters can become detached, in which case dogs are brought in to sniff out the escapees. By late December 1998, all four of Maud’s males were booming, and soon mating signs—tufts of down and feathers near the track and bowl area—were found. Then, on the island’s west facing slope, where the setting sun dapples through the trees and brown pine needles muffle one’s footsteps, Merton and others discovered a nest with three eggs under sparse bracken cover on a slope so steep the subsequent track cut up it was a winding staircase of 140 steps. The find was such a momentous event that Merton and his colleagues took no chances with the safety of their charges. The three chicks that hatched were offspring of Richard Henry, the last and only known surviving Fiordland kākāpō. “We’ve waited more than 20 years for this nest,” Merton said at the time. “It must succeed!” And so the intervention began. Every time the mother, named Flossie, left the nest to forage—generally at around 2 or 3am—a stealthy construction crew moved in. First, a metre high retaining wall was erected on the lower side of the nest to prevent the eggs from rolling down the hill. Next a plywood roof was added. Then a drain was dug on the upslope to divert any possible flooding. A piece of plastic pipe became an entrance tunnel, and an infra red beam, wired to a door chime, was placed across the entrance to alert nest minders when the mother left for her nightly perambulations. A miniature video surveillance camera was placed inside the nest to keep an electronic eye on the chicks. Later, a play ground was added. It was as if a person living in a shanty had left for a short walk and returned to find a prefab house with a sundeck, and a sand pit for the kids. Not showing the least surprise, Flossie and the youngsters took the alterations in their goosestep stride. All the while, a roster of nest minders camped in a tent 80 metres away, ready to dash in to deal with any emergency. Electronic surveillance and nest minding would become standard procedure with all subsequent nests. A fabric scoop on the end of a ski pole makes a useful device for extracting chicks from deep hideaways when weighing and measuring is to be carried out. Females feed young chicks (such as the 12 day old in the bottom photograph) by regurgitating the soft parts of plants, including fruit and shoots, but older chicks are given less digested fruit and seeds.

24.document_title: Kākāpō: Bird on the Brink - Conservation Efforts and Recovery Success
24.document_summary: This comprehensive document chronicles the remarkable conservation journey of the kākāpō, New Zealand's critically endangered flightless nocturnal parrot. Once abundant throughout New Zealand's islands, the species declined dramatically to just 18 males in Fiordland by the 1980s, with only 62 birds remaining by the early 2000s due to introduced predators and historical human hunting. The breakthrough came with the discovery of a 200-strong population on Stewart Island in 1977, including the first identified female since the early 1900s. The recovery program involved relocating all surviving kākāpō to predator-free island sanctuaries including Whenua Hou, Maud Island, and Little Barrier Island between 1982-1992. Key conservation innovations include helicopter access to remote populations, hand-rearing of chicks, inter-island transfers, electronic surveillance systems, and supplementary feeding programs. The species' unique lekking courtship behavior, where males inflate and boom low-frequency calls from elaborately maintained bowl-shaped arenas, was crucial to understanding their breeding patterns. Despite their appearance as ecological relics, kākāpō demonstrate adaptability and have become marathon survivors with lifespans potentially exceeding 60 years. The dedicated recovery team has achieved significant breeding successes, transforming wild kākāpō into managed refugees in their own homeland. The long-term vision includes establishing free-living, self-sustaining populations on subantarctic islands like Campbell Island, representing an unprecedented turning point in the species' survival.

After receiving encouraging reports from Buckingham for nearly a month, Nora’s foster chick started to lose condition, and on May 13 it had to be rescued a second time, and transferred to Auckland Zoo to join the other two. For the next 35 days all was well. Regular “plunket faxes” arrived in our office from the zoo, plotting steady weight gains in the three chicks. It was a time of great excitement, and some nervousness. Would these birds be the first successfully hand reared kakapo? Would they survive the transition back to the wild? Ultimately, would they help the species “turn the corner” and escape the threat of extinction? Louise Joyce, a Television New Zealand journalist who visited the zoo weekly for nearly three months to record the progress of the chicks, takes up the story in April, when only two chicks had been transferred . . . Maud Island’s VIP bird, Hoki, gets a large, predator proof aviary to herself, and plenty of attention from her caretakers. 25.document_title: The Kakapo of Codfish Island: Conservation, Hand-Rearing, and Species Recovery
25.document_summary: This comprehensive document chronicles critical conservation efforts to save the kakapo, one of the world's rarest parrots, from extinction. In March 1992, with only 50 kakapo remaining and just 15 known females, the Department of Conservation launched a rescue mission on Codfish Island after El Niño-driven gales threatened chick survival. Don Merton coordinated the transfer of critically underweight chicks to Auckland Zoo for artificial rearing, including a challenging rescue of two chicks from an inaccessible nest beneath a boulder. At Auckland Zoo, Curator Mick Sibley supervised intensive hand-rearing of three chicks—Alf, BJ, and Nora's foster chick—providing round-the-clock care with specialized feeding every two hours using soya bean-based porridge. The programme achieved remarkable success in raising multiple chicks together but faced tragic setbacks, including deaths from acute respiratory problems caused by food particle inhalation. The surviving chick Hoki was successfully transferred to Maud Island, serving as a crucial research subject and potential nucleus for a captive breeding population. The recovery programme gained invaluable insights into kakapo development and breeding requirements, with the Department of Conservation recognizing that intervention, monitoring, supplementary feeding, and nest protection are essential for species survival. This conservation effort mirrors successful strategies used with black robins, offering hope that kakapo can return from the brink of extinction.

26.document_title: Kokako: New Zealand's Endangered Forest Bird - Conservation History, Recovery Programs, and Breeding Efforts
26.document_summary: This comprehensive document chronicles the history, biology, and conservation efforts of the kokako, an endemic New Zealand wattlebird belonging to the ancient Callaeidae family. It covers two species: the blue-wattled North Island kokako (Callaeas wilsoni) and the orange-wattled South Island kokako (Callaeas cinerea), formally declared extinct in 2004. The document details kokako behavior, including their distinctive grey plumage, black mask, vivid blue wattles, melodious calls, weak flying abilities, omnivorous diet, and role as dispersers of large-seeded forest plants. A pivotal turning point came with the 1989-1997 Kokako Recovery Management programme, a collaborative effort between the Department of Conservation and Forest Research Institute across three forest blocks (Kaharoa, Rotoehu, and Mapara). This study conclusively demonstrated that predation from introduced predators such as ship rats, possums, stoats, and hawks was the primary cause of kokako decline. The programme identified that reducing possums and ship rats to very low levels could allow managed kokako populations to survive on the mainland. By 2005, 615 breeding pairs existed nationwide, with management goals of 1000 pairs by 2020. The document describes successful kokako transfers to islands and mainland locations, establishing populations on Little Barrier and Tiritiri-Matangi. The Kaharoa Kokako Trust exemplifies success, growing from 12 pairs to 137 territory-holding birds in a decade. Conservation efforts involving pest control, ecosystem restoration, mist-netting, bird tracking, and dedicated fieldwork have been instrumental in supporting kokako recovery.

27.text:
[Page 1] It is four in the morning, and I am sitting alone on the rain soaked soil of an island at the edge of Foveaux Strait, hunched against the pre dawn cold and endless southwesterlies. I have been in the thick blackness of this southern night for six hours already, waiting for the approaching dawn to silhouette the forest canopy with patches of grey. My only company lies a couple of metres away, in a tangle of rotting rata stumps and roots: a tiny grey chick which looks as cold and disconsolate as I feel. It is H2, a seven day old kakapo and one of the very latest additions to the embattled parrot’s population. While I shiver in layers of expensive polypropylene and synthetic fabrics, H2 has only the finest coating of grey down for warmth and resembles nothing more than a patch of mould on the forest floor. As a volunteer nest minder, I am spending two weeks looking after this fragile addition to the kakapo world while its mother, Heather, forages in the surrounding rimu forest of Codfish Island/Whenua Hou. Fatigued by 10 days of scant and intermittent sleep and up to four hours’ walking on waterlogged tracks each day, I find my biggest challenge is simply to stay awake. It’s rough and it’s raw, but what I’m doing is the reality of conservation in this country. Forget photo opportunities and cuddling one of the world’s rarest birds. Saving this species requires patience, sturdy boots and getting used to rivulets of water trickling down your neck. 27.document_title: Minders: The Kakapo Caregivers of Codfish Island - Conservation and Intensive Management
27.document_summary: This comprehensive document chronicles the extraordinary kakapo conservation efforts on Codfish Island/Whenua Hou, focusing on the landmark 2002 breeding season. Over 100 volunteer nest minders from around the world participated in intensive 24-hour surveillance of 24 nests, resulting in 26 chicks hatching with 24 surviving—a 39% increase in the world kakapo population from 62 to 86 birds. The nest minders maintained constant vigilance, acted as surrogate parents during female foraging periods, and used innovative equipment like heat pads and infrared monitoring systems. The Department of Conservation-led intervention programme involved detailed monitoring, video surveillance, nightly chick weighing, and hand-rearing of struggling chicks. Despite harsh conditions—steep boggy tracks, cold nights, and minimal sleep—volunteers found the opportunity invaluable. The document profiles individual kakapo mothers (Heather, Ruth, Nora, Flossie) and their distinct parenting behaviors. A 1999 aerial poison drop eradicated rats, dramatically improving nesting success. With a chick mortality rate of just 8%, the 2002 season represented the most significant breakthrough for kakapo recovery since their rediscovery in 1977, demonstrating that intensive human intervention can successfully secure this endangered species' survival.

28.document_title: Mason Bay Marram: Ecological Restoration and Community Conflict on Stewart Island
28.document_summary: This article explores the ecological restoration efforts at Mason Bay on Stewart Island's west coast, where the Department of Conservation launched a herbicide eradication program in 2001 to remove invasive marram grass. Farmers had deliberately planted marram from the 1930s-1960s to stabilize dunes, but the aggressive grass now smothers native vegetation including the endangered pingao sedge. Dr. Mike Hilton, a leading dune ecologist, documents the project's progress while investigating how possums spread the invasive Russell lupin. The eradication effort faces significant community opposition from long-standing Stewart Islanders who view the marram-covered dunes as part of their heritage. Scientists argue that native dune-binding plants like pingao should replace marram to restore natural dune dynamics and support endangered species. DOC staff work to bridge the communication gap between scientific data and local sentiment. University students participate in restoration efforts, collecting soil samples and removing invasive species, celebrating Mason Bay's transformative power and its geomorphically unparalleled active dune system.
