30.document_title: Falcon of the Dawn
30.document_summary: This article chronicles the ascension of Te Atairangikaahu as the sixth Maori King in 1966, following the death of King Koroki. Te Atairangikaahu, born Princess Piki of Tainui, became the first female leader of the Kingitanga movement, a pan-tribal coalition established in the mid-19th century to counter political marginalization and land dispossession. The article traces the movement's origins and early monarchs, highlighting how Te Atairangikaahu fulfilled an ancestor's prophecy. Despite humble beginnings, she became the longest-serving head of the tribal confederation and instrumental in securing Tainui's historic 1995 raupatu settlement with the Crown. She was also the first Maori to be made a dame and helped inspire a broader Maori cultural renaissance, particularly the revival of te reo Maori.

31.text:
[Page 14] Rangatiratanga—that vexing word, promised in Te Tiriti and, Maori would say, never kept. Erimana Taniora traced its origins in his testimony at Panguru. ‘Raranga’ means to bind or weave; ‘tira’ is a group, such as a hapu. A rangatira is one whose role is to lead and unite a hapu and maintain its mana, and rangatiratanga is the process by which that happens. Rangatiratanga releases human potential—and for Taniora, this was a crucial point. If you are prevented from exercising your function in life, what chance do you have to flourish as a human being? The Waitangi Tribunal has heard this line of argument before, and has spoken strongly in its favour. In its report on the Wai 262 claim concerning Maori traditional knowledge, the tribunal wrote about the failure of governing structures in New Zealand to recognise the iwi role of guardianship or kaitiakitanga, one of the functions of rangatiratanga. The tribunal wrote: “If iwi and hapu are unable to exercise their kaitiaki obligations, they are deprived of a core aspect of their culture… Without kaitiakitanga, Maori are lost.” In his covering letter for the Wai 262 report, then chairman of the Waitangi Tribunal Justice Joe Williams laid down a gauntlet when he wrote: “ What we saw and heard in sittings over many years left us in no doubt that unless it is accepted that New Zealand has two founding cultures, not one; unless Maori culture and identity are valued in everything government says and does; and unless they are welcomed into the very centre of the way we do things in this country, nothing will change. Maori will continue to be perceived, and know they are perceived, as an alien and resented minority, a problem to be managed with a seemingly endless stream of taxpayer funded programmes, but never solved.” Solving the problem, say Ngapuhi, involves a question of honour. In 2010, when the Wai 1040 claim began, the fiery Ngapuhi matriarch Titewhai Harawira told the Waitangi Tribunal that her tupuna were bound by rules of ‘kupu mana’—your word is your bond—and they signed Te Tiriti believing the Crown would honour its word, too. “The Crown, however, has acted with deceit and dishonour, seeking to suppress us and take what it wanted, even those things we agreed to share,” she said. “We don’t want to stand here and argue about which Crown or what Government. We don’t need to. Every single one of them has been part of a lie that festers within our history.” [sidebar 1] If those words sound like anti Pakeha fanaticism, consider this statement made in 1847, a mere seven years after the Treaty was signed, in a letter to the British Colonial Office: “I am grieved beyond the power of expression at the attempted violation of the Treaty, and must never again plead the honour and integrity of Her Majesty’s Government. This appears to have been lost or never to have been possessed.” Who wrote those words of damning disappointment? The Rev Henry Williams, the missionary who translated the Treaty into Maori, explained it to the Ngapuhi chiefs, and acted as the Crown’s intermediary in persuading the chiefs to sign. [Chapter break] At this moment , New Zealand is in the midst of a constitutional review. Unlike most countries, we do not have a single constitutional document, but several, of which the Treaty of Waitangi is considered foundational. Ngapuhi assert that the country picked the wrong foundation, and that it is He Whakaputanga, not the English language Treaty with assumption of ceded sovereignty, that should be the constitutional footing on which this country rests. its To write this story, I needed to go back to the north, to the place where the foundations were laid. I suspect that to resolve the sovereignty question will require us all to ‘go back’ in some way—anathema though that is for many non Maori, whose mantra is to “put the past behind us” and who, by those words, align themselves with the discarders of history. The view from the other side of the Treaty page is, “Ma te tika te he ka tika”—we need to right the wrong. What would it mean if the tribunal were to find in favour of Ngapuhi’s claim? I cannot begin to guess, but I suspect that things would look very different in Waitangi at dawn on Independence Day. The post A Sovereign Act appeared first on New Zealand Geographic .
{}

31.document_title: Ngapuhi Sovereignty: He Whakaputanga, the Declaration of Independence, and Constitutional Foundations of New Zealand
31.document_summary: This comprehensive document collection examines Ngapuhi's assertion of sovereignty and their claim that Māori never ceded sovereignty to Britain. The materials trace Ngapuhi's political development in the early 19th century, focusing on their diplomatic engagement with European powers and the formation of Te Whakaminenga (a confederation) around 1807. Central to the narrative is He Whakaputanga (the Declaration of Independence), signed in 1835 by 34 rangatira with British Resident James Busby's facilitation, which the authors argue should serve as New Zealand's constitutional foundation rather than the Treaty of Waitangi. The documents explore the cultural and political significance of these declarations, drawing parallels to Scotland's Declaration of Arbroath, and emphasize that Ngapuhi's whakaputanga was a manifesto of self-determination asserting independence while seeking external protection. The collection includes discussion of Ngapuhi's 2010 Waitangi Tribunal claim (Wai 1040) questioning the government's authority to govern, the sacred nature of moko marks as royal seals, and the concept of rangatiratanga (chieftainship authority) as essential for Māori flourishing. It also features Rev Henry Williams' 1847 letter expressing disappointment in the Crown's violation of the Treaty, and argues that the Crown's historical dismissal of the Treaty covenant has caused 170 years of suffering.

32.document_title: Waka Jumper, Mahi and Chilly Bin Added to Oxford English Dictionary
32.document_summary: The Oxford English Dictionary has added several New Zealand words and phrases to its latest update, including "waka jumper" (a member of Parliament who switches parties during a term), "mahi" (work or activity in Māori contexts), "chilly bin" (portable insulated container), and various te reo Māori terms like "tikanga," "kapa haka," and "Aotearoan." The addition reflects the increasing use of te reo Māori in New Zealand society and media. While experts celebrate the inclusion of Māori words as a sign of language normalization, some, including Māori Language Commission chief executive Ngahiwi Apanui, expressed concerns about "Aotearoan," viewing it as inconsistent with Māori orthographic conventions. Linguists note this represents the evolving and distinctive nature of New Zealand English.

[Page 1] Māori AI expert Dr Karaitiana Taiuru shares his favourite whakataukī 2024 03 18 22:44:07+13:00 Dr Karaitiana Taiuru. Tino rangatiratanga: mō tātou, ā, mō kā uri ā muri ake nei. It is the whakataukī (Māori proverb) that means most to Māori data, AI and technology ethicist Dr Karaitiana Taiuru (Ngāi Tahu, Ngāti Kahungunu, Ngāti Toa). Translated to English, it means "the ability to create and control our destiny for generations to come". It links in well with his work and family life, Taiuru told RNZ Nights. For his work, it reminded Taiuru why he still does what he does and that there was a new generation of children who will not know life without AI and it was "our role to create the new normal for them". Taiuru applies a te ao Māori perspective to AI. https://www.rnz.co.nz/national/programmes/nig new generation of children who will not know life without AI and it was "our role to create the new normal for them". Taiuru applies a te ao Māori perspective to AI. https://www.rnz.co.nz/national/programmes/nig hts/audio/2018930609/whakatauki of the week with karaitiana taiuru Listen to the full interview on Nights "We already know that internationally, there's bias against minority peoples so what I do, in conjunction with international best practices with artificial intelligence and other technologies, is bring that Māori voice and Te Tiriti o Waitangi considerations to play." There were "a number" of cultural values that needed to be considered in terms of AI, he said. Many Māori have moko (facial tattoos) so understanding how that was considered with facial technologies was a big factor. In his personal life, the whakataukī applied to his whānau. "For me, I consider that I have an opportunity to create wealth and opportunities for my children and also for my grandchildren. "I live by that rule. I make that sure my children have the opportunities that I didn't always have, make sure they have access to education, financial resources, a home, and part of my planning in life is that my grandchildren will also have the same access and all going well in life, I should see my great grandchildren and maybe great great grandchildren whom I will also ensure that they have equal access. "And I know my children also that they consider the same sort of philosophies in life where they want to protect their whānau as well for the future." Taiuru said the whakataukī came out of working groups around the South Island when Ngāi Tahu was trying to identify a new tribal vision that would be carried into the future. It came after settlements with the Crown in 1996. "That whakataukī was the key whakataukī that came out of those hui." Related

He highlights the importance of understanding cultural factors like moko (facial tattoos) in facial recognition technology. Personally, the whakataukī guides his commitment to creating wealth and opportunities for his whānau across multiple generations, ensuring access to education, financial resources, and housing. The whakataukī originated from Ngāi Tahu working groups developing a tribal vision following the 1996 Crown settlements.

[Page 1] Te Hunga Rōia Māori co president Natalie Coates. Māori lawyers are rejecting comments by the Minister of Justice, saying "unique" court rulings recognising tikanga Māori could cost the country investment. Te Hunga Rōia Māori, the Māori Law Society, disagreed with the minister, saying tikanga Māori isn't a "bolt on" that makes New Zealand law "bespoke" in a negative sense, and it actually strengthens the rule of law. Last week, Paul Goldsmith said he was worried New Zealand was developing a "bespoke" legal system that incorporated concepts of tikanga Māori. He emphasised the government was "absolutely prepared" to legislate "over the top of judgements" it needed to, in order to provide more clarity. On behalf of the organisation of Māori lawyers, co presidents Natalie Coates and Tai Ahu have today written an open letter saying tikanga is the first law of Aotearoa and has been recognised for generations in statutes, court decisions and Treaty jurisprudence. "All legal systems are, by definition, shaped by their own histories and values. The common law itself is "bespoke" to the communities that develop it." They explain that for New Zealand, that meant a legal system grounded in both tikanga Māori and the common law tradition. "Far from being a weakness, this is a source of strength and legitimacy." The implication of the minister's comments, that tikanga was "inherently unpredictable", was wrong they said, explaining that tikanga can be and is discerned by the courts, guided by precedent, evidence and resources. "Judicial recognition of tikanga has been careful, principled, and incremental. It is anchored in the same legal standards of fairness, reasonableness, good faith, and proportionality that underpin all judicial reasoning." They said they were more disturbed that the remarks had come from the Minister of Justice, saying it was inappropriate for a member of the executive to threaten a change of legislation in the event particularly reasoning was deployed by the courts. "Such statements risk eroding public confidence in the courts and amount to a veiled threat to judicial independence a far greater danger to the rule of law than the incorporation of tikanga." The lawyers were also concerned by the minister pointing to the Marine and Coastal Area Act (MACA) legislation as an example of the government making changes to legislation. Goldsmith had told RNZ the government had already demonstrated its willingness to overturn court decisions "if required", citing the Marine and Coastal Area Act. The government is forging ahead with plans to change the law governing New Zealand's foreshore and seabed, despite a Supreme Court ruling last year that appeared to undercut the rationale for the change. Minister of Justice Paul Goldsmith. The Māori Law Society said it was "misleading" to claim the amendments were about clarification and certainty. "Framing these amendments as part of any quest for "certainty" misrepresents their actual purpose and diverts attention from the ongoing denial of Māori property rights recognised at law." They said what actually created instability was a government that routinely legislated over court decisions it doesn't like. The lawyers referenced other countries where First Nations rights or customary law were written into their constitution, such as Canada, Australia and South Africa. "None of these countries have seen investment dry up as a result. Likewise, there is no evidence that the application of tikanga is stifling investment in Aotearoa." On the contrary, they indicated Māori had a long and proven record of co investing with international partners, from the Sealord fisheries settlement to the recently announced $1 billion partnership between Waikato Tainui and Brookfield. "Te Hunga Rōia Māori rejects the suggestion that economic certainty would be maximised by excluding tikanga from our legal system." RNZ reported on Goldsmith's comments over the weekend. He told RNZ tikanga Māori was increasingly addressed in the courts and legislation, representing a "unique strand in New Zealand's legal landscape, alongside countries we compare ourselves with internationally". He said having law that recognised "who we are as a nation" and reflecting "our unique circumstances" was a good thing, but the implications of that legal development should also be considered. "A core foundation of our success as a nation is predictability in the law," he said. "To be a successful modern economy, we need to attract investment to this country domestically and internationally. "Such serious, long term investment requires predictability and certainty in our institutions." In response to the Māori Law Society, he had nothing further to add except to indicate he wasn't referring to particular examples of a loss of investment, but to a risk that should be considered. Ellis v R the role of tikanga The original comments were made by Goldsmith at an event hosted by the Law Association. Law News reported the comments had been in response to a question from the audience citing an article by New Zealand Initiative chair Roger Partridge calling for parliamentary intervention "to restore appropriate boundaries and legal certainty" following the Ellis v R decision in 2022. Goldsmith responded by referencing the government's moves on MACA, and on the issue of addressing judgements, told the audience "there'll be more in this space", reported Law News. But there were no specific examples given. Coates was also one of the lawyers who represented Peter Ellis in the successful appeal to quash his convictions, an appeal the Supreme Court ruled could continue despite his death a departure from common law norms. Coates had been brought on by Ellis' legal team to consider tikanga as part of the appeal. Under tikanga, the customary rules which govern Māori life, Ellis would have a right to clear his name or re establish his mana, even if dead. In te ao Māori, mana and reputation carries on in whakapapa, rather than an individual's life. Speaking to RNZ on Monday, Coates explained the Supreme Court had essentially confirmed tikanga as part of the common law of the country, and it could inform the development of law here. She said the judges took into account a range of factors when deciding whether the case should continue, but she didn't think tikanga was the "decisive factor." She acknowledged it was significant because the Supreme Court articulated it clearly, but in her opinion it wasn't "new" and thinks the significance or the effect of the ruling was over inflated. "We've got cases dating back to not long after courts were established in Aotearoa recognising custom in various different ways." She said people cite the case as a "turn the wold around" type case but it didn't "break the wheel" and "send our whole legal system into chaos." Coates didn't know what else the minister might be considering when it came to legislating "over the top", but that was what was concerning at a broad level, she said. "It's just kind of this general veiled threat around overturning cases that stand on or emphasise tikanga, and so that's sort of concerning in terms of the boundaries of what the executive should be saying to the courts." She understood tikanga without us having to explain it and when a hospital midwife made her negative comment about our choice to keep the placenta, the carer corrected her without her or us losing face, which is a skilled and culturally appropriate way to correct a mistake of that nature," the mother stated. A former midwife with no relation to this birth, now, a well child nurse Sharron Wipiti said it was "crazy" that there were cultural breaches because she only knew tikanga as being a strict practice. When Wipiti was younger, she said there was no consideration for tikanga when a māmā was in labour. "You got on the bed, you had your baby, and they just got rid of the placenta. I never knew there was such thing as keeping the placenta." But it is something she had learnt since "regaining being Māori," which is what got her and another midwife to create the Hapū Wānanga in Taranaki a programme to help wāhine hapū to reclaim traditional birthing practices. Regardless, Wipiti said consent everything. Communication and environment a point of concern The complaint stated the strategies staff and the obstetric used to "motivate" the woman to deliver her baby were damaging. Multiple staff members said the tone and manner of the experienced registrar were not unusual but can be taken as "unsympathetic" in a situation. The interventions were necessary, the mother agreed, but raised concerns around the need for tikanga of manaakitanga. 38.document_title: Health NZ Southern Made Multiple Breaches During Māori Mum's Labour - HDC Report
38.document_summary: A Deputy Health and Disability Commissioner report details multiple breaches by Health NZ Southern during a Māori mother's labour in 2017. The hospital staff dismissed the mother's cultural wishes regarding placenta retention and proceeded with an episiotomy without proper informed consent, leaving her feeling violated. Key breaches included: lack of consent for umbilical cord blood testing (violating Right 7(10) of the Code), failure to respect cultural safety and te ao Māori beliefs regarding tapu (sacred) practices, and inadequate communication during emergency procedures. The mother developed PTSD symptoms and received ACC compensation. In response, Health NZ Southern implemented nine changes including cultural safety training, new Māori cultural education roles, amended cord blood testing policies requiring informed consent, and the introduction of a 'Hua Oranga' midwifery performance appraisal tool to improve cultural competency and respectful care.

39.document_title: Trans and Non-Binary New Zealanders: Violence, Discrimination, and Health Support Framework
39.document_summary: This comprehensive document combines research findings and policy recommendations addressing the crisis facing trans and non-binary New Zealanders. The Counting Ourselves survey of 2,631 participants (56% non-binary, 22% trans men, 22% trans women) reveals: 19% threatened with physical violence in the past four years, 8% experienced deliberate physical violence, and 77% reported high psychological distress—six times the general population rate. Over half seriously considered suicide and one in ten attempted it. Trans women and disabled individuals face disproportionately higher rates of violence, with 40% experiencing sexual violence. The document outlines a comprehensive health and support framework based on five key principles: Mauri (health, education, housing services), Mana (legal gender change, gender-affirming healthcare access), Tapu (expanded healthcare availability, violence protection), and Tikanga (anti-discrimination, healthcare worker training). It provides mental health and support resources including crisis helplines (1737, Lifeline 0800 543 354), sexual violence services, and specialized community support. Personal accounts illustrate the pervasive impact of anti-trans sentiment on daily life, employment, housing, and mental health, with 16% relocating for safety and nearly one in five experiencing homelessness.

41.document_title: Supreme Court allows appeal of customary marine title judgment
41.document_summary: The Supreme Court has allowed an appeal of a Court of Appeal decision regarding customary marine title (CMT) under the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act, calling the previous ruling "unduly narrow." The Supreme Court will restate the Section 58 test to better reflect the act's reconciliatory purpose and recognition of Māori rights under the Treaty of Waitangi. Key issues addressed include: (1) who "holds" an area in accordance with tikanga, requiring an integrated relationship with the seascape; (2) proof of exclusive use and occupation from 1840 to present without substantial interruption. Applicants must first prove they hold the area according to tikanga and have continuously used it since 1840. If successful, the burden shifts to opponents to prove the claim is invalid. Non-substantial interference should not prevent CMT granting.

1.fileDescription: Kaitiakitanga is a foundational Māori concept of guardianship and environmental stewardship rooted in the worldview that humans are part of nature. A kaitiaki is a guardian recognized by tangata whenua to care for natural areas such as lakes, forests, and waterways. Traditional conservation practices include temporary rāhui (resource restrictions), use of the lunar calendar (maramataka) for planting and harvesting, sustainable hunting and fishing, and blessing of mauri stones by tohunga (priests). Key spiritual concepts include mana (spiritual power), tapu (spiritual restriction), and mauri (life force). Today, kaitiakitanga is experiencing renewal as iwi (tribes) restore ecosystems and apply traditional knowledge in modern contexts. Practical examples include Ngāi Tahu's guardianship of pounamu resources, Ngāti Toa's fishery restoration at Pukerua Bay, and multi-tribal efforts to stop river pollution and protect endangered species. The document outlines challenges in collaborating with non-Māori stakeholders and details legislative frameworks such as the Resource Management Act 1991 and Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004 that incorporate kaitiakitanga principles. Kaitiakitanga offers perspectives on environmental stewardship and kinship with nature, enabling Māori to fulfill ancestral responsibilities while contributing to broader environmental sustainability.

chunkHighlights.text: Tiaki

The word tiaki is the basis of the longer word kaitiakitanga. Tiaki means to guard. It also means to preserve, foster, protect and shelter. So, notions of care and protection are at the heart of kaitiakitanga, and give
it its conservation ethic.

chunkHighlights.text: By Te Ahukaramū Charles Royal

Understanding kaitiakitanga Kaitiakitanga means guardianship and
protection. It is a way of managing the environment, based on the Māori world view. A kaitiaki is a guardian. This can be a person or group that cares for an area such as a lake or forest. They are given that role by the local iwi . Māori world view In the Māori world view, people are closely connected to the land and nature. Kaitiakitanga is based on this idea of humans as part of the natural world. Traditional practices In the past, people followed traditional practices when they were hunting, fishing, growing or finding food. These helped them to care for the environment. They included: temporary bans (rāhui) on taking food from an area using the lunar calendar (maramataka) to decide when to plant and harvest taking only what was needed hunting and fishing only for food, not as sport using bird snares at the right time – for example, not when the birds were breeding. Mana, tapu and mauri Mana means spiritual power. If a forest has mana , it will have plenty of flowers, fruit and birds. Tapu can mean spiritual restriction. Sometimes rāhui (restrictions) are needed to help the mana of the forest. A rāhui might stop people taking birds, fish or fruit from a certain area, or at a certain time. Mauri means life force. This must be protected in forests, rivers, gardens, lakes and the sea. Special mauri stones, which tohunga (priests) said prayers over, were used to preserve this force. Kaitiakitanga today Today there is growing interest in kaitiakitanga. Iwi are restoring their environment and culture, and using traditional ideas in the modern world. Ngāi Tahu are guardians of pounamu (greenstone) in the South Island. Te Āti Awa ki Taranaki made a claim to the government to stop pollution in their fishing areas. Four iwi (Ngāti Kahungunu, Rangitāne, Muaūpoko and Ngāti Raukawa) have come together to stop the Manawatū River being polluted. The Te Rarawa people are working to save the kūkupa (New Zealand pigeon). Kaitiakitanga has also been included in some laws,
such as the Resource Management Act 1991.

9.fileDescription: Kennedy Warne reflects on his deep personal connection to the Hauraki Gulf in New Zealand, tracing memories from childhood through his grandfather's swordfishing boat. He explores the concept of guardianship and stewardship through the Inuit legend of the mother of the sea—a story about how people's disrespect for the ocean causes the sea's bounty to disappear until a shaman restores harmony by combing her hair. Warne connects this ancient wisdom to the Māori concept of kaitiakitanga, arguing it represents a profound stewardship that goes beyond mere resource management. He observes a growing movement of individuals taking environmental responsibility into their own hands, becoming "ministers of the environment" by caring for wetlands, forests, and oceans. The essay emphasizes humanity's forgotten relationship with the sea and calls for a return to reverence and respect for the natural world.

[Page 3] From 1865, the government acquired hundreds of thousands of hectares of Tairāwhiti land by force. When Ngāti Porou resisted land sales, officials used the Native Lands Act to confiscate vast chunks of land—by splitting it into individual titles, or tying it up in complicated leases. Since then, permissive land use legislation and targeted subsidies have centred profits for landowners or leaseholders—mainly Pākehā or overseas investors in farming or forestry. In the early 1900s the land was burnt off for farming. When the pasture slipped off the hills it was replanted in pine. But this is some of the softest, steepest land in the world. Every few decades, when the pine is harvested, it’s like pushing on a wound. Clocking that cycle, as well as poor official oversight and increasingly severe storms driven by the climate crisis, many locals were not surprised when Cyclone Gabrielle tore strips off bare hillsides in February last year, pulling swathes of pine plantation down with it. Afterwards, former National minister Hekia Parata, herself Ngāti Porou, led a ministerial inquiry into land use in Tairāwhiti. Her report calls the use of land here an “environmental disaster, hiding in plain sight”. The report recommends a credit system to incentivise native forests, investment in climate adaptation, tighter forestry legislation and support for Māori to use their land. Transition to more sustainable land use, it says, is urgent; the list of ills reads almost like a post mortem. “Sedimentation from more than a thousand untreated gullies, trees, logs and slash off hills that should never be plantation planted or clear felled, waterways choked with debris flows, riverbeds aggraded, coastlines suffocated and dangerous, roads and bridges unfit, unpassable, and many broken. ## Te Tikanga o 'Kaitiakitanga'

Ko **kaitiakitanga** tētahi kupu Māori e whakamārama ana i te **tiakitanga, te ārai, te pupuri, me te manaaki** i te taiao — he ara whakahaere i te taiao, i ahu mai i te tirohanga ao Māori. [[1]](cite://1/1)

### Te Hanganga o te Kupu

Ko te kurupae **'kai'** e tohu ana ki tētahi tangata e mahi ana i tētahi mahi. Nō reira, ko te **kaitiaki** he tangata, he rōpū rānei e tiaki ana, e ārai ana, e pupuri ana i tētahi taonga, i tētahi wāhi rānei. [[2]](cite://2/1) Ko ngā atua o te ao tūroa ngā kaitiaki tuatahi — ko Tāne, hei tauira, ko ia te kaitiaki o te ngahere. Ko ērā atu kaitiaki katoa e whai ana i tēnā tauira. [[2]](cite://2/2)

### Te Hononga ki te Ao Tūroa

I roto i te tirohanga ao Māori, he tino tūhono ngā tāngata ki te whenua me te taiao. Ko kaitiakitanga te kōrero o tēnā hononga i roto i te ao hou. [[3]](cite://3/1) He āhua rerekē tēnei i te tiakitanga o te ao Pākehā — i te ao Māori, ko ngā tāngata he wāhanga o te taiao, ā, he hononga ōritetanga tō rāua. [[4]](cite://4/1)

### Ngā Tikanga ā-Mahi

I ngā rā o mua, ko ēnei ngā tikanga i whāia e ngā tāngata hei tiaki i te taiao: [[1]](cite://1/2)

- **Rāhui** — he aukati ūnga ki tētahi rohe ki te tiaki i ngā rauemi
- **Maramataka** — he hātepe marama hei tohu i ngā wā tika mō te māra me te hauhake
- Ko te tango noa iho i ngā mea e hiahiatia ana — kaua te nui rawa atu
- Ko te hī ika me te mahi tahi i ngā kararehe mō te kai anake, kaua hei hākinakina

### Ngā Ariā Tūāhuru

E toru ngā ariā matua e hāngai ana ki kaitiakitanga: [[1]](cite://1/3)

- **Mana** — te mana wairua; ki te ora te ngahere, ka tipu ngā hua, ka rere ngā manu
- **Tapu** — te ārai wairua; ko ngā rāhui tētahi āhua o tēnei
- **Mauri** — te mauri ora; me tiaki tēnei i ngā ngahere, awa, māra, roto me te moana

### Kaitiakitanga i Ēnā Rā

Ehara kaitiakitanga i te mea mō te taiao anake — ka taea anō te āta tiaki i ngā taonga tuku iho, pērā i ngā **korowai**, **mere pounamu**, me ngā **pukapuka whakapapa**. Ko tēnā taonga, nā tēnā tangata i tīmata, ka huri hei taonga nō ōna uri katoa, ā, ka tiakina e tētahi kaitiaki i runga i te ingoa o te rōpū. [[5]](cite://5/1)

### Kaitiakitanga i roto i ngā Ture

Kua whakaurua kaitiakitanga ki roto i ētahi ture o Aotearoa. Ko te **Resource Management Act 1991** e whakamārama ana i kaitiakitanga hei 'te whakamahi o te tiakitanga e ngā tangata whenua o tētahi rohe e ai ki ngā tikanga Māori mō ngā rauemi ā-taiao me ngā rauemi ā-tinana; ā, koia anō te tikanga o te āta tiaki.' [[6]](cite://6/1)

Ka āhei anō a kaitiakitanga ki ērā kore-Māori ki te whakaaro anō mō tōna hononga ki te taiao, me tōna ahuatanga whakamahana i tēnei ao e tūkino ana te taiao. [[7]](cite://7/1)

---

He pātai āku: kei te hiahia koe ki te mōhio atu mō ngā tikanga ā-mahi o kaitiakitanga i ēnei rā — arā, ngā mahi a ngā iwi i tēnei wā hei tiaki i ō rātou taonga?

[Page 1] By Te Ahukaramū Charles Royal Understanding kaitiakitanga Kaitiakitanga means guardianship and protection. It is a way of managing the environment, based on the Māori world view. A kaitiaki is a guardian. This can be a person or group that cares for an area such as a lake or forest. They are given that role by the local iwi . Māori world view In the Māori world view, people are closely connected to the land and nature. Kaitiakitanga is based on this idea of humans as part of the natural world. Traditional practices In the past, people followed traditional practices when they were hunting, fishing, growing or finding food. These helped them to care for the environment. They included: temporary bans (rāhui) on taking food from an area using the lunar calendar (maramataka) to decide when to plant and harvest taking only what was needed hunting and fishing only for food, not as sport using bird snares at the right time for example, not when the birds were breeding. Mana, tapu and mauri Mana means spiritual power. If a forest has mana , it will have plenty of flowers, fruit and birds. Tapu can mean spiritual restriction. Sometimes rāhui (restrictions) are needed to help the mana of the forest. A rāhui might stop people taking birds, fish or fruit from a certain area, or at a certain time. Mauri means life force. This must be protected in forests, rivers, gardens, lakes and the sea. Special mauri stones, which tohunga (priests) said prayers over, were used to preserve this force. Kaitiakitanga today Today there is growing interest in kaitiakitanga. Iwi are restoring their environment and culture, and using traditional ideas in the modern world. Ngāi Tahu are guardians of pounamu (greenstone) in the South Island. Te Āti Awa ki Taranaki made a claim to the government to stop pollution in their fishing areas. Four iwi (Ngāti Kahungunu, Rangitāne, Muaūpoko and Ngāti Raukawa) have come together to stop the Manawatū River being polluted. The Te Rarawa people are working to save the kūkupa (New Zealand pigeon). Kaitiakitanga has also been included in some laws, such as the Resource Management Act 1991. Kaitiakitanga means guardianship, protection, preservation or sheltering. It is a way of managing the environment, based on the traditional Māori world view.

1.document_title: Kaitiakitanga: Māori Guardianship, Environmental Stewardship, and Traditional Conservation Practices
1.document_summary: Kaitiakitanga is a foundational Māori concept of guardianship and environmental stewardship rooted in the worldview that humans are part of nature. A kaitiaki is a guardian recognized by tangata whenua to care for natural areas such as lakes, forests, and waterways. Traditional conservation practices include temporary rāhui (resource restrictions), use of the lunar calendar (maramataka) for planting and harvesting, sustainable hunting and fishing, and blessing of mauri stones by tohunga (priests). Key spiritual concepts include mana (spiritual power), tapu (spiritual restriction), and mauri (life force). Today, kaitiakitanga is experiencing renewal as iwi (tribes) restore ecosystems and apply traditional knowledge in modern contexts. Practical examples include Ngāi Tahu's guardianship of pounamu resources, Ngāti Toa's fishery restoration at Pukerua Bay, and multi-tribal efforts to stop river pollution and protect endangered species. The document outlines challenges in collaborating with non-Māori stakeholders and details legislative frameworks such as the Resource Management Act 1991 and Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004 that incorporate kaitiakitanga principles. Kaitiakitanga offers perspectives on environmental stewardship and kinship with nature, enabling Māori to fulfill ancestral responsibilities while contributing to broader environmental sustainability.

2.text:
[Page 11] Legislation Kaitiakitanga has been included in some legislation. The Resource Management Act 1991 aims to enable sustainable management of environmental resources. It states that people managing resources under the act must take kaitiakitanga into account. The act defines kaitiakitanga as ‘the exercise of guardianship by the tangata whenua of an area in accordance with tikanga Māori in relation to natural and physical resources; and includes the ethic of stewardship’. Kaitiakitanga was also included in the Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004, where it has the same meaning.

13.document_title: Ngā Tamariki: Māori Childhood, Education, and Youth Development - Traditional Practices to Contemporary Change
13.document_summary: This comprehensive document explores Māori childhood, education, and youth development across traditional, colonial, and contemporary periods in New Zealand. It examines traditional Māori child-rearing practices where children were raised collectively by extended whānau and hapū, cherished as the tribe's future, and educated through observation, play, and formal instruction at whare wānanga. Traditional practices included birth rituals like the tohi ceremony and the tamaiti whāngai (customary fostering) system, where grandparents and extended family served as primary educators. European influence through mission schools (early 19th century) and native schools (1867) transformed Māori childhood by introducing literacy, English language, new discipline methods, and European values. Mid-20th century urbanization disrupted traditional family structures, leading to health disparities and social challenges. The document addresses contemporary issues including child abuse and describes legislative reforms, particularly the 1989 Children, Young Persons and their Families Act, which incorporated Māori customs into child welfare systems through family group conferences. Modern cultural preservation efforts include kōhanga reo (Māori-language pre-schools) established in 1982, kura kaupapa Māori (Māori-language schools), and iwi and hapū initiatives providing scholarships and cultural immersion for Māori youth.

14.document_title: New Zealand Rivers: Comprehensive Guide to Geography, Ecology, Culture, and Conservation
14.document_summary:
This comprehensive document explores New Zealand's extensive river systems across both the North and South Islands, covering over 180,000 kilometres of mapped rivers including the Waikato (425 km) and Clutha (largest by volume). It details river formation through high rainfall, glacial activity, and geological processes, describing distinct river types: deep, fast-flowing rivers in the North Island hills and wide, braided rivers in the South Island's east.

The document emphasizes the profound cultural significance of rivers to Māori people, including their roles in exploration, transportation, food sources, and spiritual traditions involving taniwha (river spirits). It documents European settlement impacts including military conquest, transport use, 19th-century gold rushes, and industrial/agricultural pollution.

The content examines ecological transformations over two centuries, detailing how introduced species like rainbow trout, brown trout, and salmon impacted native fish populations. It describes the creation of eight artificial lakes along the Waikato River through hydroelectric dams (1945-1970s) and habitat loss through forest clearance. Conservation efforts are discussed, from late 19th-century catchment protection through the 1941 Soil Conservation Act to the 1981 Wild and Scenic Rivers Amendment protecting 12 rivers.

Modern challenges including invasive species like didymo, dairy farming impacts on water quality, and off-road vehicle use are addressed. The document highlights Māori guardianship cases involving the Waikato and Whanganui rivers, explores rivers' cultural significance through 19th and 20th-century art, literature, and film, and examines contemporary management practices including jet boat tourism, riparian protection through native tree planting, and regional council monitoring.

15.document_title: Kaumātua – The Role of Māori Elders in Traditional and Modern Society
15.document_summary: Kaumātua are respected elders in Māori society who serve as vital storehouses of tribal knowledge, genealogy, and traditions. They hold multiple roles including guardians of tikanga (Māori customs), leaders of whānau (family) and rūnanga (tribal councils), nurturers of children, and dispute resolvers. Traditionally, kaumātua raised grandchildren, arranged marriages, and provided guidance on ceremonial and daily matters, transmitting cultural knowledge through storytelling, waiata (songs), and mentorship. The document explores their significance in traditional Māori stories (Māui, Tāwhaki, Toi) where they appear as knowledge keepers and nurturers. While life expectancy changes have affected the age threshold for kaumātua status (historically 30s-40s, now typically mid-60s+), their role remains vital. In modern times, urbanization in the 20th century caused cultural dislocation and threatened knowledge transmission. Contemporary solutions include community initiatives such as Te Arataki Manu Kōrero o Tainui and kaumātua flats, which preserve cultural knowledge, maintain elders' active participation in community life, and sustain their leadership roles. Despite challenges, kaumātua remain essential to Māori cultural identity and tribal mana (prestige).

Protecting historic and spiritual sites like Mahinapua seems straightforward, as does finding ways for mana whenua to have leadership roles in the care of local conservation areas, including restoration of mahinga kai sites. Then there’s the customary harvesting of kai and resources, like plants for rongoā or weaving, that is essential for cultural survival, but which is only permitted on conservation land on an ad hoc basis.

16.document_title: Stewardship Land Reclassification in New Zealand: Conservation, Māori Rights, and the Old Ghost Road
16.document_summary: This comprehensive document collection examines New Zealand's stewardship land—nine percent of Aotearoa's total land area—through interconnected narratives spanning conservation policy, indigenous rights, and economic development. The collection begins with the Old Ghost Road project in the Mokihinui Gorge, illustrating how stewardship land's lower protection status both threatened and enabled conservation initiatives, ultimately generating $4 million annually for local communities after Meridian Energy abandoned its proposed dam project. The documents trace the government's 2021 fast-tracked reclassification process, which proposed appointing expert panels to assess stewardship land within eight months. This initiative sparked significant controversy, particularly from Ngāi Tahu iwi, who filed urgent High Court proceedings citing consultation breaches and Treaty of Waitangi violations. The historical context reveals how the Crown's 1859 acquisition of the West Coast from Poutini Ngāi Tahu for £300 left the iwi with only 4,000 hectares despite claiming 151,757 hectares, with 87% of their territory now managed by DOC with minimal iwi input. The collection explores the tension between traditional conservation frameworks and contemporary approaches that integrate mātauranga (Māori knowledge) and recognize Māori cultural values extending beyond preservation to include economic and commercial use on ancestral land. Through case studies such as Lake Mahinapua, the documents examine how mana whenua and national assessment panels are collaboratively developing integrated conservation models that respect rangatiratanga while addressing concerns about mining interests and the Stockton Coal Mine on Denniston Plateau.

17.text:
[Page 9] If everyone foraged, would we strip the land? Wellington author Johanna Knox (Ngāti Tukorehe, Ngāti Raukawa ki te Tonga, Ngāti Ranginui, Tangata Tiriti), who wrote the book on foraging in New Zealand, thinks that eating the environment is a pretty good way of reconnecting with it. She reckons foraging could resurrect the idea of the commons—not just the tragedy of it. It could bring back the concept of places that are used and maintained by people for each other—and for future generations. That idea has been largely lost from the Pākehā world, but it’s remained intact in te ao Māori. Despite the destruction of traditional food gathering areas, despite the theft of land, the depletion of resources, and the loss of kōrero about how different species are prepared—despite all of that, the philosophy of how to gather food sustainably remains intact. It’s the concept of kaitiakitanga. “A big difference between Western environmentalism and Māori kaitiakitanga is how they see humans in the environment,” says Knox. “So in Pākehā conservation, it’s like, ‘We must keep these areas pristine. Nobody can take anything from here,’ but in te ao Māori it’s like, ‘People are part of the landscape. It’s a reciprocal relationship, so of course we’re taking stuff.’ McKenzie and Mikhail Shatura, head chef at downtown Auckland restaurant Ahi, taste the morning’s foraging. Shatura assembles a dish of quail, chickweed, huruhuru whenua and ureure. Foraged ingredients don’t form the bulk of a dish, says McKenzie, but they bring the flavours of a place onto the plate. “These are supporting characters,” he says. “So I come at foraging from the perspective that if you get right out there and involve yourself in the landscape—which means taking what you can, but respectfully and sustainably and at the same time giving back—that’s just a really good way to do things.” Raglan ecologist and rongoā practitioner Mahuru Wilcox (Ngāti Awa, Ngāti Ranginui) echoes Knox. She forages native plants traditionally used for medicinal purposes for her small business, Hau Botanicals. “How can you teach people to value something if you can’t connect to it?” she asks. “These [plants] are valued because they were important as kai or as rongoā or they were important as ancestors, as tūpuna. If you’re really thinking of our world around us as our tūpuna, as our ancestors, how would you respect your tūpuna? So using those principles for how you connect.” Even in the most densely populated parts of the city, plants move through the cycles of the year. Retreating into their roots to conserve water, springing forth with new shoots. Exploding into colour for a week or two. “It’s such a reminder in your daily life as a human that everything has a season,” says Wilcox. Over time, you start to see it: the living calendar, the shifts in weather and sunlight reflected in the plants changing, day by day, in all the gaps between the fixed and immobile parts of the city.

17.document_title: The Weed Eaters: Urban and Rural Foraging in New Zealand
17.document_summary: This comprehensive article explores the growing practice of foraging in New Zealand, examining both urban and rural contexts. The piece follows multiple narratives: in Auckland, forager Bella Burgess leads a Facebook community group on Maungawhau/Mount Eden, teaching participants to identify and harvest edible wild plants including vetch, wild brassica, pūhā, nasturtium, oxalis, and onion weed while emphasizing ethical foraging practices. In Canterbury, Peter Langlands scouts for elderflower and wild parsnips for restaurants, demonstrating how roadsides and berms provide abundant biodiversity and foraged ingredients. The article features interviews with professional foragers like Nate McKenzie and Rico Birndt who maintain sustainable harvesting practices. It highlights the cultural and philosophical dimensions of foraging, connecting it to Māori philosophy of kaitiakitanga—a reciprocal relationship with the environment—and contrasting this with Western conservation approaches. The piece explores the underlying human desire for self-reliance and independence from modern systems, noting how the surge in foraging interest during COVID-19 lockdowns reflects deeper needs for connection and resilience. The article showcases how edible plants grow abundantly in plain sight throughout New Zealand's towns and cities, challenging cultural hesitation about harvesting from public spaces while advocating for sustainable practices and "feral parks" instead of manicured lawns.

Recognition from others, knowing one’s worth, a sense of mana—these are as essential to human wholeness as food, security and companionship, the previous three. Kearns gave Maslow’s category a further spin, speaking of the mutual esteem that grows between people and place. He spoke of how repeated engagements lead to pride and care of a space, further creating a sense of belonging. In time, an ethic of kaitiakitanga, or guardianship, develops. Of all nights to hear that message—only an hour earlier I had thrown in my lot with the Friends, paid my membership and offered my services. I could see a direct cause and effect at work. 18.document_title: Pilgrim at Oakley Creek: Urban Nature, Memory, and Human Flourishing
18.document_summary: This comprehensive collection of interconnected essays by Kennedy Warne explores the transformative power of Oakley Creek (Te Auaunga) in Auckland, New Zealand, examining it through multiple lenses: personal pilgrimage, human psychology, historical memory, and place attachment. The work chronicles Warne's six-month photographic journey from winter to summer solstice, inspired by contemplative writers and Zen philosophy, demonstrating how mindful observation of urban nature fosters deep ecological connection. The essays apply Maslow's hierarchy of needs to show how urban green spaces fulfill fundamental human requirements—from physiological exercise and emotional security to social belonging and self-actualization—while highlighting the critical importance of preserving these spaces as Auckland's open space availability declines. Through archival research and personal narrative, Warne traces the layered histories converging at Oakley Creek, including indigenous Māori heritage, colonial discoveries, the legacy of Carrington Psychiatric Hospital, and the story of patient Rolfe Hattaway whose artistic vision inspired modernist artists. The collection advocates for kaitiakitanga (guardianship) and "locaphilia"—binding oneself to place through loving attention, storytelling, and ceremonial engagement—demonstrating how individuals can expand a place's narrative and experience meaningful homecoming through relationship-based environmental engagement.

19.document_title: Between a Rock and a Hard Place
19.document_summary: This article examines the contentious Denniston Plateau mining debate, which pits resource extraction against environmental preservation. With 6.1 million tonnes of bituminous coal beneath a 150-hectare site, the proposed open-cast mine would generate 14 million tonnes of CO2 emissions when burned—equivalent to New Zealand's annual dairy herd emissions. The article explores the tension between economic benefits ($46 million in salaries for a struggling West Coast region) and environmental costs, including mercury, selenium, arsenic emissions, and climate change contributions. It presents three perspectives: exploitation versus preservation, and a Māori concept of land as taonga (treasure and resource), emphasizing guardianship (kaitiakitanga) and respect for the land's living essence. The author questions whether this traditional approach might offer a less-destructive path to prosperity.

Warne connects this ancient wisdom to the Māori concept of kaitiakitanga, arguing it represents a profound stewardship that goes beyond mere resource management. He observes a growing movement of individuals taking environmental responsibility into their own hands, becoming "ministers of the environment" by caring for wetlands, forests, and oceans. The essay emphasizes humanity's forgotten relationship with the sea and calls for a return to reverence and respect for the natural world.

21.document_title: Eyes in the Land: Dune Lakes, Wetlands, and Indigenous Stewardship in Northland
21.document_summary: This comprehensive collection explores New Zealand's dune lakes and wetlands in Northland, examining their ecological significance and cultural importance to iwi communities. The articles document indigenous stewardship and scientific conservation efforts, featuring Lake Ngatu and NIWA scientist Paul Champion's research on unique flora including kuta sedge and tuatara plants. Key threats include invasive species such as hornwort, Egeria densa, Gambusia affinis, and grass carp. The collection emphasizes kaitiakitanga (environmental stewardship) as the foundation for restoration, incorporating ecological and cultural dimensions. Monitoring strategies using the LakeSPI bio-assessment tool are detailed, alongside management approaches including herbicide applications and freshwater mussel restoration. The narrative incorporates the Māori proverb "Te roto tāpokopoko, he wai whakahuihui, he pukenga ora" (a dune lake is an oasis that gathers and grows life) and explores te mana o te repo (the mana of wetlands) as intermediaries between Tāne (forests) and Tangaroa (seas). Community engagement initiatives like "Get to Know Your Dune Lake" days link lake conservation to Māori traditions and reconnect communities with their ancestral lands.

22.document_summary: This comprehensive document collection explores the ecological, cultural, and conservation significance of kōura (New Zealand freshwater crayfish) through multiple interconnected narratives. It traces the historical role of kōura in Māori diet and culture, documenting how Māori ancestors practiced kaitiakitanga (environmental stewardship) by translocating crayfish across the country for centuries to ensure food security. The document examines kōura's ecological importance as ecosystem engineers that control invasive species and restore waterway health. It details the dramatic decline of kōura populations due to trout predation, forest clearing, invasive species (particularly brown bullhead catfish and marron), and water quality degradation, with some populations experiencing up to 99% decline. The collection highlights contemporary restoration efforts led by iwi and freshwater biologists using adapted traditional harvesting methods like the tau kōura technique. It features innovative approaches including John Hollows' professional kōura farming operations in Southland wetlands, which demonstrate sustainable aquaculture, and Kāti Huirapa rūnanga's initiatives to reconnect whānau with traditional food sources. The document emphasizes that mātauranga (Māori knowledge) remains essential for freshwater conservation and advocates for transferring ecosystem management responsibility back to indigenous communities.

23.document_title: New Zealand's Eel Crisis: Conservation, Māori Guardianship, and the Fight to Restore Tuna Migration
23.document_summary: This comprehensive collection examines the critical decline of New Zealand's eel populations (tuna) and conservation efforts to restore migration pathways. Eels, which have sustained Māori culture for generations as relations and ancestors, face unprecedented threats from hydroelectric dams, river barriers, turbines, and water intakes. Key narratives include researchers monitoring glass eel migrations on the Ashley River, Kāti Huirapa and Kāti Irakehu whānau's traditional guardianship at Wairewa/Lake Forsyth, and Ngāti Manawa iwi's struggle to protect tuna in the Rangitāiki River despite multiple dams. The articles detail mitigation strategies including trap-and-transfer programs, fish-friendly turbines, bypass pipes, gravity gates, and community-led fish ladder installations. They highlight dedicated individuals like Maurice Toetoe and Willie Tai, who have rescued and transported thousands of eels annually. A central tension emerges between New Zealand's renewable energy goals—seeking 70% increased production by 2050—and the imperative to protect culturally significant eel populations. The collection emphasizes that eels represent integral aspects of Māori identity, spirituality, and survival, requiring power companies and policymakers to implement lasting solutions beyond temporary interventions.

24.text:
[Page 12] Beyond these customary conceptions of Māori culture, there is the question of economic and commercial use. One of the core principles of Western conservation—protecting land against human intervention—does not map to Māori values regarding the natural world. You descend from the land through whakapapa, and your livelihood and survival depend upon that land, too. In the modern world, this aspect of the culture can take the form of iwi businesses, whose profits go back into each tribe. The preference is for those businesses to happen on ancestral land. Why? To combat urbanisation, and fragmentation. Places of cultural significance—your home marae, where your dead are buried, where knowledge is passed on—those places are often a long way from good jobs. On Te Tai Poutini, the median annual income is $26,400, and the total population decreased between 2013 and 2018. [Chapter Break]

24.document_title: Stewardship Land Reclassification in New Zealand: Conservation, Māori Rights, and the Old Ghost Road
24.document_summary: This comprehensive document collection examines New Zealand's stewardship land—nine percent of Aotearoa's total land area—through interconnected narratives spanning conservation policy, indigenous rights, and economic development. The collection begins with the Old Ghost Road project in the Mokihinui Gorge, illustrating how stewardship land's lower protection status both threatened and enabled conservation initiatives, ultimately generating $4 million annually for local communities after Meridian Energy abandoned its proposed dam project. The documents trace the government's 2021 fast-tracked reclassification process, which proposed appointing expert panels to assess stewardship land within eight months. This initiative sparked significant controversy, particularly from Ngāi Tahu iwi, who filed urgent High Court proceedings citing consultation breaches and Treaty of Waitangi violations. The historical context reveals how the Crown's 1859 acquisition of the West Coast from Poutini Ngāi Tahu for £300 left the iwi with only 4,000 hectares despite claiming 151,757 hectares, with 87% of their territory now managed by DOC with minimal iwi input. The collection explores the tension between traditional conservation frameworks and contemporary approaches that integrate mātauranga (Māori knowledge) and recognize Māori cultural values extending beyond preservation to include economic and commercial use on ancestral land. Through case studies such as Lake Mahinapua, the documents examine how mana whenua and national assessment panels are collaboratively developing integrated conservation models that respect rangatiratanga while addressing concerns about mining interests and the Stockton Coal Mine on Denniston Plateau.

25.text:
[Page 4] Ngāti Kuri, another iwi from the Far North, has been on a similar journey of restoration. Wayne Petera, Ngāti Kuri’s coordinator for wai māori (freshwater), tells me that his people are awakening to the importance of the dune lakes in their rohe, and to their role as kaitiaki. Petera says the kaitiaki responsibility is an ancestral mantle laid on the shoulders of each generation. “We have no choice in the matter,” he says. “Mana requires that we act.” On the basis that Ngāti Kuri has existed for close to a thousand years, Petera says the iwi has decided it must have a thousand year vision for itself and its environment, lakes included. “We recognise that if we are the people we say we are, then we have a deep responsibility to ensure the life and well being of all of these ecological gems,” he says.

It is the whakataukī (Māori proverb) that means most to Māori data, AI and technology ethicist Dr Karaitiana Taiuru (Ngāi Tahu, Ngāti Kahungunu, Ngāti Toa). Translated to English, it means "the ability to create and control our destiny for generations to come". It links in well with his work and family life, Taiuru told RNZ Nights. For his work, it reminded Taiuru why he still does what he does and that there was a new generation of children who will not know life without AI and it was "our role to create the new normal for them". Taiuru applies a te ao Māori perspective to AI. https://www.rnz.co.nz/national/programmes/nig new generation of children who will not know life without AI and it was "our role to create the new normal for them". Taiuru applies a te ao Māori perspective to AI. https://www.rnz.co.nz/national/programmes/nig hts/audio/2018930609/whakatauki of the week with karaitiana taiuru Listen to the full interview on Nights "We already know that internationally, there's bias against minority peoples so what I do, in conjunction with international best practices with artificial intelligence and other technologies, is bring that Māori voice and Te Tiriti o Waitangi considerations to play." There were "a number" of cultural values that needed to be considered in terms of AI, he said. Many Māori have moko (facial tattoos) so understanding how that was considered with facial technologies was a big factor. In his personal life, the whakataukī applied to his whānau. "For me, I consider that I have an opportunity to create wealth and opportunities for my children and also for my grandchildren. "I live by that rule. I make that sure my children have the opportunities that I didn't always have, make sure they have access to education, financial resources, a home, and part of my planning in life is that my grandchildren will also have the same access and all going well in life, I should see my great grandchildren and maybe great great grandchildren whom I will also ensure that they have equal access. "And I know my children also that they consider the same sort of philosophies in life where they want to protect their whānau as well for the future." Taiuru said the whakataukī came out of working groups around the South Island when Ngāi Tahu was trying to identify a new tribal vision that would be carried into the future. It came after settlements with the Crown in 1996. "That whakataukī was the key whakataukī that came out of those hui." Related

Whakataukī (Māori proverbs) are a fun and powerful way to help rangatahi develop their own voices and find grounding in the "continuum of whakapapa", Dr Hinemoa Elder says. The child psychiatrist and author weaves observations from her professional life into the new book Dear Moko a child centred reshaping of her beloved 2020 whakataukī collection. https://www.rnz.co.nz/nation professional life into the new book Dear Moko a child centred reshaping of her beloved 2020 whakataukī collection. https://www.rnz.co.nz/nation al/programmes/saturday/audio/2018961498/hinemoa elder dear moko The idea that children should be "seen and not heard" first introduced to Aotearoa by Pākehā settlers is one that Elder challenges in Dear Moko. Although this "older, more colonised" message about the place of young people still prevails in New Zealand culture, it is critical that whānau seek to understand young people's actual lived experience, she says, as they did in generations past. "I'm constantly trying to tune into a tūpuna [ancestral] voice in thinking about their struggles and trying to retain at least some of the older kōrero." Most young people are just trying to please their families, she says, and are "exquisitely attuned" to how their whānau receives them. "I'm often saying to parents 'Hey, our teenagers, our rangatahi get a bit of a bad rap but actually they're very caring because they've been keeping their pain private in order to protect your feelings and they pay a big price for that'." An illustration from Dear Moko. As both a child psychiatrist and whānau advocate, Elder sees Māori around New Zealand facing "very serious challenges" when it comes to mental health, particularly in under served rural areas. "I'm really quite shocked about the degree of complexity and the amount of difficulty that our whānau are trying to absorb themselves without professional help at all. "We need to make sure that rural communities are better resourced with mental health services and these services are functioning as well as looking at prevention." [Page 1] 2024 01 29 21:53:12+13:00 Anton Matthews is the director of Hustle Group, a company operating a bunch of restaurants and catering companies in Ōtautahi Christchurch. He's also a big advocate for people learning te reo Māori, also running online course Normalising Te Reo Māori. In the next in a weekly series, he shares a favourite whakataukī, or traditional Māori aphorism, with Emile Donovan. Ko te amorangi ki mua, ko te hāpai ō ki muri The leader at the front and the workers behind the scenes This simple whakataukī, or Māori proverb, is a multi layered favourite of Matthews. While he was fortunate to grow up immersed in te ao Māori, including being educated at kohanga reo and kura kaupapa, Matthews tells Nights anyone exposed to a lot of te reo Māori quickly learns that it’s a language rich in metaphor. “There’s the literal meaning of whatever has been said, but it often takes a couple of years (sometimes it never actually dawns on us), but there is a hidden meaning there as well. “That’s what I love about whakataukī is that yep, there's that kind of surface layer literally, what is the person saying? But what's the hidden meaning? What are they really trying to explain or what sort of message or idea are they trying to convey when they use the whakataukī? That's the beauty of language, not just te reo Māori, but any language has those kinds of beautiful nuances, I think.” Matthews says he loves all sorts of different whakataukī for different reasons and occasions, but his favourite is particularly appropriate to his work in the hospitality sector. Ko te amorangi ki mua, ko te hāpai ō ki muri has two parts to it, Matthews says. Amorangi is a term that refers to recognised iwi leaders, the ones who are front and centre when leading a pōwhiri, or welcome, onto the marae. “These are the familiar faces that everyone kind of knows… these people are highly respected. They have a lot of mana. We look to them when we need guidance.” Te hāpai ō referred to in the second part of the whakataukī is the complete opposite, Matthews says.

Linguists note this represents the evolving and distinctive nature of New Zealand English.

[Page 1] 'No one should go home hungry' Manaakitanga on full display at Tuurangawaewae ByPokere Paewai Māori issues reporter 2024 09 04 05:46:28+12:00 Thousands of people have gathered at Tuurangawaewae Marae to pay their respects to Kiingi Tuheitia, but local iwi have ensured that nobody has gone hungry. One of the core beliefs at Tuurangawaewae Marae is that 'no one should go home hungry', and the people of Tainui have epitomised the Māori value of Manaakitanga or hospitality during the tangihanga of Kiingi Tuheitia. The death of Kiingi Tuheitia has been a shock, but once it was announced, they flocked to the marae. They might be in the kitchen making sandwiches, outside directing traffic or operating the livestream. Dr Rangi Mātāmua who arrived with his iwi Tūhoe said Tainui were made to host events of this scale. "I know my own people would struggle to do what they do. They don't just do it for just one event, they do this kind of national massive gatherings to continue to unite us year after year. How many events like this occur here, and they do it on the aroha and hard work of the people of Tainui." It showed their love for the kaupapa and for the other iwi who attended, he said. "They are breaking their backs to manaaki te ao Māori, I do take my hat off to them. "I fail to have words really to bestow upon them just what they've done not just today, but since the establishment of the Kiingitanga." The Kiingitanga has been a burden on the people of Tainui in many ways, but they continued to carry it with such humility, Mātāmua said. Labour MP Cushla Tangaere Manuel arrived representing her iwi Ngāti Porou and the wider Tairawhiti. "I think what you observe when you come here is that people are born into manaaki here. "Intergenerational jobs, people have their role from generations and they are just a well oiled machine," she said. Another iwi, Rangitāne, travelled up to Waikato from Wairarapa on Monday, and instead of having to return home straight after paying their respects they were hosted at Te Kauri Marae in Rāhui Pōkeka, Huntly. Rangitāne kaumātua Manahi Paewai said being welcomed onto a marae by their hosts beat traveling through the night in a bus by a wide margin. "Miharo, kātahi te miharo nā rātau i tūwhera mai ō rātau kuwaha kia noho mai mātau Rangitāne o te Wairarapa, Rangitāne o Tamaki nui a rua. 43.text:
[Page 2] “These are the people that you don't quite see; they're not familiar faces, they're not well known, they are the humble folk, that are often behind the scenes doing all the grunt work, doing all the heavy lifting. “Hāpai ō literally means to carry food, so these are the food carriers. And in so while the amorangi are at the front, the humble food carriers are at the back doing what they do.” Matthews says this whakataukī neatly demonstrates the duality and balance fundamental to te ao Māori. “Hāpai ō and amorangi are like two sides of the same coin; they are equal, but they are opposites.” This whakataukī is often used as in the context of a pōwhiri, which includes formalities followed by hospitality. [pullquote] Some of us actually do our best work behind the scenes in the shadows, getting our hands dirty, you know, peeling spuds and preparing kai. “In order for those two things to work together harmoniously, the front amorangi and the back hāpai ō actually need to be in communication constantly. They actually need each other. The amorangi can't actually perform their duties out the front, the formalities, without the food carriers out the back in the kitchen, peeling the spokes and getting all the kai ready for the visitors.” Matthews says the whakataukī is a reminder not to conflate being “at the front” with increased importance. “We're not all cut out to be out the front on show leading by example. Some of us actually do our best work behind the scenes in the shadows, getting our hands dirty, you know, peeling spuds and preparing kai. And what I love about it is that they are both worthy of mana. They're both just as important as each other. “This is a really important idea for our staff to really grab on to. From a Western point of view, sometimes we look down in retail, sometimes we look down on hospitality staff, but from a Māori point of view the skills that you're learning here working in this restaurant, whether you're in the kitchen, while you're at the front of the house serving people, these are exactly the skills that are required on the marae, and these are exactly the skills that are required for your iwi to be able to earn mana by serving manuhiri, by serving guests." This whakataukī shows that “everyone has a seat on the bus,” Matthews says. “It's this kind of this big jigsaw puzzle. And unless you've got all the pieces, then it's not really complete. And I think that that's a wonderful idea, that everyone's got their own place. No one's more important than the other. Everyone is just as important as each other and that's what I love about this whakataukī.”

45.document_summary: On February 4, 2024, hundreds of Māori gathered at the Waitangi Treaty Grounds in a powerful display of kotahitanga (unity). Led by Kiingi Tuuheitia and Rātana Tumuaki Manuao, iwi leaders from across the country assembled to voice concerns about the government's proposed Treaty principles bill. The pōwhiri featured speeches emphasizing unity and peaceful resistance, with leaders like Ngāpuhi Rangatira Matua Hone Sadler urging iwi to remain peaceful while standing firm. Bayden Barber referenced the 1990s kotahitanga movement, calling for continued strategic planning. Te Taepa Kameta criticized Minister Shane Jones's absence, while Rāhui Papa emphasized mobilizing under mana motuhake and ensuring He Whakaputanga receives equal standing with Te Tiriti. The gathering concluded with Tainui representatives singing in harmony, marking a historic moment of Māori solidarity.

1.fileDescription: Kaitiakitanga is a foundational Māori concept of guardianship and environmental stewardship rooted in the worldview that humans are part of nature. A kaitiaki is a guardian recognized by tangata whenua to care for natural areas such as lakes, forests, and waterways. Traditional conservation practices include temporary rāhui (resource restrictions), use of the lunar calendar (maramataka) for planting and harvesting, sustainable hunting and fishing, and blessing of mauri stones by tohunga (priests). Key spiritual concepts include mana (spiritual power), tapu (spiritual restriction), and mauri (life force). Today, kaitiakitanga is experiencing renewal as iwi (tribes) restore ecosystems and apply traditional knowledge in modern contexts. Practical examples include Ngāi Tahu's guardianship of pounamu resources, Ngāti Toa's fishery restoration at Pukerua Bay, and multi-tribal efforts to stop river pollution and protect endangered species. The document outlines challenges in collaborating with non-Māori stakeholders and details legislative frameworks such as the Resource Management Act 1991 and Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004 that incorporate kaitiakitanga principles. Kaitiakitanga offers perspectives on environmental stewardship and kinship with nature, enabling Māori to fulfill ancestral responsibilities while contributing to broader environmental sustainability.

chunkHighlights.text: By Te Ahukaramū Charles Royal

Understanding kaitiakitanga Kaitiakitanga means guardianship and
protection. It is a way of managing the environment, based on the Māori world view. A kaitiaki is a guardian. This can be a person or group that cares for an area such as a lake or forest. They are given that role by the local iwi . Māori world view In the Māori world view, people are closely connected to the land and nature. Kaitiakitanga is based on this idea of humans as part of the natural world. Traditional practices In the past, people followed traditional practices when they were hunting, fishing, growing or finding food. These helped them to care for the environment. They included: temporary bans (rāhui) on taking food from an area using the lunar calendar (maramataka) to decide when to plant and harvest taking only what was needed hunting and fishing only for food, not as sport using bird snares at the right time – for example, not when the birds were breeding. Mana, tapu and mauri Mana means spiritual power. If a forest has mana , it will have plenty of flowers, fruit and birds. Tapu can mean spiritual restriction. Sometimes rāhui (restrictions) are needed to help the mana of the forest. A rāhui might stop people taking birds, fish or fruit from a certain area, or at a certain time. Mauri means life force. This must be protected in forests, rivers, gardens, lakes and the sea. Special mauri stones, which tohunga (priests) said prayers over, were used to preserve this force. Kaitiakitanga today Today there is growing interest in kaitiakitanga. Iwi are restoring their environment and culture, and using traditional ideas in the modern world. Ngāi Tahu are guardians of pounamu (greenstone) in the South Island. Te Āti Awa ki Taranaki made a claim to the government to stop pollution in their fishing areas. Four iwi (Ngāti Kahungunu, Rangitāne, Muaūpoko and Ngāti Raukawa) have come together to stop the Manawatū River being polluted. The Te Rarawa people are working to save the kūkupa (New Zealand pigeon). Kaitiakitanga has also been included in some laws,
such as the Resource Management Act 1991.
