4.fileDescription: This comprehensive article explores the growing practice of foraging in New Zealand, examining both urban and rural contexts. The piece follows multiple narratives: in Auckland, forager Bella Burgess leads a Facebook community group on Maungawhau/Mount Eden, teaching participants to identify and harvest edible wild plants including vetch, wild brassica, pūhā, nasturtium, oxalis, and onion weed while emphasizing ethical foraging practices. In Canterbury, Peter Langlands scouts for elderflower and wild parsnips for restaurants, demonstrating how roadsides and berms provide abundant biodiversity and foraged ingredients. The article features interviews with professional foragers like Nate McKenzie and Rico Birndt who maintain sustainable harvesting practices. It highlights the cultural and philosophical dimensions of foraging, connecting it to Māori philosophy of kaitiakitanga—a reciprocal relationship with the environment—and contrasting this with Western conservation approaches. The piece explores the underlying human desire for self-reliance and independence from modern systems, noting how the surge in foraging interest during COVID-19 lockdowns reflects deeper needs for connection and resilience. The article showcases how edible plants grow abundantly in plain sight throughout New Zealand's towns and cities, challenging cultural hesitation about harvesting from public spaces while advocating for sustainable practices and "feral parks" instead of manicured lawns.

chunkHighlights.text: If everyone foraged, would we strip the land? Wellington author Johanna Knox (Ngāti Tukorehe, Ngāti Raukawa ki te Tonga, Ngāti Ranginui, Tangata Tiriti), who wrote the book on foraging in New Zealand, thinks that eating the environment is a pretty good way of reconnecting with it. She reckons foraging could resurrect the idea of the commons—not just the tragedy of it. It could bring back the concept of places that are used and maintained by people for each other—and for future generations.

That idea has been largely lost from the Pākehā world, but it’s remained intact in te ao Māori. Despite the destruction of traditional food-gathering areas, despite the theft of land, the depletion of resources, and the loss of kōrero about how different species are prepared—despite all of that, the philosophy of how to gather food sustainably remains intact. It’s the concept of kaitiakitanga.

“A big difference between Western environmentalism and Māori kaitiakitanga is how they see humans in the environment,” says Knox. “So in Pākehā conservation, it’s like, ‘We must keep these areas pristine. Nobody can take anything from here,’ but in te ao Māori it’s like, ‘People are part of the landscape. It’s a reciprocal relationship, so of course we’re taking stuff.’

McKenzie and Mikhail Shatura, head chef at downtown Auckland restaurant Ahi, taste the morning’s foraging. Shatura assembles a dish of quail, chickweed, huruhuru whenua and ureure. Foraged ingredients don’t form the bulk of a dish, says McKenzie, but they bring the flavours of a place onto the plate. “These are supporting characters,” he says.

“So I come at foraging from the perspective that if you get right out there and involve yourself in the landscape—which means taking what you can, but respectfully and sustainably and at the same time giving back—that’s just a really good way to do things.”

Raglan ecologist and rongoā practitioner Mahuru Wilcox (Ngāti Awa, Ngāti Ranginui) echoes Knox. She forages native plants traditionally used for medicinal purposes for her small business, Hau Botanicals.

“How can you teach people to value something if you can’t connect to it?” she asks. “These [plants] are valued because they were important as kai or as rongoā or they were important as ancestors, as tūpuna. If you’re really thinking of our world around us as our tūpuna, as our ancestors, how would you respect your tūpuna? So using those principles for how you connect.”

Even in the most densely populated parts of the city, plants move through the cycles of the year. Retreating into their roots to conserve water, springing forth with new shoots. Exploding into colour for a week or two.
“It’s such a reminder in your daily life as a human that everything has a season,” says Wilcox.
Over time, you start to see it: the living calendar, the shifts in weather and sunlight reflected in the plants changing, day by day, in all the gaps between the fixed and immobile parts of the city.

5.fileDescription: Kaitiakitanga is a foundational Māori concept of guardianship and environmental stewardship rooted in the worldview that humans are part of nature. A kaitiaki is a guardian recognized by tangata whenua to care for natural areas such as lakes, forests, and waterways. Traditional conservation practices include temporary rāhui (resource restrictions), use of the lunar calendar (maramataka) for planting and harvesting, sustainable hunting and fishing, and blessing of mauri stones by tohunga (priests). Key spiritual concepts include mana (spiritual power), tapu (spiritual restriction), and mauri (life force). Today, kaitiakitanga is experiencing renewal as iwi (tribes) restore ecosystems and apply traditional knowledge in modern contexts. Practical examples include Ngāi Tahu's guardianship of pounamu resources, Ngāti Toa's fishery restoration at Pukerua Bay, and multi-tribal efforts to stop river pollution and protect endangered species. The document outlines challenges in collaborating with non-Māori stakeholders and details legislative frameworks such as the Resource Management Act 1991 and Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004 that incorporate kaitiakitanga principles. Kaitiakitanga offers perspectives on environmental stewardship and kinship with nature, enabling Māori to fulfill ancestral responsibilities while contributing to broader environmental sustainability.

chunkHighlights.text: Legislation

Kaitiakitanga has been included in some legislation. The Resource Management Act 1991 aims to enable sustainable management of environmental resources. It states that people managing resources under the act must take kaitiakitanga into account.

The act defines kaitiakitanga as ‘the exercise of guardianship by the tangata whenua of an area in accordance with tikanga Māori in relation to natural and physical resources; and includes the ethic of stewardship’.
Kaitiakitanga was also included in the Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004, where it has the same meaning.

By Te Ahukaramū Charles Royal Understanding kaitiakitanga Kaitiakitanga means guardianship and
protection. It is a way of managing the environment, based on the Māori world view. A kaitiaki is a guardian. This can be a person or group that cares for an area such as a lake or forest. They are given that role by the local iwi . Māori world view In the Māori world view, people are closely connected to the land and nature. Kaitiakitanga is based on this idea of humans as part of the natural world. Traditional practices In the past, people followed traditional practices when they were hunting, fishing, growing or finding food. These helped them to care for the environment. They included: temporary bans (rāhui) on taking food from an area using the lunar calendar (maramataka) to decide when to plant and harvest taking only what was needed hunting and fishing only for food, not as sport using bird snares at the right time – for example, not when the birds were breeding. Mana, tapu and mauri Mana means spiritual power. If a forest has mana , it will have plenty of flowers, fruit and birds. Tapu can mean spiritual restriction. Sometimes rāhui (restrictions) are needed to help the mana of the forest. A rāhui might stop people taking birds, fish or fruit from a certain area, or at a certain time. Mauri means life force. This must be protected in forests, rivers, gardens, lakes and the sea. Special mauri stones, which tohunga (priests) said prayers over, were used to preserve this force. retrieved_chunks.text: Flax, or harakeke, holds significant cultural importance to Maori, with each pa or marae traditionally having its own flax plantation. At Papakura Marae, this tradition continues, as seen in the image where Ope Heremaia, who arrived in New Zealand from the Cook Islands 40 years ago, is cutting flax. This activity supports a group of weavers who regularly gather to practice their craft, preserving and passing down traditional Maori weaving skills. The image captures Ope Heremaia in a lush, verdant flax field, holding a large bundle of flax leaves, with the vibrant green foliage and the serene rural setting emphasizing the cultural and natural significance of flax in Maori communities.

[Page 1] Maaoridom has spent the week commemorating the eighth Maaori monarch Te Arikinui Kuini Nga wai hono i te po. The traditions and customs of the Kiingitanga trace back to the mid 1850s when iwi came together on the shores of Lake Taupoo to discuss the idea of appointing a King. The role was eventually offered to a rangatira of great mana, Pootatau Te Wherowhero who after initially declining, accepted the role. Today the home of Te Kiingitanga is Turangawaewae in Ngaaruawaahia and for many generations Waikato whaanau have devoted their entire lives to serving their monarch. One of those people is Rahui Papa, spokesperson or maangai mo te Kiingitanga. He talks to Mihingarangi at Turangawaewae.

# The History of New Zealand's National Parks

New Zealand's national parks are among the country's most treasured taonga (treasures) — extraordinary landscapes preserved for present and future generations. As of 2021, there are 13 national parks, protecting everything from volcanic peaks and ancient glaciers to deep fiords and limestone cave systems. [[1]](cite://1/1) Access to them is widely regarded as a birthright for New Zealanders. [[1]](cite://1/2)

## The Seeds of an Idea

The impulse to protect New Zealand's wild places took root in the 1860s and 1870s, when early thinkers began to worry about what settler land-clearing was doing to the natural environment. Conservation historian Paul Star notes that writer T. H. Potts proposed, in his essay *National Domains*, that large tracts of land be set aside as refuges for vulnerable native plants and animals — even floating the idea of using predator-free islands as sanctuaries. [[2]](cite://2/1)

By the time of European settlement, there were clear motivations for creating parks in New Zealand. Some settlers were troubled by the destruction of scenic landscapes as forests fell to the axe. Scientists worried about the loss of native wildlife, especially birds. And the government had an eye on the tourism potential of New Zealand's remarkable natural wonders. [[3]](cite://3/1)

## Tongariro: The First National Park

The story of New Zealand's very first national park is one of both cultural foresight and political necessity. In the 1880s, competing land claims around the Lake Taupō area put the central North Island volcanoes at risk of being divided and sold. Tūwharetoa paramount chief Horonuku Te Heuheu understood exactly what was at stake:

> 'If our mountains of Tongariro are included in the blocks passed through the Court in the ordinary way, what will become of them? They will be cut up and perhaps sold, a piece going to one pakeha and a piece to another… Tongariro is my ancestor, my tupuna; it is my head; my mana centres around Tongariro.' [[4]](cite://4/1)

In 1887, acting on the advice of his son-in-law, Tauranga politician Lawrence Marshall Grace, Horonuku signed a deed with the Crown ensuring the mountain block could never be sold. [[5]](cite://5/1) The government subsequently purchased additional Māori land to supplement the mountaintops, and Tongariro National Park was formally established by an Act of Parliament in 1894 — the fourth national park in the world. [[4]](cite://4/2)[[6]](cite://6/1)

The growing support for national parks among some Pākehā, combined with Māori determination to protect their ancestral land, had together created the conditions for this landmark moment. [[7]](cite://7/1)

## Early Expansion: Parks Before 1900

The success of Tongariro inspired rapid action. By 1900, national parks had also been created on Taranaki/Mt Egmont in the North Island, and large areas of South Island mountain lands had been set aside at Aoraki/Mt Cook and Arthur's Pass. Nearly a million hectares was reserved in Fiordland in 1905. [[8]](cite://8/1)

This early network was concentrated in mountain regions, reflecting both the scenery and the fact that such lands were less immediately useful for farming. [[8]](cite://8/2)

## Conservation Advocacy and the Scenery Preservation Act

A pivotal figure in this era was parliamentarian Harry Ell, who championed the setting aside of scenic reserves — "one hundred to one hundred and fifty acres of bush land every four or five miles… not merely for ourselves, but for the people who come after us." [[9]](cite://9/1) His persistence led to the **Scenery Preservation Act of 1903**, which established a commission to identify areas suitable for preservation, and was later amended in 1908 to accelerate the creation of scenic reserves boards. [[9]](cite://9/2)

By the time Ell left Parliament, more than 500 reserves had been created across the country, up from fewer than 100 when he arrived. Many of these early reserves — including areas at Aoraki/Mt Cook and the Paparoa Range — later became the foundations for future national parks. [[9]](cite://9/3)

## Tourism First: Parks as Playgrounds

Until the 1940s, New Zealand's national parks were managed primarily as places for recreation and tourism rather than nature conservation. [[10]](cite://10/1) They were developed broadly on the American model, which prioritised visitor enjoyment over ecological protection. [[11]](cite://11/1)

The tension between these two visions was sharply illustrated in Tongariro, where Police Commissioner John Cullen spent a decade from 1914 scattering tonnes of Scottish heather seed across the park to encourage grouse hunting and beautify the landscape. Critics were scathing, with one declaring: "We do not wish to turn Tongariro National Park into something that does not exist on earth." [[11]](cite://11/2)

Tourism entrepreneur Rodolph Wigley made a bold play in the late 1920s by constructing the grand Chateau Tongariro, complete with a gymnasium, cinema, and central heating, hoping proximity to Rotorua and the main trunk railway would ensure profitability. The timing was disastrous — the Great Depression bankrupted Wigley a year later, and the Tourist Department took over the resort in 1931. [[11]](cite://11/3) The outbreak of World War Two in 1939 brought tourism to a near-complete halt, with the Chateau transformed into a military hospital. [[11]](cite://11/4)

## The National Parks Act 1952: A New Framework

Though management boards had been set up in the 1920s for Tongariro and Egmont, there was no coordinated system across all national parks. Through the 1940s, organisations like the Forest and Bird Society and the Federated Mountain Clubs (FMC) argued for central oversight. [[12]](cite://12/1)

This advocacy resulted in the landmark **National Parks Act 1952**, which:

- Established a National Parks Authority to provide guidance and national policy [[12]](cite://12/2)
- Created individual park boards working alongside the Department of Lands and Survey [[12]](cite://12/3)
- Introduced a professional park ranger service [[12]](cite://12/4)
- Crucially, **emphasised the preservation of native plants and animals** and the control or eradication of introduced species [[12]](cite://12/5)

The number of national parks rapidly expanded from four to 10 in the years immediately following the Act. [[13]](cite://13/1)

## A Golden Age of Tramping and Hut Building

The 1950s and '60s were a golden age for outdoor recreation. Access to wild places became more affordable, and the government embarked on a massive programme of hut building, track construction, and footbridge installation. In 1960 alone, the Forest Service built an average of one backcountry hut per week. Between 1957 and 1972, it constructed 680 huts and shelters, 166 footbridges and cableways, and 4,000 kilometres of tramping tracks. [[13]](cite://13/2)

This infrastructure boom was so successful that conservationists began calling for restraint — warning that wilderness was being "tamed" by over-development. The response was the creation of designated **Wilderness Areas**: zones free of huts, tracks, bridges, and even helicopter access. The first, Otehake (12,000 hectares) in Arthur's Pass National Park, was established in 1955. [[14]](cite://14/1)

By 1974, the country's largest wilderness areas — Pembroke and Glaisnock (125,000 hectares) — were created within Fiordland National Park. [[15]](cite://15/1)

## Māori Rights and Park Management

Despite the vital role Horonuku Te Heuheu played in creating Tongariro, iwi (tribal) involvement in park management was progressively diminished after 1914, when the park was transferred from its founding trust board to the Tourist Department. Repeated requests for iwi recognition were refused for many years. [[16]](cite://16/1)

From the 1960s onwards, Māori began to reclaim greater influence over how national parks were managed. [[17]](cite://17/1) Some proposed national parks faltered or failed because they conflicted with Māori land claims before the Waitangi Tribunal. Many iwi sought the return of national park land through Treaty settlements, and management partnerships were eventually established between iwi such as Ngāi Tahu and the Department of Conservation (DOC). [[18]](cite://18/1)

## Expanding the Network: Later Parks

New parks continued to be added, reflecting changing ideas about what deserved protection. Abel Tasman National Park was created in 1942, championed by Nelson conservationist Perrine Moncrieff to mark the 300th anniversary of Tasman's arrival in New Zealand. [[19]](cite://19/1)

4.text:
[Page 9] From their earliest days New Zealanders have debated whether national parks should be havens for native plants and animals or adapted for the enjoyment of visitors. For 10 years from 1914, sporting enthusiast and Police Commissioner John Cullen spread tonnes of Scottish heather seed in Tongariro National Park to encourage grouse hunting and beautify the landscape. A critic asserted, ‘We do not wish to turn Tongariro National Park into something that does not exist on earth and I trust does not exist in heaven.’ 2 National parks in New Zealand were developed on the American model that prioritised pleasure for visitors over nature conservation. Yet shortage of funds meant that the huts in national parks suited only those ‘with the scouting spirit’. 3 In the late 1920s Wigley made a bold move to construct a hotel in Tongariro National Park. The Chateau was grand and its modern facilities included a gymnasium, a cinema and central heating. Wigley hoped that being close to Rotorua and midway between Wellington and Auckland on the main trunk railway line would ensure profitability. He also believed that successful tourist operators needed a chain of businesses in both North and South islands. Tourism in the Depression The timing was bad for grand ventures, and the economic depression bankrupted Wigley a year later. The Tourist Department took over the resort in 1931, publicising weekend excursions and importing European ski instructors. In 1938 there were 20,000 overseas visitors, 61% of them Australians. The outbreak of the Second World War in 1939 brought an immediate halt in travel for pleasure. The Chateau’s transformation into a hospital symbolised a tourist industry in ‘cold storage’. 4 Wartime petrol rationing brought resorts like Franz Josef close to bankruptcy. Government takeovers kept hotels open for an expected boom after the war. In the early 20th century most New Zealanders could afford only one or two day excursions. In the 1920s the Railways Department aggressively promoted weekend excursions which drew crowds to places like Caroline Bay in Timaru, Arthur’s Pass, Rotorua, Te Aroha , Waitomo Caves and Waihī Beach. In the 1930s, with New Zealand now one of the most motorised countries in the world, families explored further afield from South Island lakes to Far North beaches.

4.document_title: New Zealand Tourism: A Comprehensive History from the 1880s to the 2020s
4.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the evolution of New Zealand's tourism industry from the late 19th century through the 2020s. The narrative begins with the government's establishment of Rotorua as a spa resort in the 1880s, inspired by European spa culture, and the pioneering efforts of Māori entrepreneurs in tourism services. Early tourism was driven by wealthy travelers from Britain, Australia, and the United States attracted to natural landscapes including Rotorua's geysers, the Southern Alps, and Milford Sound. Key historical figures include Thomas Donne (first government tourist superintendent), Dr Arthur Wohlmann (balneologist), and Freda Du Faur (pioneering female mountaineer). The industry faced significant challenges through the World Wars, with the Treasury skeptical of tourism's economic value in the 1950s. The transformative shift came with long-haul jet aircraft service beginning in the 1960s, making New Zealand accessible to international tourists. Major developments included Auckland International Airport (1966), the Māori Arts and Crafts Institute (1963), and the Agrodome (1969). The 1980s brought deregulation and extreme adventure tourism, exemplified by bungy jumping (1988). In 1999, Tourism New Zealand launched the iconic "100% Pure New Zealand" global campaign. By 2019, nearly 3.9 million international tourists visited annually, contributing $25 billion to the economy, with tourism becoming New Zealand's top export earner. The COVID-19 pandemic halted inbound tourism in March 2020, creating uncertain long-term impacts.

10.document_title: New Zealand's Mountains: Comprehensive Guide to Geology, Ecosystems, Culture, and Recreation
10.document_summary: This comprehensive document explores New Zealand's mountains across both the South Island and North Island. It covers the geological formation of major mountain ranges including the Southern Alps (containing all 23 peaks over 3,000 metres, with Aoraki/Mt Cook as the highest at 3,724 metres), North Island volcanoes (Mt Ruapehu, Mt Taranaki, and Mt Ngāuruhoe), and other significant ranges. Mountain formation is driven by tectonic plate collision between the Pacific and Australian plates, causing rapid uplift (up to 10mm/year in the Southern Alps) and counteracted by heavy rainfall and erosion exceeding 10,000mm annually on western slopes. Glaciation over the past two million years has shaped valleys, fiords, and lakes. The alpine ecosystems feature over 600 endemic plant species above the treeline (93% endemic) and unique fauna including the kea parrot, rock wren, giant wētā, and the world's only alpine gecko. Introduced species have significantly impacted native biodiversity. Mountains hold profound cultural significance in Māori tradition as sacred places with spiritual importance and tribal identity connections. The document covers European exploration and mountaineering achievements, mountain settlement patterns (typically not exceeding 600-700 metres altitude), extensive recreation and tourism infrastructure with approximately 500,000 annual visitors to Aoraki/Mt Cook and 800+ back-country huts, and mountains' representation in art, photography, and literature.

11.document_title: Fiordland's Marine Ecosystem: Glacial Formations, Species Diversity, and Conservation Management
11.document_summary:
This comprehensive document explores New Zealand's 14 fiords in the south-west of the South Island, examining their geological origins and unique marine ecosystems. Fiords are long, narrow sea inlets with steep sides carved by glaciers approximately 20,000 years ago. When glaciers melted, seawater filled these formations, creating distinctive ecosystems characterized by a layer of fresh water from heavy rainfall sitting above salt water, which reduces sunlight penetration and creates dark conditions similar to deep ocean environments. This enables "deep water emergence," allowing deep-water species to thrive at shallow depths.

The Fiordland marine ecosystem supports exceptionally diverse marine life including over 150 fish species such as the brotula fish, Jock Stewart fish, scorpion fish, and deep-water wavyline perch, along with sponges, corals, sea stars, sea urchins, and marine mammals including New Zealand fur seals and a resident pod of 60 bottlenose dolphins in Doubtful Sound. Life concentrates in distinct zones: the upper zone (0-15m) with hardy organisms like mussels and barnacles, the lower zone (15-40m) dominated by sponges and corals, and deep basins (40m+) with sparse life.

Conservation challenges include fragmented management due to jurisdictional gaps between terrestrial and marine authorities, commercial fishing targeting blue cod, crayfish, and pāua, and increasing tourism pressures. Conservation efforts began in 1995 with the Guardians of Fiordland Fisheries and Marine Environment, followed by the Fiordland Marine Management Act 2005, which established 928,000 hectares as a special management area with eight new marine reserves.

12.text:
[Page 10] Tongariro National Park In the 1880s land was being sought by numerous claimants around the Lake Taupō area. Because the Tūwharetoa chief Horonuku had joined both Waikato and Te Kooti in fighting against the British Crown, some claimants believed this was reason enough for the Crown to treat the Taupō blocks as rebel land. Horonuku could see that he might lose the land. So in 1887, on the advice of his son in law (the Tauranga politician Lawrence Marshall Grace), he signed a deed with the government which ensured that the mountain block could never be sold. The land became New Zealand’s first national park.

12.document_summary: This comprehensive document provides an in-depth overview of Ngāti Tūwharetoa, a Māori iwi (tribe) from the central North Island of New Zealand. It traces the tribe's origins to the Te Arawa canoe and ancestral explorers Ngātoroirangi and Tia, whose legendary journeys shaped the cultural landscape of the Taupō region. The document details Chief Tūwharetoa, a 16th-century warrior and skilled carver, and the subsequent rise of the Te Heuheu dynasty as paramount chiefs in the 18th century. Key historical narratives include tribal warfare establishing Tūwharetoa mana, Māori mythology about mountain warriors competing for the maiden mountain Pīhanga, and Chief Horonuku's 1887 deed protecting the mountain block, which became New Zealand's first national park in 1894. The document describes the traditional diet based on native fish species including kōkopu, īnanga, kākahi, koura, and kōaro, which were largely displaced by introduced trout in the early 1900s. It documents the establishment of the Ngāti Tūwharetoa Trust Board in 1926 and the tribe's economic development through forestry investments and education initiatives. The document highlights geographic divisions within the iwi, particularly Ngāti Tūwharetoa ki Kawerau in the Bay of Plenty, and notes the leadership of paramount chief Sir Tumu Te Heuheu (1997-2025) and his successor Gerrard Te Rangimaheu Te Heuheu. Significant treaty settlements are documented: a 2003 settlement worth $10.5 million for Ngāti Tūwharetoa ki Kawerau, and a 2017 settlement of $25 million for the broader iwi. Census data from 1991-2013 shows tribal identification growth from 24,066 to 35,877 members.

13.text:
[Page 8] Acknowledging the need for conserving representative areas, the Guardians proposed making the whole of Sutherland Sound a marine reserve. In response, the New Zealand government passed the Fiordland Marine Management Act 2005, which ensured that 928,000 hectares were set aside as a special management area, and created eight new marine reserves. With the continued support of government and an increasing public awareness of conservation issues, there is a good chance that the fiords will remain a rich and unique environment.

13.document_title: Fiordland's Marine Ecosystem: Glacial Formations, Species Diversity, and Conservation Management
13.document_summary:
This comprehensive document explores New Zealand's 14 fiords in the south-west of the South Island, examining their geological origins and unique marine ecosystems. Fiords are long, narrow sea inlets with steep sides carved by glaciers approximately 20,000 years ago. When glaciers melted, seawater filled these formations, creating distinctive ecosystems characterized by a layer of fresh water from heavy rainfall sitting above salt water, which reduces sunlight penetration and creates dark conditions similar to deep ocean environments. This enables "deep water emergence," allowing deep-water species to thrive at shallow depths.

The Fiordland marine ecosystem supports exceptionally diverse marine life including over 150 fish species such as the brotula fish, Jock Stewart fish, scorpion fish, and deep-water wavyline perch, along with sponges, corals, sea stars, sea urchins, and marine mammals including New Zealand fur seals and a resident pod of 60 bottlenose dolphins in Doubtful Sound. Life concentrates in distinct zones: the upper zone (0-15m) with hardy organisms like mussels and barnacles, the lower zone (15-40m) dominated by sponges and corals, and deep basins (40m+) with sparse life.

Conservation challenges include fragmented management due to jurisdictional gaps between terrestrial and marine authorities, commercial fishing targeting blue cod, crayfish, and pāua, and increasing tourism pressures. Conservation efforts began in 1995 with the Guardians of Fiordland Fisheries and Marine Environment, followed by the Fiordland Marine Management Act 2005, which established 928,000 hectares as a special management area with eight new marine reserves.

14.text:
[Page 2] Fishing and tourism threaten life in the fiords. A group called the Guardians of Fiordland Fisheries and Marine Environment was formed in 1995 to make sure that the area is not harmed. The government established a large marine management area in Fiordland in 2005. Remote and rugged, the inner reaches of the 14 fiords (also spelt fjords) of south west New Zealand are unique. Fiordland’s climate, vegetation and topography have combined with oceanic influences to create habitats and biological communities that have no counterpart anywhere in the world.

[Page 4] In the 1880s, there was a risk that ownership of the central North Island volcanoes would be disputed in the Māori Land Court. Tūwharetoa chief Horonuku Te Heuheu said, ‘If our mountains of Tongariro are included in the blocks passed through the Court in the ordinary way, what will become of them? They will be cut up and perhaps sold, a piece going to one pakeha and a piece to another. They will become of no account, for the tapu will be gone. Tongariro is my ancestor, my tupuna; it is my head; my mana centres around Tongariro.’ 1 The first national park Tongariro In 1887, following suggestions from some prominent Pākehā , the paramount chief of the Ngāti Tūwharetoa tribe, Horonuku Te Heuheu, made an agreement wirh the Crown that the central North Island volcanoes would become a national park. Different tribes were disputing ownership of the peaks of Ruapehu, Ngāuruhoe and Tongariro, and there was a danger that they would be divided and sold. Horonuku’s action ensured that Tūwharetoa’s ancestral mountains would remain untouched, even if they were no longer directly controlled by the tribe. The government bought more Māori land to supplement the mountaintops, and Tongariro National Park was established by an 1894 act.

15.document_title: New Zealand National Parks: Comprehensive Guide to Conservation, Heritage, and Recreation
15.document_summary: This comprehensive document provides an extensive overview of New Zealand's national parks system, tracing its evolution from 1894 to 2002. New Zealand has 13-14 national parks ranging from Fiordland (1,260,288 hectares) to Abel Tasman (23,703 hectares). Tongariro National Park, established in 1894, was New Zealand's first national park, created through an agreement between Ngāti Tūwharetoa chief Horonuku Te Heuheu and the Crown to preserve ancestral volcanoes. The document traces the significant shift from initial recreation and tourism focus to conservation and ecological protection, with the National Parks Act 1952 establishing centralized management. Key parks discussed include Abel Tasman (160,000 annual visitors), Kahurangi (517,335 hectares, established 1996), Westland Tai Poutini with glaciers, Aoraki/Mount Cook (3,724m), Mount Aspiring, Fiordland, and Rakiura. The document emphasizes the evolving role of Māori in park management, including name changes reflecting indigenous heritage and the 2014 disestablishment of Urewera National Park. Scientific understanding of ecology influenced policy changes, particularly the 1980 National Parks Act emphasizing ecosystem protection. Several parks are designated UNESCO World Heritage Sites. The parks protect rare plants and animals, with biodiversity preservation efforts including endangered species like takahē, kākāpō, and kiwis. Tourism remains significant with 1.7 million overseas visitors in 2017. Each park offers diverse recreational opportunities including tramping, mountaineering, skiing, and water activities, while balancing public access with environmental protection.

[Page 2] In 1887 Tūwharetoa paramount chief Horonuku Te Heuheu made an agreement with the government about Tongariro, Ngāuruhoe and Ruapehu mountains. They became the basis of Tongariro National Park, established in 1894. The Tourist Department developed the park as a visitor destination. Iwi involvement in park management was limited, and diminished after 1914 when the park was transferred from the founding trust board to the Tourist Department. 16.document_title: Te tāpoi Māori – Māori Tourism: Evolution, Cultural Preservation, and Business Development in New Zealand
16.document_summary: This document traces the evolution of Māori involvement in New Zealand tourism from the 19th century through the early 2000s. Initially, Māori controlled thermal tourism in the central North Island, earning substantial income as guides and operators. The Pink and White Terraces near Rotorua were major attractions until Mt Tarawera's 1886 eruption destroyed them. By the early 20th century, the government had purchased most thermal lands, shifting power from Māori to the Department of Tourist and Health Resorts. Māori transitioned from independent operators to employees and cultural exhibits. The Māori Arts and Crafts Institute, established by Parliament in 1963 at Whakarewarewa, became central to preserving and promoting Māori culture through carving traditions and performance arts. By the early 2000s, Māori tourism experienced significant resurgence with diverse businesses like Whale Watch Kaikōura and Tamaki Tours, representing a return to Māori control. By 2008, over 350 Māori tourism businesses operated in New Zealand, with 65% being self-employed operations. Tourism has significantly contributed to maintaining Māori language and cultural practices while generating economic opportunities.

17.document_title: The Volcanic Plateau Region: Comprehensive Study of Geology, Māori Heritage, Tourism, and Economic Development in New Zealand's Taupō and Rotorua Areas
17.document_summary: This comprehensive document analyzes New Zealand's Volcanic Plateau region across geological, cultural, economic, and social dimensions. The region stretches from the Bay of Plenty coast to Mt Ruapehu, encompassing Rotorua and Taupō, featuring three major volcanoes and significant geothermal features including Lake Taupō (623 km²). The volcanic history spans 1.5 million years, including the Taupō eruption (232 CE) and Tarawera eruption (1886). Māori settlement dates from around 1300, with Te Arawa (Rotorua) and Ngāti Tūwharetoa (Lake Taupō) as main tribal groups descended from the Te Arawa canoe. Tourism developed from the 19th century, with Rotorua becoming a government-built spa town and the 1887 gift of three mountains establishing Tongariro National Park. The economy encompasses forestry, farming (after cobalt fertilizer resolved soil deficiencies in 1935), trout fishing (introduced 1887), and geothermal/hydroelectric power generation. Population grew from 5,100 in 1906 to 98,187 in 2013, with Rotorua expanding from under 1,000 in 1896 to 53,265 by 2013. Māori comprise 34.6% of the plateau population versus 14.9% nationally. The region has become a global adventure tourism destination featuring zorbing, bungy jumping, and the Tongariro Crossing. Educational institutions, health services, and cultural heritage preservation through museums and the School of Māori Arts and Crafts (1927) are highlighted. Environmental challenges include lake pollution and nutrient runoff from agriculture. Geological hazards from Pacific Plate subduction create ongoing volcanic risks including lahars. Te Arawa and Ngāti Tūwharetoa maintain significant Crown relationships through land ownership agreements and parliamentary representation via electorates established in 1919 and 1963.

18.text:
[Page 12] From the 1970s Māori issues, including Māori land legislation, became much more prominent in New Zealand’s political life. A shift in political attitudes to focus on preventing further sales of Māori land led to the revision of Māori land law proposed by the 1978 McCarthy Commission. The resulting legislation, Te Ture Whenua Maori (Maori Land Act) 1993, was the first piece of Māori land legislation to include a reference to the Treaty of Waitangi. Its preamble acknowledged the special relationship between the Māori people and the Crown established by the treaty, affirmed that it is desirable to recognise that land is a taonga tuku iho (treasure handed down) of special significance to Māori people, and promoted retention, occupation, development, and use of land for the benefit of its owners, their whānau and their hapū .

18.document_title: Māori Land Court: Historical Evolution and Legislative Development from Treaty of Waitangi to Te Ture Whenua Maori Act 1993
18.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the complete history and evolution of the Māori Land Court (Te Kōti Whenua) and Māori land tenure in New Zealand from the Treaty of Waitangi (1840) through 1993. The document covers three major periods: (1) The transformation from communal tribal land ownership to individual titles following the Native Lands Act 1862, which established courts to issue legal titles and introduced the 10-owner rule, resulting in massive land alienation—by the early 20th century, only 2 million of 27 million hectares remained in Māori ownership; (2) The legislative evolution from 1873-1909, including the abolition of the 10-owner rule under the Native Lands Act 1873, which inadvertently created fragmented titles with numerous owners, and the passage of approximately 560 acts dealing with Māori land, despite protective measures like the "taihoa" policy, over 800,000 hectares were sold; (3) The transformation from 1920-1993, where by 1920 only 19 acres per Māori remained, prompting the court to shift from land acquisition to land development support, culminating in the Te Ture Whenua Maori Act 1993—the first Māori land legislation referencing the Treaty of Waitangi and emphasizing land retention and development. The court's primary objectives evolved from facilitating land transfers to retaining Māori land ownership and promoting effective land use, while maintaining jurisdiction over marae governance and cultural matters.

19.document_title: Southland Region: Comprehensive Guide to Geography, History, Economy, Culture, and Demographics
19.document_summary: This comprehensive document provides an in-depth exploration of New Zealand's Southland region across multiple dimensions. It covers geography including Fiordland National Park (1.2 million hectares), diverse terrain, and harsh climate with high rainfall. The document traces Southland's history from early Māori settlement under chiefs Rākaihautū and Tamatea through European colonization beginning with Captain James Cook in 1770 and the Treaty of Waitangi in 1840. It details unique flora and fauna including endemic insect species, rare birds like takahē and kākāpō, and marine mammals such as Hector's dolphins. The economic narrative spans from gold rushes and agricultural development in the 1870s-1880s through freezing works, dairy expansion, and modern infrastructure including railways and the Homer Tunnel. By 2013, Southland had 93,339 residents with Invercargill as the major urban center. Primary industries—agriculture (17% of workforce), manufacturing (16.8%), and fishing—remain central to the economy, with over 670,000 dairy cows by 2012. The region is characterized by strong Scottish Presbyterian heritage, distinctive cultural identity, and sporting achievements, particularly in rugby where Southland produced over 50 All Blacks.

23.document_title: Māori Forest Knowledge and Traditional Uses of Native New Zealand Plants
23.document_summary: This comprehensive document explores Māori forest knowledge, traditions, and the traditional uses of native New Zealand plants. It is centered on Tāne, the god of the forest, and details how Māori utilized forest resources across multiple categories. The document covers food sources including aruhe fern root, berries, karaka kernels, tawa, taraire, and various forest fruits, along with detailed preparation methods such as the 12-hour toxin removal process for karaka. It describes medicinal applications including rimu bark for wounds and pōhutukawa nectar for sore throats. Building materials are extensively documented, featuring tōtara and kauri for canoes and tree ferns for house posts. The text explains the spiritual significance of forests through the concept of mauri (life force) and illustrates respect for Tāne through the Rātā tradition, emphasizing proper rites before harvesting trees. Major forest trees including tōtara, kauri, beech, kahikatea, and rimu are described with their specific uses. The document also covers weaving plants (harakeke, wharariki, nīkau, tī, kiekie) and their applications in basket and net making. It highlights Māori's deep environmental knowledge, reverence for forests' beauty and spiritual presence, and documents seasonal migration patterns and harvesting practices. The text notes that indigenous forest cover has declined from 80% to 24.8% over centuries, underscoring the historical importance of these traditional practices.

25.document_title: New Zealand's Mountains: Comprehensive Guide to Geology, Ecosystems, Culture, and Recreation
25.document_summary: This comprehensive document explores New Zealand's mountains across both the South Island and North Island. It covers the geological formation of major mountain ranges including the Southern Alps (containing all 23 peaks over 3,000 metres, with Aoraki/Mt Cook as the highest at 3,724 metres), North Island volcanoes (Mt Ruapehu, Mt Taranaki, and Mt Ngāuruhoe), and other significant ranges. Mountain formation is driven by tectonic plate collision between the Pacific and Australian plates, causing rapid uplift (up to 10mm/year in the Southern Alps) and counteracted by heavy rainfall and erosion exceeding 10,000mm annually on western slopes. Glaciation over the past two million years has shaped valleys, fiords, and lakes. The alpine ecosystems feature over 600 endemic plant species above the treeline (93% endemic) and unique fauna including the kea parrot, rock wren, giant wētā, and the world's only alpine gecko. Introduced species have significantly impacted native biodiversity. Mountains hold profound cultural significance in Māori tradition as sacred places with spiritual importance and tribal identity connections. The document covers European exploration and mountaineering achievements, mountain settlement patterns (typically not exceeding 600-700 metres altitude), extensive recreation and tourism infrastructure with approximately 500,000 annual visitors to Aoraki/Mt Cook and 800+ back-country huts, and mountains' representation in art, photography, and literature.

26.text:
[Page 5] Rakiura National Park, created in 2002, is New Zealand’s most recent national park. It covers 157,000 hectares about 85% of the island’s land area. The island has a long history of reserves. Following failed attempts to encourage settlement and development, all forested crown land was set aside as a state forest in 1886 and by the early 1900s the majority of the island’s land had reserve status. Areas in eastern parts of the island, around Halfmoon Bay and Codfish Island (Whenuahou), are also conservation land but are not part of the National Park. On the eastern coast, around East Cape and Port Adventure, there is a large tract of land owned by the Rakiura Māori Land Trust.

26.document_title: Stewart Island/Rakiura: Comprehensive Guide to New Zealand's Third Largest Island
26.document_summary: Stewart Island/Rakiura is New Zealand's third largest island located south of the South Island. The Māori name "Rakiura" means "glowing skies," referencing the aurora australis, while the English name honors William Stewart, first mate of the sealer Pegasus. Covering 1,680 square kilometers with approximately 85% protected as Rakiura National Park (established 2002), the island features diverse vegetation zones from coastal shrublands to alpine tussock lands, with over half covered by podocarp and hardwood forests. The island supports exceptional biodiversity including 15,000 southern tokoeka (Stewart Island kiwi), kākāpō, three penguin species, fur seals, and sea lions, with 21 endemic alpine plant species. Historically, Polynesians reached the island by the late 1200s, with permanent Māori settlement following primarily around coastal areas for fishing and harvesting tītī (muttonbirds). European contact began with James Cook in 1770, followed by sealers, whalers, and missionaries. Since the 1850s, the island's economy has centered on sheep farming, timber milling, and fishing, with fishing becoming dominant by 2013. Tourism evolved from the 1890s to a major industry attracting 30,000 annual visitors. Key geographic features include Paterson Inlet (8,900 hectares), Mason Bay with 200-metre dunes, Ulva Island (predator-free scenic reserve), Port Pegasus with granite domes, and the Southern Circuit tramping track (71.5 km). Oban (Halfmoon Bay) serves as the main township with 378 residents in 2013.

27.text:
[Page 2] The conception of wilderness in New Zealand largely mirrored what would emerge in the United States’ Wilderness Act of 1964. Here, the legislation dictated that any land set aside as a wilderness area “shall be kept and maintained in a state of nature”—that meant no buildings, ski tows, maintained tracks, trails, roads, vehicles or horses. McCaskill played a major role in establishing the first wilderness area, Otehake (12,000 hectares) in Arthur’s Pass National Park in 1955. These were followed by Te Tatau Pounamu and Hauhungatahi in Tongariro National Park in the early 1960s—these too were small, each being less than 10,000 hectares.

27.document_title: Hunt for the Wilder Places: New Zealand's Wilderness Areas, Policy, and Indigenous Land Management
27.document_summary: This comprehensive document explores New Zealand's wilderness areas through historical, philosophical, and policy perspectives. It traces how American conservation philosophy, particularly through Olaus Murie's 1949 visit, influenced the establishment of New Zealand's 11 official wilderness areas. Key milestones include the National Parks Act 1952, the first wilderness area at Otehake in 1955, and the 1981 Rotoiti conference. New Zealand adopted stricter wilderness criteria than the US, requiring minimum sizes of at least two days' foot travel with no huts, tracks, bridges, or aerial access. The document examines wilderness as both a historical construct and personal concept—a "state of mind and heart" rather than objective designation. It addresses tensions between resource development and conservation, overuse challenges, and the evolution from seven wilderness areas in 1981 to 11 by 2006. A critical focus is recognizing Māori perspectives on wilderness management, challenging Western concepts that render Indigenous homes invisible. Te Urewera National Park's 2014 settlement with Tūhoe represents a transformative model where land is recognized as a legal entity with mana and mauri, with Tūhoe as guardians and governors. This approach offers solutions for balancing protection and flexibility while incorporating Indigenous worldviews into New Zealand's conservation policy.

28.text:
[Page 4] Ell’s greatest parliamentary successes, however, concerned the preservation of New Zealand’s native fauna and flora. At a time when forests were still falling to the axe and the fire to make way for grazing, he unrelentingly championed the setting aside of scenic reserves—“one hundred to one hundred and fifty acres of bush land every four or five miles . . . not merely [for] ourselves, but for the people who come after us. When once the bush is destroyed there will be no possibility of restoring it to its native beauty.” Largely as a result of his persistence, the Scenery Preservation Act was passed in 1903, providing for a commission to investigate which areas were suitable for preservation. This legislation was amended in 1908 to provide for the formation of scenic reserves boards, thereby accelerating the setting aside of areas of scenic value. By the time Ell left Parliament 11 years later, more than 500 reserves had been created throughout the country; there had been fewer than 100 when he entered. It was a remarkable period for New Zealand conservation, a time when people were slowly waking up to the thoughtless destruction of the settler years. The two pronged case Ell put for reserves was the precursor of the conservationist argument so familiar in New Zealand today: preservation of native wildlife and provision for outdoor recreation. 44.document_title: Hunt for the Wilder Places: New Zealand's Wilderness Areas, Policy, and Indigenous Land Management
44.document_summary: This comprehensive document explores New Zealand's wilderness areas through historical, philosophical, and policy perspectives. It traces how American conservation philosophy, particularly through Olaus Murie's 1949 visit, influenced the establishment of New Zealand's 11 official wilderness areas. Key milestones include the National Parks Act 1952, the first wilderness area at Otehake in 1955, and the 1981 Rotoiti conference. New Zealand adopted stricter wilderness criteria than the US, requiring minimum sizes of at least two days' foot travel with no huts, tracks, bridges, or aerial access. The document examines wilderness as both a historical construct and personal concept—a "state of mind and heart" rather than objective designation. It addresses tensions between resource development and conservation, overuse challenges, and the evolution from seven wilderness areas in 1981 to 11 by 2006. A critical focus is recognizing Māori perspectives on wilderness management, challenging Western concepts that render Indigenous homes invisible. Te Urewera National Park's 2014 settlement with Tūhoe represents a transformative model where land is recognized as a legal entity with mana and mauri, with Tūhoe as guardians and governors. This approach offers solutions for balancing protection and flexibility while incorporating Indigenous worldviews into New Zealand's conservation policy.

Plans are already underway to amend the Conservation Act to modernise land management and support a government priority to unleash economic growth on conservation land. 56.document_title: Who Should Make Decisions Over Conservation Land?
56.document_summary: The New Zealand Minister of Conservation has proposed significant changes to decision-making authority over national parks and conservation land. The proposals include amending the Conservation Act to modernize land management and support economic growth initiatives. Most controversially, the Minister is proposing a new National Conservation Policy Statement that would grant him sole decision-making powers over the conservation estate, effectively removing authority from statutory bodies like the NZ Conservation Authority. Critics argue this represents an unprecedented shift that strips away democratic processes and prioritizes commercial interests over conservation. The Federated Mountain Clubs have condemned the move as fundamentally altering how conservation land is managed, though the policy has only undergone limited consultation so far.

57.text:
[Page 1] Six proposals referred to the New Zealand Conservation Authority (NZCA) to consider the suitability of adding 4298 hectares of land to existing national parks. 63 proposals for disposal investigations, covering up to 3352 hectares of land. 151 proposals for protection under the Reserves Act covering 192,973 hectares of land, including historic and scenic reserves. 157 proposals for protection under the Conservation Act, including increased clarity through classification as conservation parks, and additional protections for ecological areas. Potaka said the changes were the most significant reclassification since DOC's inception in 1987. "The vast majority of areas will finally have the accurate classification as they deserve, reflecting their conservation and cultural values. "Existing rights on stewardship land such as concessions for tourism activities, mining, and grazing licences, for example can continue. "Reclassifying this land will deliver more certainty on land use options for our tourism, farming, mining and hunting sectors. New concessions will be easier to obtain." Potaka said the new classifications would provide certainty and clarity for those operating on these areas. "I am particularly excited about the creation of the 181,000ha Tarahanga e Toru Historic Reserve, which recognises the significance of the area for Poutini Ngāi Tahu, alongside protecting the extensive natural and recreational values. "The reserve does not result in a change in ownership, decision making, or joint management and public access remains the same." New Zealand First's deputy leader Shane Jones. New Zealand First wants 'unfettered development' Shane Jones Jones said New Zealand First had a long standing remit that a lot of stewardship land should be taken off the Department for Conservation and "opened up for unfettered development." "It was only shoved in DOC in 1987 because people were too lazy back there to find a better home for it. "Obviously we're pro mining, pro extraction and this decision never went through Cabinet so it's fair to say that it's not aligned with the party stance on stewardship land." However, Jones acknowledged Potaka was entitled to make the changes. "Technically speaking, I'm advised that Tama has the total authority under the DOC Act. As you know, I don't like DOC, and I've been invited to take these more fundamental concerns to the next election. "I accept you can't get your way every time, but know this from me, we are a pro extractive, pro mining, pro development, pro jobs party." ACT leader David Seymour said the government had to work within the reality of the Ngāi Tahu settlement that did provide for some claim on the divestment of public land. "We've supported a wider deal that allows a lot more activity. I think that's a good thing. If it also comes with transfer to iwi, we've had a history of treaty settlements for a long time. "Sometimes some public land goes to Māori, probably not the way I would do it if I could start New Zealand 180 years ago but it's where we are." 58.text:
[Page 1] You don't invest in conservation land 'by flogging it off', Forest and Bird says ByCheckpoint 2024 11 15 19:00:36+13:00 Without checks and balances in place "we could see things like helicopter landings in remote areas of the Darran Mountains in Fiordland," Richard Capie said. Forest and Bird is concerned a government proposal could lead to a sell off of conservation land. The government has just released a proposal to "modernise New Zealand's conservation management system". The aim, it says, is to cut red tape, maximise benefits from commercial activity on public conservation land, and make it easier to dispose of or swap whenua. The plan would also give the minister more powers to decide the fate of the estate. The Department of Conservation (DOC) is the country's biggest land manager with an estate of 8.7 million hectares, including 15,000 kilometres of tracks. In an earlier briefing to the minister, DOC said it was managing more assets than it could afford to and its funding had not kept pace. https://www.rnz.co.nz/national/programmes/checkpoint/a udio/2018964370/forest and bird speaks on new govt conservation pro posal Forest and Bird general manager of advocacy Richard Capie told Checkpoint New Zealand did need to make changes in how conservation land was managed and some of the proposals sensibly looked to streamline the process. "But we also need to keep our focus on improving conservation and biodiversity and what the government's announced this morning is pretty heavily on commercialisation of public conservation land and actually really light on how conservation's going to be improved." There were also some red flags in the details of the proposal and fast track decision making did not work in the conservation area, he said. "At present we have something called the New Zealand Conservation Authority and independent expert conservation decision makers, who make decisions on plans so they're actually like a check and balance there to make sure that some of the key decisions that are made about what we're going to do with our public conservation land is really carefully thought through we don't want more fast track style decision making on that project." The proposals wanted to take the principals such as those used on the Ruataniwha Dam proposal and apply them more broadly to conservation land, he said. Capie said DOC's budget was slashed at the beginning of the year and we are in the middle of a biodiversity and climate crisis. "In the discussion paper the minister talks about three to four billion dollars of income coming in through tourism on public conservation land and yet we're massively underfunding it. "The way to fund it is to actually do that properly not by flogging off the land to the highest bidder." Giving ministerial decision making on things like area plans and amenity zones, it risked seeing large scale rezoning of conservation land to be more permissive, he said. "If we don't have those checks and balances in place with an independent expert group then we could see things like helicopter landings in remote areas of the Darran Mountains in Fiordland." Choices need to be made but the key word was conservation which meant looking after biodiversity, he said. "Absolutely we need to invest in that, but you don't invest in it by flogging it off." It is possible to allow changes for commercial activity, but it must be done in the right place and in the right way, he said. The Environmental Defence Society policy director Raewyn Peart said the conservation system was no longer fit for purpose and the government's proposal was a welcome first step towards modernising it. But the society had concerns, she said. "The proposal to make it easier to exchange conservation land is of some concern and needs further thought. Any exchanges need to be subject to robust considerations and should not include land with high conservation values," she said in a statement. "There is an urgent need for more money for conservation and EDS supports some access charging in principle. However, the details will need to be carefully worked through to ensure that New Zealanders are not excluded from accessing conservation areas." In a statement, Tourism Industry Aotearoa chief executive Rebecca Ingram said there was a lot to digest in the proposals. It would be getting the views of its members before making a submission, she said. "It's very important that consideration of access charging also recognises that the International Visitor Levy is now $100 and will generate tens of millions of dollars of funding for conservation and visitor management on the conservation estate." 59.document_title: Tourist Trap: Why Charging Entry Fees at Iconic NZ Natural Attractions Could Have Hidden Costs
59.document_summary: New Zealand's government proposes charging international tourists $20-$40 entry fees at iconic natural attractions including Aoraki-Mount Cook, Tongariro Crossing, Milford Sound, and Cathedral Cove, targeting $60 million annually. While complementing the international visitor levy (IVL) tripled to $100, this approach raises concerns about conservation funding equity. Less-known sites lacking revenue-generating capacity may suffer reduced investment, and the decentralized fee system could undermine strategic conservation efforts. The proposal risks signaling a broader agenda to make public conservation lands financially self-sufficient, potentially compromising their intrinsic ecological and wellbeing values beyond economic metrics.

Once the next implementation plan is finalised, this and the existing ANZBS (Aotearoa New Zealand Biodiversity Strategy) will be submitted to the Convention on Biological Diversity as our national biodiversity strategy and action plan." Staff from the Department of Conservation (DOC) are attending the conference as part of New Zealand's delegation, along with officials from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade, the Ministry for Primary Industries and the Environmental Protection Authority. Conservation minister Tama Potaka did not attend the conference. He said he was confident the officials attending were well placed to represent the government's position on how targets will be achieved. Capie was unimpressed with the lack of ministerial attendance at the conference. "Other nations are sending their ministers and heads of state. We're sending a tiny delegation. It speaks volumes." Conservation minister Tama Potaka. Policy target mismatch One of the agreement's key targets is the '30 by 30' target to conserve 30 percent of land, water and sea by 2030. Both Capie and Kingdon Bebb said government policy was at odds with achieving this. Around 30 percent of the country's land mass is managed by DOC, and has some level of protection. Marine protection was different, Kingdon Bebb said. "Despite having the fifth largest ocean territory on the planet, New Zealand currently protects less than one percent of our marine environment, which is pretty shocking," she said. Plans to create a Kermadec marine sanctuary were halted in March. Had the sanctuary gone ahead, the percentage of protected marine areas would have jumped to close to 15 percent, Kingdon Bebb said. Proposed protections for the Hauraki Gulf have also been weakened, with commercial fishing to be allowed in some protected areas. Fast track legislation and proposed reforms to the Resource Management Act are at odds with some of the targets, Capie said. Part of one target calls for no loss to the extent or condition of indigenous land, wetland, freshwater ecosystems, and marine and coastal habitats that have been identified as having high biodiversity value. "We are currently putting through changes in our [resource management] system to enable mining and quarrying in wetlands," he said. Forest & Bird's Richard Capie Projects that had already been rejected due to environmental concerns may still be able to go ahead under the proposed fast tracking legislation. Kingdon Bebb said Trans Tasman Resources' plan to mine the seabed off Taranaki was among the projects previously rejected due a lack of controls to protect the environment Potaka said the Fast track Approvals Bill excluded a range of land, including high value conservation land, national parks, national reserves, nature reserves, scientific reserves, wilderness areas, sanctuary areas, Ramsar sites, and marine reserves. Under the proposed legislation, expert panels will assess each application. "For land and waters that are in scope, the Bill provides the ability for the panel to decline where adverse impacts are significant enough to outweigh the purpose of the Bill," Potaka said. "In their assessment, the panel must consider reports from DOC, with advice on relevant conservation matters. The panel can consider and set conditions to manage risks to species and conservation values, as they see appropriate.". There is no penalty for failing to meet the 2030 targets. 60.document_title: New Zealand Accused of 'Waffle' and No Plan to Hit Targets for Global Biodiversity Agreement
60.document_summary: New Zealand faces criticism from environmental advocates for lacking a concrete action plan to meet its commitments under the UN Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework signed in 2022. WWF-New Zealand and Forest & Bird argue the government submitted only "waffle" and empty platitudes with no financial commitment or domestic policy implementation strategy. Key concerns include: the '30 by 30' target to conserve 30% of land, water, and sea by 2030 is undermined by government policies; New Zealand protects less than 1% of its marine environment despite having the fifth-largest ocean territory; proposed Fast-track Approvals Bill and RMA reforms contradict biodiversity targets; and the government sent only a small delegation to the Colombia summit rather than ministerial representation. While the Department of Conservation stated a fully-fleshed action plan is still being developed, critics argue current policies prioritize mining and development over environmental protection, putting the country at odds with its international commitments.

61.text:
[Page 1] Conservation Minister Tama Potaka. Unease is building over law changes that could see Conservation Boards sidelined. However, Conservation Minister Tama Potaka said Conservation Boards and the New Zealand Conservation Authority will continue to play an important role in the way conservation land is managed. The 15 boards across New Zealand are made up of local people nominated by their communities or iwi, and appointed by the minister to monitor DOC's work in their regions and advise the NZ Conservation Authority ( Te Pou Atawhai o te Taiao). The authority in turn provides DOC and the minister with independent policy advice. no metadata The boards have a statutory role in reviewing DOC's regional management plans and the authority must approve National Park plans. In its submission on the government's plan to "modernise" conservation land management, the West Coast (Tai Poutini) Conservation Board said there was serious concern at the proposal to remove significant functions from both the boards and the NZCA. Those functions included the need for the boards and the authority to approve conservation management plans and strategies as well as park plans, board chair Mike Legge submitted. "These approvals would be given directly to the Minister of Conservation without the input of either the Conservation Boards or the NZCA. "This board also has concerns that the proposed draft document also appears to limit input by iwi. " The Conservation Authority, currently headed by Edward Ellison (Ngāi Tahu), also has strong misgivings about the proposed legislation. "Firstly, we consider the theme for the National Conservation Policy Statement 'modernising the conservation system' is a misleading title, " the authority submitted. "The proposed document is more of an enabling document, promoting economic development over conservation values. "The proposal will reduce the role of the NZCA and Conservation Boards therefore the public voice in statutory planning and advisory functions is much reduced." It was not clear how the proposed actions would result in better conservation outcomes, or how they would ensure that biodiversity was protected, the authority said. "We again reiterate our disappointment in the lack of engagement with the NZCA, Conservation Boards, iwi and the public ... in preparing this policy; we believe the feedback we and others have provided has been largely ignored." And at the meeting of the West Coast Conservation Board last month, the minister's absence at the last two meetings of board chairs in Wellington was a further cause for disappointment. There had been a question mark hanging over whether the regular meeting should go ahead both this year and last, Legge said. "The minister was invited but he didn't turn up ... didn't put an apology in, which was very disappointing. It's a really valuable meeting especially for new chairs and DOC always puts on some good topical presentations." LDR asked the minister's office if his no show reflected an uncertain future for Conservation Boards. That was not the case and no snub was intended, a spokesperson said. The board chairs' meeting early this year had coincided with the lead up to Waitangi commemorations, while the October one had clashed with a prior engagement. "The minister values Conservation Boards and the vital role they play in ensuring local voices are heard in conservation. He regularly engages with the New Zealand Conservation Authority (NZCA) and appreciates updates from Chair Edward Ellison, " the spokesperson said. The NZCA and Conservation Boards would remain key advisers under the conservation law reforms, providing input on the National Conservation Policy Statement and area plans, with the minister required to consider their feedback. "These changes create a single, coherent system where the government sets the rules and accountable for decisions. This avoids the current misalignment where plans can restrict activities that align with good conservation outcomes." Statutory checks and safeguards would remain, ensuring conservation lands were protected while allowing practical, balanced use that reflects government policy, the minister's spokesperson said. The Conservation Acts (Land Management) Amendment Bill is set to be introduced to is Parliament at the end of the year. LDR is local body journalism co funded by RNZ and NZ On Air. 61.document_summary: New Zealand's proposed conservation law reforms threaten to sideline Conservation Boards and the New Zealand Conservation Authority (NZCA) by removing their statutory approval functions. The 15 regional Conservation Boards, composed of local community and iwi representatives, currently review DOC's regional management plans and advise on conservation policy. Under the proposed Conservation Acts (Land Management) Amendment Bill, these approval powers would transfer directly to the Conservation Minister, bypassing board and authority input. The West Coast Conservation Board and NZCA have expressed serious concerns, arguing the changes prioritize economic development over conservation values and reduce public voice in statutory planning. The NZCA warns the reforms lack engagement with stakeholders and may not ensure better conservation outcomes or biodiversity protection. Minister Tama Potaka maintains the boards will remain key advisers, though critics view the changes as a significant reduction in their role.

63.document_title: Conservation Minister Defends Centralising Decision-Making Powers
63.document_summary: Conservation Minister Tama Potaka has defended proposals to grant him sole decision-making powers over New Zealand's conservation estate through a new National Conservation Policy Statement. The proposed changes would amend the Conservation Act to modernize land management and support economic growth on conservation land, while removing decision-making authority from statutory bodies like the NZ Conservation Authority. Critics argue this strips away democratic processes and prioritizes commercial interests. Potaka justifies the centralization as necessary to reduce bureaucratic delays, citing cases where applicants wait 5-7 years for decisions. He aims to streamline processes by consolidating two separate systems (conservation and national parks policies) into one ministerial decision-making framework while maintaining environmental protection. First reading is expected within six months.

1.fileDescription: This comprehensive document provides an extensive overview of New Zealand's national parks system, tracing its evolution from 1894 to 2002. New Zealand has 13-14 national parks ranging from Fiordland (1,260,288 hectares) to Abel Tasman (23,703 hectares). Tongariro National Park, established in 1894, was New Zealand's first national park, created through an agreement between Ngāti Tūwharetoa chief Horonuku Te Heuheu and the Crown to preserve ancestral volcanoes. The document traces the significant shift from initial recreation and tourism focus to conservation and ecological protection, with the National Parks Act 1952 establishing centralized management. Key parks discussed include Abel Tasman (160,000 annual visitors), Kahurangi (517,335 hectares, established 1996), Westland Tai Poutini with glaciers, Aoraki/Mount Cook (3,724m), Mount Aspiring, Fiordland, and Rakiura. The document emphasizes the evolving role of Māori in park management, including name changes reflecting indigenous heritage and the 2014 disestablishment of Urewera National Park. Scientific understanding of ecology influenced policy changes, particularly the 1980 National Parks Act emphasizing ecosystem protection. Several parks are designated UNESCO World Heritage Sites. The parks protect rare plants and animals, with biodiversity preservation efforts including endangered species like takahē, kākāpō, and kiwis. Tourism remains significant with 1.7 million overseas visitors in 2017. Each park offers diverse recreational opportunities including tramping, mountaineering, skiing, and water activities, while balancing public access with environmental protection.

2.fileDescription: This comprehensive historical document chronicles Richard Henry's pioneering role in New Zealand's conservation movement and the establishment of island sanctuaries for endangered native birds. Henry, a self-taught field naturalist, became curator of Resolution Island, New Zealand's first reserve for native flora and fauna established in 1891. The document explores the ecological crisis of the late 19th century when mustelids (stoats, ferrets, and weasels) devastated native bird populations. From 1894 to 1908, Henry captured and relocated 572 kakapo and kiwi to Resolution Island, developing innovative methods that became foundational to modern wildlife conservation. The narrative details subsequent conservation efforts on Secretary and Resolution Islands in Fiordland, including stoat eradication programs and wildlife reintroduction initiatives led by the Department of Conservation. It contextualizes Henry's work within New Zealand's broader ecological history, showing how Polynesian settlement and European colonization devastated native species. Modern conservation efforts demonstrate the effectiveness of removing invasive predators to restore island ecosystems, with simulations suggesting female kakapo numbers could reach 150 within two to four decades if islands are used as sanctuaries.

chunkHighlights.text: The idea of preserving remnants of the original New Zealand for future generations began to take shape in the 1860s and 1870s. According to Paul Star, a conservation historian at Otago University, Potts suggested in his seminal essay National Domains that large tracts of land should be set aside to be used as refuges for vulnerable native animals and plants. He also hit on the idea of converting islands still free of introduced species into refuges.

chunkHighlights.text: In the 1880s, there was a risk that ownership of the central North Island volcanoes would be disputed in the Māori Land Court. Tūwharetoa chief

Horonuku Te Heuheu said, ‘If our mountains of Tongariro are included in the blocks passed through the Court in the ordinary way, what will become of them? They will be cut up and perhaps sold, a piece going to one pakeha and a piece to another. They will become of no account, for the tapu will be gone. Tongariro is my ancestor, my tupuna; it is my head; my mana centres around Tongariro.’
The first national park – Tongariro

In 1887, following suggestions from some prominent Pākehā , the paramount chief of the Ngāti Tūwharetoa tribe, Horonuku Te Heuheu, made an agreement wirh the Crown that the central North Island volcanoes would become a national park. Different tribes were disputing ownership of the peaks of Ruapehu, Ngāuruhoe and Tongariro, and there was a danger that they would be divided and sold.

Horonuku’s action ensured that Tūwharetoa’s ancestral mountains would remain untouched, even if they were no longer directly controlled by the tribe. The government bought more Māori land to supplement the mountaintops, and Tongariro National Park was established by an 1894 act.
