47.text:
[Page 2] targets was not.. That was still being worked on by local and central government, she said. "The plan will include actions to deliver on our national targets. Once the next implementation plan is finalised, this and the existing ANZBS (Aotearoa New Zealand Biodiversity Strategy) will be submitted to the Convention on Biological Diversity as our national biodiversity strategy and action plan." Staff from the Department of Conservation (DOC) are attending the conference as part of New Zealand's delegation, along with officials from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade, the Ministry for Primary Industries and the Environmental Protection Authority. Conservation minister Tama Potaka did not attend the conference. He said he was confident the officials attending were well placed to represent the government's position on how targets will be achieved. Capie was unimpressed with the lack of ministerial attendance at the conference. "Other nations are sending their ministers and heads of state. We're sending a tiny delegation. It speaks volumes." Conservation minister Tama Potaka. Policy target mismatch One of the agreement's key targets is the '30 by 30' target to conserve 30 percent of land, water and sea by 2030. Both Capie and Kingdon Bebb said government policy was at odds with achieving this. Around 30 percent of the country's land mass is managed by DOC, and has some level of protection. Marine protection was different, Kingdon Bebb said. "Despite having the fifth largest ocean territory on the planet, New Zealand currently protects less than one percent of our marine environment, which is pretty shocking," she said. Plans to create a Kermadec marine sanctuary were halted in March. Had the sanctuary gone ahead, the percentage of protected marine areas would have jumped to close to 15 percent, Kingdon Bebb said. Proposed protections for the Hauraki Gulf have also been weakened, with commercial fishing to be allowed in some protected areas. Fast track legislation and proposed reforms to the Resource Management Act are at odds with some of the targets, Capie said. Part of one target calls for no loss to the extent or condition of indigenous land, wetland, freshwater ecosystems, and marine and coastal habitats that have been identified as having high biodiversity value. "We are currently putting through changes in our [resource management] system to enable mining and quarrying in wetlands," he said. Forest & Bird's Richard Capie Projects that had already been rejected due to environmental concerns may still be able to go ahead under the proposed fast tracking legislation. Kingdon Bebb said Trans Tasman Resources' plan to mine the seabed off Taranaki was among the projects previously rejected due a lack of controls to protect the environment Potaka said the Fast track Approvals Bill excluded a range of land, including high value conservation land, national parks, national reserves, nature reserves, scientific reserves, wilderness areas, sanctuary areas, Ramsar sites, and marine reserves. Under the proposed legislation, expert panels will assess each application. "For land and waters that are in scope, the Bill provides the ability for the panel to decline where adverse impacts are significant enough to outweigh the purpose of the Bill," Potaka said. "In their assessment, the panel must consider reports from DOC, with advice on relevant conservation matters. The panel can consider and set conditions to manage risks to species and conservation values, as they see appropriate.". There is no penalty for failing to meet the 2030 targets. However, previous concerns have been raised that allowing further degradation to New Zealand's environment could butt up against free trade agreements with the UK and European Union. [Page 1] Plans to grant Conservation Minister sole authority over land ByNinetonoon 2025 09 01 13:23:18+12:00 Fears plan will give minister sole authority over conservation land Conservation Minister Tama Potaka. https://www.rnz.co.nz/national/prog rammes/ninetonoon/audio/2019002317/plans for conservation minister to make all decisions The conservation estate could end up subject to political whims under a proposal to grant the Conservation Minister sole authority over the land, Federated Mountain Clubs say. The FMC told Nine to Noon a proposed National Conservation Policy Statement would strip away democratic process and prioritise commercial interests, while stripping decision making from the public and the current statutory body the New Zealand Conservation Authority. At present, delivery of different strategies and management plans were approved by the National Conservation Authority or local Conservation Boards, which were often made up of government and iwi representatives, and members of the public. FMC board member Allan Brent said for a long time these bodies had provided a public voice with extensive local knowledge. "These proposals stand to throw all of that away and go back to a situation where public conservation land our land is treated like Crown land that governments of the day can do as they will with," Brent said. The FMC said the proposed reforms undermine Aotearoa's public whenua by "stripping away democratic process and prioritising commercial interests". "Governments can, legitimately, propose fundamental changes to how we care for our conservation land but only after real dialogue with New Zealanders. That has not happened here," Brent said. One of the government's stated objectives of the proposal was to provide certainty for those who operated on Conservation land, he said. The FMC supported that objective, but did not think the government's proposal was the way to achieve it, Brent said. "They are going to be under all sort of pressures of the moment, so it is a real compromise on that fundamental commitment to preservation and conservation in perpetuity." The proposal is out for targeted consultation at present and will go to Cabinet and then through the Select Committee process next year. The Department of Conservation confirmed the new proposed National Conservation Policy Statement combined the current Conservation General Policy which was approved by the Minister with the National Parks General Policy. It also said area plans would replace current regional plans and they too would require ministerial approval rather than by the New Zealand Conservation Authority. The Conservation Minister, Tama Potaka, had also been approached for a response. In a press release last month, Prime Minister Christopher Luxon said many New Zealanders already run businesses on the conservation estate, such as guided walks, ski fields, filming documentaries, grazing sheep and cattle, or hosting concerts and building cell phone towers. "But to do any of that, you need a concession and the concessions regime is totally broken, often taking years to obtain or renew and leaving businesses in a cycle of bureaucratic limbo," Luxon said. "Outdated rules mean we've got examples of modern E bike users being turned away from potential touring opportunities because they have to be considered as proper vehicles. And tourism on the Routeburn is being held up because the trail crosses artificial boundaries, with different rules and different limits." He said his government will "fix the Conservation Act" to unleash a fresh wave of concessions in locations where that makes sense. chunkHighlights.text: National parks
By Nancy Swarbrick
New Zealand has 13 national parks. They protect some of the country’s most scenic landscapes:
Aoraki/Mount Cook National Park – the highest mountain, Aoraki/Mt Cook
Westland Tai Poutini National Park – Fox and Franz Josef glaciers
Whanganui National Park – the Whanganui River
Kahurangi National Park – limestone landscapes and deep caves
Tongariro National Park – the volcanic peaks of Tongariro, Ruapehu and Ngāuruhoe
Fiordland National Park – Milford Sound and many other fiords.
The parks are also home to many rare plants and animals. Visitors enjoy walking, mountain climbing, boating, snow sports and many other activities.

5.fileDescription: This comprehensive collection examines New Zealand's forest ecosystems from historical transformation to contemporary conservation challenges. The documents trace dramatic landscape change from native forest wilderness to agricultural farmland within a century of European settlement, driven by kauri milling, refrigeration technology, and colonial ideology. A central focus is the shift in primary threats from historical human exploitation to invasive species, including exotic weeds, pests, and pathogens like Phytophthora taxon Agathis (PTA) causing kauri dieback disease. The collection features perspectives from environmental activists like Stephen King, who protested logging at Pureora Forest in 1978 and now works with restoration efforts, alongside scientific experts discussing "ecological integrity" versus pragmatic acceptance of "blended ecosystems." Key case studies include Deans Bush in Canterbury, Hinewai Reserve on Banks Peninsula where gorse is used as a nurse canopy for native regeneration, and Riccarton Bush—a rare remnant of pre-human Canterbury lowland forest. The documents emphasize integrating Māori knowledge (mātauranga Māori) with Western science, community-based conservation at multiple scales, and coordinated public education to combat invasive threats. Overall, the collection argues that New Zealand's environmental and cultural future depends on learning to be "fluent in the language of place" through engagement with native forests while acknowledging complex realities of modern ecological management.

chunkHighlights.text: Six years later, Premier Julius Vogel took up the conservation cause, championing an act that would allow for the creation of state forests and the appointment of a forest conservator. He argued for conservation on

utilitarian grounds—the forests’ role in preventing soil erosion and land desiccation, in providing a sustainable supply of timber, in stabilising watersheds and regulating climate—but he also spoke of forests’ intrinsic value. They helped shape the “beauty, healthfulness and pleasure-bestowing qualities” of the nation, Vogel told Parliament.

It would be another 25 years, however, before the country had legislation enabling land to be set aside for its “non-productive” qualities. Tourism was one of the motivations behind the passage of the Scenery Preservation Act of 1903. Its boosters believed there was a golden egg of revenue to be had, and New Zealand’s scenery was the goose that would lay it. Hardline pastoralists grudgingly conceded that people seemed to like our natural landscapes, but argued that nothing must stand in the way of settlement.

chunkHighlights.text: Tongariro National Park

Tongariro was New Zealand’s first national park. In 1887 Horonuku Te Heuheu, paramount chief of Ngāti Tūwharetoa, signed a deed with the Crown to safeguard the volcanic peaks of Tongariro, Ngāuruhoe and Ruapehu. More land was added, and the park was established by statute in 1894. In 2019 its total area was 78,618 hectares.

It is New Zealand’s most visited national park, and one of the most visible – on a fine day its snow-covered peaks are an arresting sight for people travelling through the central North Island by road, rail or air. The park’s landscapes are diverse. As well as the volcanic mountains, barren lava flows, snowfields and hot springs exist side by side.

7.fileDescription: Lake Taupō, situated atop a 350km geothermal zone in New Zealand's North Island, offers thrilling adventure sports opportunities against a backdrop of dramatic geological history. The region, shaped by the catastrophic Oruanui eruption 26,500 years ago, features geysers, silica terraces, and mud pools. Adventure enthusiasts can enjoy jetboating through narrow canyons, whitewater rafting, bungy jumping, and skydiving. South of Taupō lies Tongariro National Park, New Zealand's oldest national park and a dual World Heritage Site established in 1894. The park offers multi-day tramping tracks, the famous Tongariro Crossing, mountain-biking trails, and opportunities for hunting and fly-fishing. More relaxed activities include lake cruises, golf, and learning about the region's volcanic and cultural heritage.

chunkHighlights.text: South of Taupō is New Zealand’s oldest national park, designated a dual World Heritage Site due to its cultural and natural significance. In 1887, Ngāti Tuwharetoa paramount chief Horonuku Te Heuheu gave the mountains of Tongariro, Ruapehu and Ngauruhoe to the Crown in order to prevent them being divided under private ownership. It was opened to the public in 1894 as Tongariro National Park.

A network of multi-day tramping tracks encircles the peaks of Ruapehu and Ngauruhoe, with many options for single-day excursions. The most famous of these, the Tongariro Crossing, showcases the variety of landscapes, from peaks and craters to steaming vents and mineral lakes. Mountain-biking tracks of various grades traverse the park, while further north, less demanding cycle trails skirt the Waikato River and Taupō lake edge.

9.fileDescription: This comprehensive document explores New Zealand's mountains across both the South Island and North Island. It covers the geological formation of major mountain ranges including the Southern Alps (containing all 23 peaks over 3,000 metres, with Aoraki/Mt Cook as the highest at 3,724 metres), North Island volcanoes (Mt Ruapehu, Mt Taranaki, and Mt Ngāuruhoe), and other significant ranges. Mountain formation is driven by tectonic plate collision between the Pacific and Australian plates, causing rapid uplift (up to 10mm/year in the Southern Alps) and counteracted by heavy rainfall and erosion exceeding 10,000mm annually on western slopes. Glaciation over the past two million years has shaped valleys, fiords, and lakes. The alpine ecosystems feature over 600 endemic plant species above the treeline (93% endemic) and unique fauna including the kea parrot, rock wren, giant wētā, and the world's only alpine gecko. Introduced species have significantly impacted native biodiversity. Mountains hold profound cultural significance in Māori tradition as sacred places with spiritual importance and tribal identity connections. The document covers European exploration and mountaineering achievements, mountain settlement patterns (typically not exceeding 600-700 metres altitude), extensive recreation and tourism infrastructure with approximately 500,000 annual visitors to Aoraki/Mt Cook and 800+ back-country huts, and mountains' representation in art, photography, and literature.

chunkHighlights.text: The network of national parks is mostly in mountain regions. By 1900, national parks had been created on Mt Tongariro and Taranaki (Mt Egmont). Large areas of South Island mountain lands had also been set aside for national parks at Aoraki/Mt Cook and Arthur’s Pass. Almost a million hectares was reserved in Fiordland in 1905.

10.fileDescription: This comprehensive document chronicles the life and legacy of Harry Ell, a pioneering conservationist who dedicated over 30 years to preserving Christchurch's Port Hills as a public asset. Growing up on a farm with the hills as his backdrop, Ell developed a lifelong passion for nature and outdoor recreation. As a Liberal politician serving 20 years in Parliament, he championed the Scenery Preservation Act (1903), which led to the creation of over 500 scenic reserves nationwide. His most ambitious achievement was realizing the Summit Road—a scenic route linking the Port Hills with networks of walking trails and biking tracks. Inspired by William Rolleston's 1873 vision, Ell championed public access rights and fought for amendments to the Public Works Act of 1900. He commissioned architect Samuel Hurst Seager to design distinctive rest houses including the Sign of the Bellbird, Sign of the Kiwi, and the grand Tudor-Gothic Sign of the Takahe. Despite persistent financial struggles, bureaucratic opposition, and conflicts with authorities like chairman William Machin, Ell's unwavering determination and personal financial sacrifice drove the project forward. He employed hundreds of unemployed workers during the Great Depression and navigated numerous challenges including vandalism and disputes with local councils. Though Ell died in 1934 before the road's official opening, his legacy endures through the Summit Road Society and ongoing conservation efforts. Today, the Port Hills are managed by the Department of Conservation, Christchurch City Council, and the Summit Road Society, with approximately 3,000 hectares under environmental protection and an annual operational budget of $300,000.

chunkHighlights.text: Ell’s greatest parliamentary successes, however, concerned the preservation of New Zealand’s native fauna and flora. At a time when forests were still falling to the axe and the fire to make way for grazing, he unrelentingly championed the setting aside of scenic reserves—“one hundred to one hundred and fifty acres of bush land every four or five miles . . . not merely [for] ourselves, but for the people who come after us. When once the bush is destroyed there will be no possibility of restoring it to its native beauty.”

Largely as a result of his persistence, the Scenery Preservation Act was passed in 1903, providing for a commission to investigate which areas were suitable for preservation. This legislation was amended in 1908 to provide for the formation of scenic reserves boards, thereby accelerating the setting aside of areas of scenic value. By the time Ell left Parliament 11 years later, more than 500 reserves had been created throughout the country; there had been fewer than 100 when he entered.

It was a remarkable period for New Zealand conservation, a time when people were slowly waking up to the thoughtless destruction of the settler years. The two-pronged case Ell put for reserves was the precursor of the conservationist argument so familiar in New Zealand today: preservation of native wildlife and provision for outdoor recreation. Many of the early reserves, such as at Mount Cook/Aoraki and in the Paparoa Range, south of Westport, formed the basis of future national parks, but perhaps of greater significance were the numerous small reserves, both rural and close to urban areas, from which people all over the country benefit more regularly.

11.fileDescription: This comprehensive document traces the evolution of New Zealand's tourism industry from the late 19th century through the 2020s. The narrative begins with the government's establishment of Rotorua as a spa resort in the 1880s, inspired by European spa culture, and the pioneering efforts of Māori entrepreneurs in tourism services. Early tourism was driven by wealthy travelers from Britain, Australia, and the United States attracted to natural landscapes including Rotorua's geysers, the Southern Alps, and Milford Sound. Key historical figures include Thomas Donne (first government tourist superintendent), Dr Arthur Wohlmann (balneologist), and Freda Du Faur (pioneering female mountaineer). The industry faced significant challenges through the World Wars, with the Treasury skeptical of tourism's economic value in the 1950s. The transformative shift came with long-haul jet aircraft service beginning in the 1960s, making New Zealand accessible to international tourists. Major developments included Auckland International Airport (1966), the Māori Arts and Crafts Institute (1963), and the Agrodome (1969). The 1980s brought deregulation and extreme adventure tourism, exemplified by bungy jumping (1988). In 1999, Tourism New Zealand launched the iconic "100% Pure New Zealand" global campaign. By 2019, nearly 3.9 million international tourists visited annually, contributing $25 billion to the economy, with tourism becoming New Zealand's top export earner. The COVID-19 pandemic halted inbound tourism in March 2020, creating uncertain long-term impacts.

chunkHighlights.text: From their earliest days New Zealanders have debated whether national parks should be havens for native plants and animals or adapted for the enjoyment of visitors. For 10 years from 1914, sporting enthusiast and Police Commissioner John Cullen spread tonnes of Scottish heather seed in Tongariro National Park to encourage grouse hunting and beautify the landscape. A critic asserted, ‘We do not wish to turn Tongariro National Park into something that does not exist on earth and I trust does not exist in heaven.’ 2

National parks in New Zealand were developed on the American model that prioritised pleasure for visitors over nature conservation. Yet shortage of funds meant that the huts in national parks suited only those ‘with the scouting spirit’. 3

In the late 1920s Wigley made a bold move to construct a hotel in Tongariro National Park. The Chateau was grand and its modern facilities included a gymnasium, a cinema and central heating. Wigley hoped that being close to Rotorua and midway between Wellington and Auckland on the main trunk railway line would ensure profitability. He also believed that successful tourist operators needed a chain of businesses in both North and South islands.
Tourism in the Depression

The timing was bad for grand ventures, and the economic depression bankrupted Wigley a year later. The Tourist Department took over the resort in 1931, publicising weekend excursions and importing European ski instructors. In 1938 there were 20,000 overseas visitors, 61% of them Australians.

The outbreak of the Second World War in 1939 brought an immediate halt in travel for pleasure. The Chateau’s transformation into a hospital symbolised a tourist industry in ‘cold storage’. 4 Wartime petrol rationing brought resorts like Franz Josef close to bankruptcy. Government takeovers kept hotels open for an expected boom after the war.

In the early 20th century most New Zealanders could afford only one- or two-day excursions. In the 1920s the Railways Department aggressively promoted weekend excursions which drew crowds to places like Caroline Bay in Timaru, Arthur’s Pass, Rotorua, Te Aroha , Waitomo Caves and Waihī Beach. In the 1930s, with New Zealand now one of the most motorised countries in the world, families explored further afield – from South Island lakes to Far North beaches.

chunkHighlights.text: The National Parks Act

Boards were set up in the 1920s to manage Tongariro and Egmont national parks, but administrative and legislative arrangements for all national parks were not co-ordinated. In the 1940s groups such as the Forest and Bird Society and Federated Mountain Clubs argued for central control.

This movement led to the National Parks Act 1952. The new law set up the National Parks Authority to provide guidance and policy. Boards oversaw individual parks in conjunction with the Department of Lands

and Survey, which provided day-to-day management through a park ranger service. The Act emphasised that native plants and animals would be preserved, and introduced species controlled or exterminated.

14.fileDescription: This article reviews "Tramping: A New Zealand History" by Shaun Barnett and Chris Maclean, which chronicles the evolution of backcountry recreation in New Zealand. Beginning with missionary William Colenso's treks in the 1840s and culminating in the 2011 opening of Te Araroa (a 3000-km walking trail), the book traces New Zealand's transformation into a trampers' paradise. Early explorers like Charlie Douglas and Arthur Harper pioneered wilderness travel, while tramping gradually gained acceptance as a leisure pursuit despite initial social stigma. The 1950s-60s marked a golden age, with rapid expansion of national parks and massive government investment in hut building and track construction. By 1960, the Forest Service built an average of one backcountry hut weekly. Today, New Zealand offers a diverse "Recreation Opportunity Spectrum" from developed paths to unmarked routes, making wilderness recreation more accessible than ever.

chunkHighlights.text: In the 1950s and 60s, tramping entered a golden age, reflected in the writings of John Pascoe, Geoffrey Orbell and the Dunedin publisher Alfred Reed, whose walking tours on “Maoriland byways” were related in a series of popular books. The number of national parks quickly grew from four to 10 within a few years of the passing of the National Parks Act (1952), and the New Zealand Forest Service entered the game in 1954 with the first of many State Forest Parks—Tararua. During these years, access to the wilderness became more affordable and the govern- ment embarked on a massive programme of hut building, track cutting and footbridge construction. In 1960 alone, the Forest Service built an average of one backcountry hut a week, for the use of both deer cullers and trampers. Between 1957 and 1972, it chalked up 680 huts and shelters, 166 footbridges and cableways, and 4000 kilometres of tramping tracks.

Such was the success of all this activity that purists began to call for restraint, warning that the wildness of remote New Zealand was being tamed by over-development. The answer to what the New Zealand Alpine Journal called “the imperceptible whittling away of solitude” was the creation of ‘Wilderness Areas’, places free of huts and other amenities, without tracks or bridges or even the possibility of a helicopter drop.

Today, we have what the Americans call a ‘Recreation Opportunity Spectrum’— choices for experiencing the backcountry tailored to every need and ability, from fully formed paths to unmarked mountain routes. Cockayne’s noble recreation ground, great laboratory and training school has never been more accessible—or, given our increasingly urban and sedentary lives, more necessary.

15.fileDescription: This comprehensive document explores New Zealand's wilderness areas through historical, philosophical, and policy perspectives. It traces how American conservation philosophy, particularly through Olaus Murie's 1949 visit, influenced the establishment of New Zealand's 11 official wilderness areas. Key milestones include the National Parks Act 1952, the first wilderness area at Otehake in 1955, and the 1981 Rotoiti conference. 17.fileDescription: This comprehensive document explores Kahurangi National Park, New Zealand's 13th national park established in 1995, through multiple interconnected narratives. The park preserves one of the country's largest wilderness tracts in north-west Nelson, encompassing 500 km of tracks across diverse ecosystems. The document chronicles a white-water rafting expedition on the Grade 5 Karamea River, where Ultimate Descents completed the first non-portaged descent through treacherous rapids, interweaving this adventure with the park's geological and ecological significance shaped by the 1929 Murchison earthquake. Kahurangi is ecologically exceptional, hosting over half of New Zealand's 2,400 native plant species (67 endemic), 80% of alpine plant species, 18 native bird species including threatened great spotted kiwi, unique Powelliphanta snails, and New Zealand's largest spider species. The park's establishment faced significant opposition from West Coast residents and mining interests, resulting in exclusions totaling 20,000 hectares for coal mining, hydroelectric operations, and gold prospecting. Contemporary challenges include possum invasions causing deforestation and native snail predation requiring $500,000 annual control efforts, conflicts between conservation regulations and recreational users on the Heaphy Track, and ongoing land claim disputes with Maori owners. The document also addresses a controversial toll road proposal that received only 3% public support, illustrating the tension between conservation and economic development in New Zealand.

chunkHighlights.text: So why has it taken so long for a huge tract of such pristine wilderness to be finally afforded full protection? Surprisingly, because Kahurangi never had an influential advocate to push the issue. Says Logan: “If north-west Nelson had been Sir Edmund Hillary’s stomping ground, it would probably have been a national park years ago.”

It is true; national parks have often been sponsored to fruition. Without the vision of Chief Te Heuheu Tukino IV, the peaks of Tongariro would not have become our first national park in 1887. An eruption may have put a stop to ex-Premier William Fox’s endless appeals for protection of the famous Pink and White Terraces at Rotomahana, but Nelson conservationist Perrine Moncrieff got her own way when Abel Tasman National Park was created in 1942 to mark the tercentenary of Tasman’s discovery of New Zealand.

Ironically, it took a surge in world metal prices to focus attention on the Kahurangi region. By the bullish early 1980s the highly mineralised parts of the area were a patchwork of prospecting, mining and exploration claims. But no single issue unified conservation support more than Australian mining giant CRNs 1981 application to bulldoze a road up to the Mt Arthur Tablelands, an expanse of tussocky downs which has always been the main route into the park for the whole Nelson area.

Guy Salmon (now chief executive of the Maruia Society) was one of those who led the charge. “We couldn’t believe that this area, ranked as a State Forest Park since 1970 in recognition of its nationally and internationally significant ecological values, didn’t have sufficient protection to keep out miners, hydrodevelopers, even Forest Service plans for huge exotic plantings!”

As a first step, the Native Forest Action Council proposed a series of ecological sanctuaries in the area. In 1988, after further lobbying to the newly formed Department of Conservation, the 83,000-hectare Tasman Wilderness Area was gazetted. It was then just a matter of time before the adjoining pieces were brought in to form a new national park.

19.fileDescription: Stewart Island/Rakiura is New Zealand's third largest island located south of the South Island. The Māori name "Rakiura" means "glowing skies," referencing the aurora australis, while the English name honors William Stewart, first mate of the sealer Pegasus. Covering 1,680 square kilometers with approximately 85% protected as Rakiura National Park (established 2002), the island features diverse vegetation zones from coastal shrublands to alpine tussock lands, with over half covered by podocarp and hardwood forests. The island supports exceptional biodiversity including 15,000 southern tokoeka (Stewart Island kiwi), kākāpō, three penguin species, fur seals, and sea lions, with 21 endemic alpine plant species. Historically, Polynesians reached the island by the late 1200s, with permanent Māori settlement following primarily around coastal areas for fishing and harvesting tītī (muttonbirds). European contact began with James Cook in 1770, followed by sealers, whalers, and missionaries. Since the 1850s, the island's economy has centered on sheep farming, timber milling, and fishing, with fishing becoming dominant by 2013. Tourism evolved from the 1890s to a major industry attracting 30,000 annual visitors. Key geographic features include Paterson Inlet (8,900 hectares), Mason Bay with 200-metre dunes, Ulva Island (predator-free scenic reserve), Port Pegasus with granite domes, and the Southern Circuit tramping track (71.5 km). Oban (Halfmoon Bay) serves as the main township with 378 residents in 2013.

chunkHighlights.text: Rakiura National Park, created in 2002, is New Zealand’s most recent national park. It covers 157,000 hectares – about 85% of the island’s land area. The island has a long history of reserves. Following failed attempts to encourage settlement and development, all forested crown land was set aside as a state forest in 1886 and by the early 1900s the majority of the island’s land had reserve status. Areas in eastern parts of the island, around Halfmoon Bay and Codfish Island (Whenuahou), are also conservation land but are not part of the National Park. On the eastern coast, around East Cape and Port Adventure, there is a large tract of land owned by the Rakiura Māori Land Trust.

retrieved_chunks.text: Six years later, Premier Julius Vogel took up the conservation cause, championing an act that would allow for the creation of state forests and the appointment of a forest conservator. He argued for conservation on utilitarian grounds—the forests’ role in preventing soil erosion and land desiccation, in providing a sustainable supply of timber, in stabilising watersheds and regulating climate—but he also spoke of forests’ intrinsic value. They helped shape the “beauty, healthfulness and pleasure-bestowing qualities” of the nation, Vogel told Parliament. It would be another 25 years, however, before the country had legislation enabling land to be set aside for its “non-productive” qualities. Tourism was one of the motivations behind the passage of the Scenery Preservation Act of 1903. Its boosters believed there was a golden egg of revenue to be had, and New Zealand’s scenery was the goose that would lay it. Hardline pastoralists grudgingly conceded that people seemed to like our natural landscapes, but argued that nothing must stand in the way of settlement.

retrieved_chunks.text: Tongariro National Park Tongariro was New Zealand’s first national park. In 1887 Horonuku Te Heuheu, paramount chief of Ngāti Tūwharetoa, signed a deed with the Crown to safeguard the volcanic peaks of Tongariro, Ngāuruhoe and Ruapehu. More land was added, and the park was established by statute in 1894. In 2019 its total area was 78,618 hectares. It is New Zealand’s most visited national park, and one of the most visible – on a fine day its snow-covered peaks are an arresting sight for people travelling through the central North Island by road, rail or air. The park’s landscapes are diverse. As well as the volcanic mountains, barren lava flows, snowfields and hot springs exist side by side.

retrieved_chunks.text: South of Taupō is New Zealand’s oldest national park, designated a dual World Heritage Site due to its cultural and natural significance. In 1887, Ngāti Tuwharetoa paramount chief Horonuku Te Heuheu gave the mountains of Tongariro, Ruapehu and Ngauruhoe to the Crown in order to prevent them being divided under private ownership. [Page 2] In the 1950s and 60s, tramping entered a golden age, reflected in the writings of John Pascoe, Geoffrey Orbell and the Dunedin publisher Alfred Reed, whose walking tours on “Maoriland byways” were related in a series of popular books. The number of national parks quickly grew from four to 10 within a few years of the passing of the National Parks Act (1952), and the New Zealand Forest Service entered the game in 1954 with the first of many State Forest Parks—Tararua. During these years, access to the wilderness became more affordable and the govern ment embarked on a massive programme of hut building, track cutting and footbridge construction. In 1960 alone, the Forest Service built an average of one backcountry hut a week, for the use of both deer cullers and trampers. Between 1957 and 1972, it chalked up 680 huts and shelters, 166 footbridges and cableways, and 4000 kilometres of tramping tracks. Such was the success of all this activity that purists began to call for restraint, warning that the wildness of remote New Zealand was being tamed by over development. The answer to what the New Zealand Alpine Journal called “the imperceptible whittling away of solitude” was the creation of ‘Wilderness Areas’, places free of huts and other amenities, without tracks or bridges or even the possibility of a helicopter drop. Today, we have what the Americans call a ‘Recreation Opportunity Spectrum’— choices for experiencing the backcountry tailored to every need and ability, from fully formed paths to unmarked mountain routes. Cockayne’s noble recreation ground, great laboratory and training school has never been more accessible—or, given our increasingly urban and sedentary lives, more necessary.

Tourism was one of the motivations behind the passage of the Scenery Preservation Act of 1903. Its boosters believed there was a golden egg of revenue to be had, and New Zealand’s scenery was the goose that would lay it. # The History of New Zealand's National Parks

New Zealand's national parks are among the country's most treasured taonga (treasures) — landscapes so magnificent, ecologically significant, or scientifically remarkable that they are considered worth protecting permanently for all New Zealanders. As of 2021, the country has 13 national parks, stretching from the far north to the deep south. [[1]](cite://1/1)

![embed-1](embed://1)

## The Beginning: Tongariro and the Gift of the Mountains

The story of New Zealand's national parks begins with an extraordinary act of generosity and foresight by a Māori rangatira (chief). In the 1880s, the volcanic peaks of Tongariro, Ngāuruhoe and Ruapehu in the central North Island were at risk of being broken up and sold as the Māori Land Court began scrutinising ownership of surrounding blocks. [[2]](cite://2/1)

Horonuku Te Heuheu, paramount chief of Ngāti Tūwharetoa, understood what was at stake. He is reported to have said: *"If our mountains of Tongariro are included in the blocks passed through the Court in the ordinary way, what will become of them? They will be cut up and perhaps sold, a piece going to one pakeha and a piece to another. They will become of no account, for the tapu will be gone. Tongariro is my ancestor, my tupuna; it is my head; my mana centres around Tongariro."* [[2]](cite://2/2)

In 1887, acting on advice from his son-in-law, the Tauranga politician Lawrence Marshall Grace, Horonuku signed a deed with the Crown ensuring the mountain block could never be sold. [[3]](cite://3/1) The government then purchased additional Māori land to supplement the mountain tops, and Tongariro National Park was formally established by an Act of Parliament in 1894 — the country's first national park, and one of the earliest in the world. [[4]](cite://4/1)[[2]](cite://2/3) By 2019, the park had grown to 78,618 hectares. [[5]](cite://5/1)

It's worth noting, however, that while the park was founded in part through Māori initiative, Iwi involvement in its management was progressively reduced — particularly after 1914, when the park was transferred from the founding trust board to the Tourist Department. Repeated requests for iwi recognition were refused for many years. [[6]](cite://6/1)

## Why National Parks? The Early Motivations

The creation of Tongariro reflected a confluence of interests. Some Pākehā settlers were growing alarmed that forest clearing for farming was destroying spectacular scenery. A few scientists worried about the loss of native plants and birdlife. And the government was increasingly aware of the tourism potential of New Zealand's natural wonders. [[7]](cite://7/1)

These motivations weren't always in perfect harmony. New Zealand's early national parks were developed on the American model, which prioritised visitor enjoyment over nature conservation. [[8]](cite://8/1) The debate between those who saw parks as recreational playgrounds and those who valued them as ecological sanctuaries would run for decades.

A vivid example: for 10 years from 1914, sporting enthusiast and police commissioner John Cullen spread tonnes of Scottish heather seed throughout Tongariro National Park to encourage grouse hunting and "beautify" the landscape. One critic retorted: *"We do not wish to turn Tongariro National Park into something that does not exist on earth and I trust does not exist in heaven."* [[8]](cite://8/2)

## The Second National Park: Egmont/Taranaki

The forest surrounding Mount Taranaki had actually been protected by a provincial reserve as early as 1875, as authorities watched the rapid destruction of bush across the district. In 1900, the area within six miles (9.6 kilometres) of the summit was formally designated New Zealand's second national park, in recognition of its spectacular landscapes and forests. [[9]](cite://9/1)

## Scenic Preservation and Building the Framework

A broader legal framework for landscape protection emerged in the early 1900s. The Scenery Preservation Act of 1903 — championed in Parliament by Henry Ell — set up a commission to investigate which areas were suitable for preservation. Ell argued passionately for reserves: *"not merely for ourselves, but for the people who come after us. When once the bush is destroyed there will be no possibility of restoring it to its native beauty."* [[10]](cite://10/1)

The 1903 legislation was amended in 1908 to create scenic reserve boards, accelerating the setting aside of areas of scenic value. By the time Ell left Parliament, more than 500 reserves had been created, up from fewer than 100 on his arrival. Many of these early reserves — including at Aoraki/Mount Cook and in the Paparoa Range — would later form the basis of future national parks. [[10]](cite://10/2)

Tourism was also a powerful driver. Premier Julius Vogel had earlier championed the cause of state forests and conservation on utilitarian grounds, including their role in preventing soil erosion, sustaining timber supply, and — crucially — their contribution to the nation's "beauty, healthfulness and pleasure bestowing qualities." [[11]](cite://11/1)

## Tourism, the Chateau, and the Depression Years

Until the 1940s, national parks were managed primarily as places for recreation and tourism. [[12]](cite://12/1) In the late 1920s, tourist operator Rodolph Wigley made the bold move to construct a grand hotel — the Chateau — inside Tongariro National Park, complete with a gymnasium, cinema and central heating. The timing proved disastrous: the economic depression bankrupted Wigley within a year, and the Tourist Department took over the resort in 1931. [[8]](cite://8/3)

The Second World War brought tourism to an abrupt halt. Petrol rationing pushed some resorts like Franz Josef close to bankruptcy, and the Chateau was converted into a hospital — a symbol, as one account put it, of a tourist industry in 'cold storage.' [[8]](cite://8/4)

## The National Parks Act 1952: A Turning Point

The post-war period brought significant change. Advocacy groups including the Forest and Bird Society and Federated Mountain Clubs pushed for better coordination of national park management. This led to the landmark National Parks Act (1952), which established the National Parks Authority to provide central guidance and policy. [[13]](cite://13/1)

Crucially, the Act shifted emphasis: it stated that native plants and animals would be *preserved*, and introduced species controlled or exterminated. [[13]](cite://13/2) This was a meaningful pivot from the recreation-first approach of earlier decades.

The Act also ushered in a golden age of park creation. The number of national parks grew rapidly from four to 10 in just a few years. [[14]](cite://14/1) Between 1957 and 1972, an extraordinary programme of hut building, track cutting and footbridge construction expanded public access to the backcountry — the New Zealand Forest Service built an average of one backcountry hut a week in 1960 alone, ultimately chalking up 680 huts and shelters, 166 footbridges and cableways, and 4,000 kilometres of tramping tracks. [[14]](cite://14/2)

### Parks Established in the 1950s and '60s

Among the major parks created in this era was **Fiordland National Park**, established in 1952. At more than 1.2 million hectares, it is New Zealand's largest national park, encompassing Milford Sound, the Sutherland Falls, and Lakes Manapōuri and Te Anau. It is also the heart of Te Wāhipounamu South West New Zealand World Heritage Area. [[15]](cite://15/1)[[16]](cite://16/1)

## Wilderness Areas: A New Concept

As parks became more accessible, some conservationists worried that the wildness of remote New Zealand was being steadily tamed. The answer was the creation of 'Wilderness Areas' — zones entirely free of huts, maintained tracks, roads, vehicles, or even helicopter access. [[14]](cite://14/3)

Mirroring the United States' Wilderness Act of 1964, the first such area — Otehake (12,000 hectares) — was established within Arthur's Pass National Park in 1955, followed by Te Tatau Pounamu and Hauhungatahi in Tongariro National Park in the early 1960s. [[17]](cite://17/1)

[Page 12] Tongariro National Park Tongariro was New Zealand’s first national park. In 1887 Horonuku Te Heuheu, paramount chief of Ngāti Tūwharetoa, signed a deed with the Crown to safeguard the volcanic peaks of Tongariro, Ngāuruhoe and Ruapehu. More land was added, and the park was established by statute in 1894. In 2019 its total area was 78,618 hectares. It is New Zealand’s most visited national park, and one of the most visible on a fine day its snow covered peaks are an arresting sight for people travelling through the central North Island by road, rail or air. The park’s landscapes are diverse. As well as the volcanic mountains, barren lava flows, snowfields and hot springs exist side by side.

[Page 9] From their earliest days New Zealanders have debated whether national parks should be havens for native plants and animals or adapted for the enjoyment of visitors. For 10 years from 1914, sporting enthusiast and Police Commissioner John Cullen spread tonnes of Scottish heather seed in Tongariro National Park to encourage grouse hunting and beautify the landscape. A critic asserted, ‘We do not wish to turn Tongariro National Park into something that does not exist on earth and I trust does not exist in heaven.’ 2 National parks in New Zealand were developed on the American model that prioritised pleasure for visitors over nature conservation. Yet shortage of funds meant that the huts in national parks suited only those ‘with the scouting spirit’. 3 In the late 1920s Wigley made a bold move to construct a hotel in Tongariro National Park. The Chateau was grand and its modern facilities included a gymnasium, a cinema and central heating. Wigley hoped that being close to Rotorua and midway between Wellington and Auckland on the main trunk railway line would ensure profitability. He also believed that successful tourist operators needed a chain of businesses in both North and South islands. Tourism in the Depression The timing was bad for grand ventures, and the economic depression bankrupted Wigley a year later. The Tourist Department took over the resort in 1931, publicising weekend excursions and importing European ski instructors. In 1938 there were 20,000 overseas visitors, 61% of them Australians. The outbreak of the Second World War in 1939 brought an immediate halt in travel for pleasure. The Chateau’s transformation into a hospital symbolised a tourist industry in ‘cold storage’. 4 Wartime petrol rationing brought resorts like Franz Josef close to bankruptcy. Government takeovers kept hotels open for an expected boom after the war. In the early 20th century most New Zealanders could afford only one or two day excursions. In the 1920s the Railways Department aggressively promoted weekend excursions which drew crowds to places like Caroline Bay in Timaru, Arthur’s Pass, Rotorua, Te Aroha , Waitomo Caves and Waihī Beach. In the 1930s, with New Zealand now one of the most motorised countries in the world, families explored further afield from South Island lakes to Far North beaches.

4.document_title: New Zealand Tourism: A Comprehensive History from the 1880s to the 2020s
4.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the evolution of New Zealand's tourism industry from the late 19th century through the 2020s. The narrative begins with the government's establishment of Rotorua as a spa resort in the 1880s, inspired by European spa culture, and the pioneering efforts of Māori entrepreneurs in tourism services. Early tourism was driven by wealthy travelers from Britain, Australia, and the United States attracted to natural landscapes including Rotorua's geysers, the Southern Alps, and Milford Sound. Key historical figures include Thomas Donne (first government tourist superintendent), Dr Arthur Wohlmann (balneologist), and Freda Du Faur (pioneering female mountaineer). The industry faced significant challenges through the World Wars, with the Treasury skeptical of tourism's economic value in the 1950s. The transformative shift came with long-haul jet aircraft service beginning in the 1960s, making New Zealand accessible to international tourists. Major developments included Auckland International Airport (1966), the Māori Arts and Crafts Institute (1963), and the Agrodome (1969). The 1980s brought deregulation and extreme adventure tourism, exemplified by bungy jumping (1988). In 1999, Tourism New Zealand launched the iconic "100% Pure New Zealand" global campaign. By 2019, nearly 3.9 million international tourists visited annually, contributing $25 billion to the economy, with tourism becoming New Zealand's top export earner. The COVID-19 pandemic halted inbound tourism in March 2020, creating uncertain long-term impacts.

11.document_title: New Zealand's Threatened Species: Conservation Status, Strategies, and Recovery Efforts
11.document_summary: This comprehensive document provides an overview of New Zealand's threatened species and conservation efforts. It defines threatened species as native plants and animals with critically low populations facing extinction risk, with New Zealand having 2,788 threatened species (37% of birds, 34% of plants). Main causes of decline include habitat destruction, invasive predators like rats and possums, and over-harvesting. New Zealand uses an eight-tier classification system for conservation status based on threats, endemism, vulnerability, and cultural importance. Conservation strategies include island sanctuaries, pest control, captive breeding, and habitat restoration. Notable successes include the black robin recovery (7 to 250 individuals), takahē recovery program, and tuatara reintroduction programs. The document presents case studies of endangered species including the Mahoenui giant wētā, Peraxilla mistletoes, kiwi, and tuatara. About 30% of New Zealand is protected conservation land. Recent efforts have expanded beyond visible species to include freshwater fish and plants, with a shift toward restoring entire habitats. Key challenges include funding limitations, many species poorly understood (1,455 fungi species classified as 'data deficient'), an estimated 50,000 unidentified native species potentially at risk, and preventing 'zombie species' that survive only in cultivation.

Many such areas are nearshore and offshore islands. Because these have been protected from habitat destruction, predators or weeds, remnant populations of threatened species are still found.

The West Coast extends over 500 kilometres along the South Island's western coast with only 32,148 residents spread across 8.7% of the land area. Geologically, the region features sedimentary rocks, coal measures, distinctive karst landforms like Pancake Rocks, and sits along the Alpine Fault. The landscape was shaped by glaciation, with high rainfall (2,000-3,000mm annually near coast, exceeding 10,000mm in mountains) supporting native forests and abundant wildlife including endangered kiwi species. Historically, Māori settlement began after 1250-1300 CE, with pounamu (greenstone) discovery becoming significant. Various iwi, including Waitaha, Ngāti Wairangi, and Poutini Ngāi Tahu, occupied the region. European exploration began with Abel Tasman (1642) and James Cook (1770), followed by the transformative gold rush triggered by alluvial gold discovery near Hokitika in mid-1864, which peaked at approximately 28,700 residents by late 1867. The region became a cradle of socialism and labour activism, particularly through coal miners' strikes like the 1908 Blackball strike. Economically, the region developed through resource extraction including gold mining (peaking at 15+ tonnes in 1866-67), coal mining (reaching 1 million tonnes by 1907), and timber production. Modern development includes dairy farming, commercial fishing (whitebaiting, blue cod, groper), and tourism. The 1965 Haast Pass road opening transformed the region into a major tourist destination. The region is home to 1.9 million hectares of protected areas including five national parks. Cultural heritage includes literary works by Keri Hulme and Eleanor Catton, strong rugby traditions, and a thriving craft sector including pounamu carving. The Māori community experienced renaissance following the 1998 Ngai Tahu Claim Settlement Act, which returned control of pounamu resources and provided financial settlements.

14.text:
[Page 10] Managing the 70% of New Zealand that is not conservation land has major implications for threatened species. Until the 1980s this land was mainly developed for farming and other production. But in 1991 the Resource Management Act changed the focus to the sustainable management of resources. However, this only addresses the negative environmental impact of new developments, rather than restoring already degraded habitats. Still, city councils and regional councils are required to consider conservation values, and many have begun to restore certain habitats. The New Zealand Biodiversity Strategy, launched in 2000, aimed to conserve New Zealand’s diversity of species, and to include the whole community in the effort. For example, throughout New Zealand there are local schemes to control predators in areas of native bush. The strategy also recognised that these projects must cut across map boundaries, and should not be the sole responsibility of the Department of Conservation. For example, the black billed gull, considered to be in serious decline, nests on South Island riverbeds which are not conservation lands. The regional council, Environment Canterbury, is now involved in saving the gull, among other species.

14.document_title: New Zealand's Threatened Species: Conservation Status, Strategies, and Recovery Efforts
14.document_summary: This comprehensive document provides an overview of New Zealand's threatened species and conservation efforts. It defines threatened species as native plants and animals with critically low populations facing extinction risk, with New Zealand having 2,788 threatened species (37% of birds, 34% of plants). Main causes of decline include habitat destruction, invasive predators like rats and possums, and over-harvesting. New Zealand uses an eight-tier classification system for conservation status based on threats, endemism, vulnerability, and cultural importance. Conservation strategies include island sanctuaries, pest control, captive breeding, and habitat restoration. Notable successes include the black robin recovery (7 to 250 individuals), takahē recovery program, and tuatara reintroduction programs. The document presents case studies of endangered species including the Mahoenui giant wētā, Peraxilla mistletoes, kiwi, and tuatara. About 30% of New Zealand is protected conservation land. Recent efforts have expanded beyond visible species to include freshwater fish and plants, with a shift toward restoring entire habitats. Key challenges include funding limitations, many species poorly understood (1,455 fungi species classified as 'data deficient'), an estimated 50,000 unidentified native species potentially at risk, and preventing 'zombie species' that survive only in cultivation.

15.document_title: New Zealand's Economy and Environment: From Agricultural Expansion to Sustainable Resource Management and Carbon Neutrality
15.document_summary: This comprehensive document examines New Zealand's complex relationship between its economy and natural environment, tracing historical transformations and contemporary challenges. It documents the country's evolution from native ecosystems to a pastoral-based economy beginning in the 19th century, with major industries including agriculture, tourism, and mining heavily dependent on environmental resources. The document traces the critical shift from prioritizing economic development (pre-1970s through the 1980s "Think Big" program) to implementing environmental protections, marked by key legislation including the Environment Act 1986 and Resource Management Act 1991. It addresses the paradox of New Zealand's "clean and green" international branding and carbon neutrality initiatives against the reality of having the sixth-largest ecological footprint globally at 7.7 hectares per person—significantly exceeding the 2.7-hectare global average. New Zealand ranks 12th globally for per capita greenhouse gas emissions, with emissions rising 25% since 1990 and exceeding Kyoto Protocol targets. Major emission sources include methane and nitrous oxide from intensive agriculture (50% of emissions) and carbon dioxide from transport and power generation. The analysis covers resource sectors including hydroelectric power, mining, and pastoral agriculture, while discussing unintended consequences like soil erosion from agricultural intensification. The document concludes by questioning whether New Zealand's environmental image reflects genuine sustainability or represents greenwashing.

16.document_title: Stewart Island/Rakiura: Comprehensive Guide to New Zealand's Third Largest Island
16.document_summary: Stewart Island/Rakiura is New Zealand's third largest island located south of the South Island. The Māori name "Rakiura" means "glowing skies," referencing the aurora australis, while the English name honors William Stewart, first mate of the sealer Pegasus. Covering 1,680 square kilometers with approximately 85% protected as Rakiura National Park (established 2002), the island features diverse vegetation zones from coastal shrublands to alpine tussock lands, with over half covered by podocarp and hardwood forests. The island supports exceptional biodiversity including 15,000 southern tokoeka (Stewart Island kiwi), kākāpō, three penguin species, fur seals, and sea lions, with 21 endemic alpine plant species. Historically, Polynesians reached the island by the late 1200s, with permanent Māori settlement following primarily around coastal areas for fishing and harvesting tītī (muttonbirds). European contact began with James Cook in 1770, followed by sealers, whalers, and missionaries. Since the 1850s, the island's economy has centered on sheep farming, timber milling, and fishing, with fishing becoming dominant by 2013. Tourism evolved from the 1890s to a major industry attracting 30,000 annual visitors. Key geographic features include Paterson Inlet (8,900 hectares), Mason Bay with 200-metre dunes, Ulva Island (predator-free scenic reserve), Port Pegasus with granite domes, and the Southern Circuit tramping track (71.5 km). Oban (Halfmoon Bay) serves as the main township with 378 residents in 2013.

20.document_title: The Volcanic Plateau Region: Comprehensive Study of Geology, Māori Heritage, Tourism, and Economic Development in New Zealand's Taupō and Rotorua Areas
20.document_summary: This comprehensive document analyzes New Zealand's Volcanic Plateau region across geological, cultural, economic, and social dimensions. The region stretches from the Bay of Plenty coast to Mt Ruapehu, encompassing Rotorua and Taupō, featuring three major volcanoes and significant geothermal features including Lake Taupō (623 km²). The volcanic history spans 1.5 million years, including the Taupō eruption (232 CE) and Tarawera eruption (1886). Māori settlement dates from around 1300, with Te Arawa (Rotorua) and Ngāti Tūwharetoa (Lake Taupō) as main tribal groups descended from the Te Arawa canoe. Tourism developed from the 19th century, with Rotorua becoming a government-built spa town and the 1887 gift of three mountains establishing Tongariro National Park. The economy encompasses forestry, farming (after cobalt fertilizer resolved soil deficiencies in 1935), trout fishing (introduced 1887), and geothermal/hydroelectric power generation. Population grew from 5,100 in 1906 to 98,187 in 2013, with Rotorua expanding from under 1,000 in 1896 to 53,265 by 2013. Māori comprise 34.6% of the plateau population versus 14.9% nationally. The region has become a global adventure tourism destination featuring zorbing, bungy jumping, and the Tongariro Crossing. Educational institutions, health services, and cultural heritage preservation through museums and the School of Māori Arts and Crafts (1927) are highlighted. Environmental challenges include lake pollution and nutrient runoff from agriculture. Geological hazards from Pacific Plate subduction create ongoing volcanic risks including lahars. Te Arawa and Ngāti Tūwharetoa maintain significant Crown relationships through land ownership agreements and parliamentary representation via electorates established in 1919 and 1963.

22.document_title: Te tāpoi Māori – Māori Tourism: Evolution, Cultural Preservation, and Business Development in New Zealand
22.document_summary: This document traces the evolution of Māori involvement in New Zealand tourism from the 19th century through the early 2000s. Initially, Māori controlled thermal tourism in the central North Island, earning substantial income as guides and operators. The Pink and White Terraces near Rotorua were major attractions until Mt Tarawera's 1886 eruption destroyed them. By the early 20th century, the government had purchased most thermal lands, shifting power from Māori to the Department of Tourist and Health Resorts. Māori transitioned from independent operators to employees and cultural exhibits. The Māori Arts and Crafts Institute, established by Parliament in 1963 at Whakarewarewa, became central to preserving and promoting Māori culture through carving traditions and performance arts. By the early 2000s, Māori tourism experienced significant resurgence with diverse businesses like Whale Watch Kaikōura and Tamaki Tours, representing a return to Māori control. By 2008, over 350 Māori tourism businesses operated in New Zealand, with 65% being self-employed operations. Tourism has significantly contributed to maintaining Māori language and cultural practices while generating economic opportunities.

23.text:
[Page 10] Tongariro National Park In the 1880s land was being sought by numerous claimants around the Lake Taupō area. Because the Tūwharetoa chief Horonuku had joined both Waikato and Te Kooti in fighting against the British Crown, some claimants believed this was reason enough for the Crown to treat the Taupō blocks as rebel land. Horonuku could see that he might lose the land. So in 1887, on the advice of his son in law (the Tauranga politician Lawrence Marshall Grace), he signed a deed with the government which ensured that the mountain block could never be sold. The land became New Zealand’s first national park.

23.document_title: Ngāti Tūwharetoa: History, Leadership, Cultural Heritage, and Contemporary Development
23.document_summary: This comprehensive document provides an in-depth overview of Ngāti Tūwharetoa, a Māori iwi (tribe) from the central North Island of New Zealand. It traces the tribe's origins to the Te Arawa canoe and ancestral explorers Ngātoroirangi and Tia, whose legendary journeys shaped the cultural landscape of the Taupō region. The document details Chief Tūwharetoa, a 16th-century warrior and skilled carver, and the subsequent rise of the Te Heuheu dynasty as paramount chiefs in the 18th century. Key historical narratives include tribal warfare establishing Tūwharetoa mana, Māori mythology about mountain warriors competing for the maiden mountain Pīhanga, and Chief Horonuku's 1887 deed protecting the mountain block, which became New Zealand's first national park in 1894. The document describes the traditional diet based on native fish species including kōkopu, īnanga, kākahi, koura, and kōaro, which were largely displaced by introduced trout in the early 1900s. It documents the establishment of the Ngāti Tūwharetoa Trust Board in 1926 and the tribe's economic development through forestry investments and education initiatives. The document highlights geographic divisions within the iwi, particularly Ngāti Tūwharetoa ki Kawerau in the Bay of Plenty, and notes the leadership of paramount chief Sir Tumu Te Heuheu (1997-2025) and his successor Gerrard Te Rangimaheu Te Heuheu. Significant treaty settlements are documented: a 2003 settlement worth $10.5 million for Ngāti Tūwharetoa ki Kawerau, and a 2017 settlement of $25 million for the broader iwi. Census data from 1991-2013 shows tribal identification growth from 24,066 to 35,877 members.

Westland Tai Poutini National Park Located halfway down the West Coast of the South Island, Westland Tai Poutini National Park covers 131,978 hectares. Its magnificent sights include snow capped mountains and glaciers, and wild beaches. Landforms and vegetation The park’s mountains have permanent snowfields that feed many glaciers, including the famous Fox and Franz Josef glaciers. The lowlands are covered by dense rainforest, mainly rimu. Near the coast are lakes, wide river mouths and wetlands. Wildlife Alpine moths, black alpine cicadas and the mountain ringlet butterfly live in the higher areas, and there are endangered rowi (Ōkārito brown kiwi) in the lowland forest. The coastal wetlands, notably the Ōkārito Lagoon, are home to wading birds including the kōtuku (white heron). Lake Māpōurika is a refuge for the threatened crested grebe (kāmana). Recreation Walking tracks allow visitors to get close to the glaciers and see views of the mountains and sea. At Welcome Flat, on the way to Copland Pass, there are hot springs. Mountaineering and ski touring are drawcards, and there are also scenic flights.

42.document_title: Hunt for the Wilder Places: New Zealand's Wilderness Areas, Policy, and Indigenous Land Management
42.document_summary: This comprehensive document explores New Zealand's wilderness areas through historical, philosophical, and policy perspectives. It traces how American conservation philosophy, particularly through Olaus Murie's 1949 visit, influenced the establishment of New Zealand's 11 official wilderness areas. Key milestones include the National Parks Act 1952, the first wilderness area at Otehake in 1955, and the 1981 Rotoiti conference. New Zealand adopted stricter wilderness criteria than the US, requiring minimum sizes of at least two days' foot travel with no huts, tracks, bridges, or aerial access. The document examines wilderness as both a historical construct and personal concept—a "state of mind and heart" rather than objective designation. It addresses tensions between resource development and conservation, overuse challenges, and the evolution from seven wilderness areas in 1981 to 11 by 2006. A critical focus is recognizing Māori perspectives on wilderness management, challenging Western concepts that render Indigenous homes invisible. Te Urewera National Park's 2014 settlement with Tūhoe represents a transformative model where land is recognized as a legal entity with mana and mauri, with Tūhoe as guardians and governors. This approach offers solutions for balancing protection and flexibility while incorporating Indigenous worldviews into New Zealand's conservation policy.

43.text:
[Page 5] The Rotoiti conference concluded with the Federated Mountain Clubs issuing a shopping list of 10 large wilderness areas. Each proposal was for more than 30,000 hectares, and in total they covered three per cent of the country’s land area. By 1985, the Wilderness Advisory Group chaired by ‘Bing’ Lucas of Lands and Survey had hammered out New Zealand’s wilderness policy. It was more purist than that of the United States, where if land had the potential to revert back to a wild state, it could be included. In the States, this was a conscious decision to ensure that there would be some wilderness areas east of the Mississippi River. Smaller areas and horses and tracks were also permitted. As a result, there are more than 750 wilderness areas in the US today. They range in size from the two hectare Pelican Island Wilderness in Florida to the more than 3.67 million hectares of Wrangell St Elias Wilderness in Alaska.

56.document_title: Forest and Bird Opposes Government Conservation Land Proposal
56.document_summary: Forest and Bird has raised concerns about the government's proposal to modernize New Zealand's conservation management system, warning it could lead to a sell-off of conservation land. The proposal aims to cut red tape, maximize commercial activity on public conservation land, and make it easier to dispose of or swap land. Richard Capie, Forest and Bird's general manager of advocacy, argues that while some streamlining is sensible, the proposal is heavily focused on commercialization rather than improving conservation and biodiversity. Key concerns include removing checks and balances through fast-track decision-making, giving ministers more power over conservation decisions, and risking large-scale rezoning of conservation land. Capie emphasizes that investment in conservation should not come "by flogging off the land." The Department of Conservation manages 8.7 million hectares but faces underfunding. The Environmental Defence Society supports modernization but also has concerns about land exchanges and access charging. Public submissions are open until February 28, 2025.

57.text:
[Page 1] The Minister of Conservation has put forward proposals that would change the way decisons are made about national parks and conservation land. Plans are already underway to amend the Conservation Act to modernise land management and support a government priority to unleash economic growth on conservation land. Now, the Minister has is also proposing changes that would give him sole decision making powers over the conservation estate through a new National Conservation Policy Statement that critics say would strip away democratic process and prioritise commercial interests. The policy has only gone out for limited consultation at this stage, but the plan would remove the decision making authority of several statutory bodies. Federated Mountain Clubs, who are on the current decision making body the NZ Conservation Authority, have described the move as unprecedented and a fundamental shift in how conservation land is managed.

61.text:
[Page 1] You don't invest in conservation land 'by flogging it off', Forest and Bird says ByCheckpoint 2024 11 15 19:00:36+13:00 Without checks and balances in place "we could see things like helicopter landings in remote areas of the Darran Mountains in Fiordland," Richard Capie said. Forest and Bird is concerned a government proposal could lead to a sell off of conservation land. The government has just released a proposal to "modernise New Zealand's conservation management system". The aim, it says, is to cut red tape, maximise benefits from commercial activity on public conservation land, and make it easier to dispose of or swap whenua. The plan would also give the minister more powers to decide the fate of the estate. The Department of Conservation (DOC) is the country's biggest land manager with an estate of 8.7 million hectares, including 15,000 kilometres of tracks. In an earlier briefing to the minister, DOC said it was managing more assets than it could afford to and its funding had not kept pace. https://www.rnz.co.nz/national/programmes/checkpoint/a udio/2018964370/forest and bird speaks on new govt conservation pro posal Forest and Bird general manager of advocacy Richard Capie told Checkpoint New Zealand did need to make changes in how conservation land was managed and some of the proposals sensibly looked to streamline the process. "But we also need to keep our focus on improving conservation and biodiversity and what the government's announced this morning is pretty heavily on commercialisation of public conservation land and actually really light on how conservation's going to be improved." There were also some red flags in the details of the proposal and fast track decision making did not work in the conservation area, he said. "At present we have something called the New Zealand Conservation Authority and independent expert conservation decision makers, who make decisions on plans so they're actually like a check and balance there to make sure that some of the key decisions that are made about what we're going to do with our public conservation land is really carefully thought through we don't want more fast track style decision making on that project." The proposals wanted to take the principals such as those used on the Ruataniwha Dam proposal and apply them more broadly to conservation land, he said. Capie said DOC's budget was slashed at the beginning of the year and we are in the middle of a biodiversity and climate crisis. "In the discussion paper the minister talks about three to four billion dollars of income coming in through tourism on public conservation land and yet we're massively underfunding it. "The way to fund it is to actually do that properly not by flogging off the land to the highest bidder." Giving ministerial decision making on things like area plans and amenity zones, it risked seeing large scale rezoning of conservation land to be more permissive, he said. "If we don't have those checks and balances in place with an independent expert group then we could see things like helicopter landings in remote areas of the Darran Mountains in Fiordland." Choices need to be made but the key word was conservation which meant looking after biodiversity, he said. "Absolutely we need to invest in that, but you don't invest in it by flogging it off." It is possible to allow changes for commercial activity, but it must be done in the right place and in the right way, he said. The Environmental Defence Society policy director Raewyn Peart said the conservation system was no longer fit for purpose and the government's proposal was a welcome first step towards modernising it. But the society had concerns, she said. "The proposal to make it easier to exchange conservation land is of some concern and needs further thought. Any exchanges need to be subject to robust considerations and should not include land with high conservation values," she said in a statement. "There is an urgent need for more money for conservation and EDS supports some access charging in principle. However, the details will need to be carefully worked through to ensure that New Zealanders are not excluded from accessing conservation areas." In a statement, Tourism Industry Aotearoa chief executive Rebecca Ingram said there was a lot to digest in the proposals. It would be getting the views of its members before making a submission, she said. "It's very important that consideration of access charging also recognises that the International Visitor Levy is now $100 and will generate tens of millions of dollars of funding for conservation and visitor management on the conservation estate." 62.document_title: New Auckland Convention Centre Tipped to Spark Tourism Recovery to Pre-Covid Levels
62.document_summary: The New Zealand International Convention Centre (NZICC) on Auckland's Hobson Street is projected to open in February 2026, marking a decade-long development. As the country's largest indoor conference space, it is expected to attract 33,000 international conference visitors annually, contributing $90 million in new economic spending. The centre has already secured 23 events through 2028, including the International Coral Reef Symposium with 23,000 delegates. Industry leaders emphasize the centre's role in off-peak tourism recovery and regional economic growth, with visitors bringing family members to explore other areas of New Zealand. Conservation Minister Tama Potaka has defended proposals which would give him sole decision making powers over the conservation estate. Plans are already underway to amend the Conservation Act to modernise land management and support a government priority to unleash economic growth on conservation land. Now, the minister is also proposing changes that would give him sole decision making powers over the conservation estate through a new National Conservation Policy Statement that critics say would strip away democratic process and prioritise commercial interests. The poli cy has only gone out for limited consultation at this stage, but would remove the decisionmaking authority of several statutory bodies. Federated Mountain Clubs, which is on the current decision making body the NZ Conservation Authority, has described the move as unprecedented and a fundamental shift in how conservation land is managed. https://www.r nz.co.nz/national/programmes/ninetonoon/audio/2019003948/who shoul d make decisions over conservation land Potaka said under the current model, decision making could take a lot of time and a pragmatic approach was needed. "When we stand back and look at people who are applying to do things in their states and are sometimes waiting five, six, seven years to get a decision, that's completely unacceptable," he said. "We're cutting bureaucracy, streamlining back office processes and maintaining environmental protection." He said many decisions also went to the minister already. "There are two systems operating right now the conservation policy and the national parks policy. One of them goes to the minister, the other one goes to the New Zealand Conservation Authority, and what we're saying is actually just have one system." 64.document_title: Bringing Kiwi Back to the Capital: Wellington's Successful Breeding Program
64.document_summary: The Capital Kiwi Project in Wellington has successfully reintroduced kiwi birds to the capital city after many years. Operating across 23,000 hectares, the project has released 139 of its permitted 250 birds, with 20 monitored via radio transmitters. This spring marks a significant milestone with five kiwi chicks hatched in the wild, with predictions of up to 14 by season's end. Kiwi ranger Jeff Hall and trainee dog Ash track and monitor the chicks' development. The project focuses on pest control, particularly managing stoats to under 5% to protect vulnerable chicks. Once kiwi reach 1.2kg within 6-8 months, they can defend themselves against predators. The initiative represents a major conservation success for New Zealand's national bird.

chunkHighlights.text: In the 1880s, there was a risk that ownership of the central North Island volcanoes would be disputed in the Māori Land Court. Tūwharetoa chief

Horonuku Te Heuheu said, ‘If our mountains of Tongariro are included in the blocks passed through the Court in the ordinary way, what will become of them? They will be cut up and perhaps sold, a piece going to one pakeha and a piece to another. They will become of no account, for the tapu will be gone. Tongariro is my ancestor, my tupuna; it is my head; my mana centres around Tongariro.’
The first national park – Tongariro

In 1887, following suggestions from some prominent Pākehā , the paramount chief of the Ngāti Tūwharetoa tribe, Horonuku Te Heuheu, made an agreement wirh the Crown that the central North Island volcanoes would become a national park. Different tribes were disputing ownership of the peaks of Ruapehu, Ngāuruhoe and Tongariro, and there was a danger that they would be divided and sold.

Horonuku’s action ensured that Tūwharetoa’s ancestral mountains would remain untouched, even if they were no longer directly controlled by the tribe. The government bought more Māori land to supplement the mountaintops, and Tongariro National Park was established by an 1894 act.
